items.prompt: A 24-year-old swimmer has 2 days of severe otalgia and marked pain with tragal manipulation. Otoscopy shows diffuse external auditory canal edema and debris; the canal is nearly occluded, and the tympanic membrane is difficult to visualize. He is afebrile, has no diabetes or immune suppression, and has no cellulitis beyond the canal. Which is the best initial management?
choices: Topical non-ototoxic antimicrobial therapy with analgesia; place an ear wick if edema prevents reliable drop delivery
Routine oral antipseudomonal antibiotics because Pseudomonas is a common pathogen
Urgent CT of the temporal bone and prolonged systemic antipseudomonal therapy
Empiric systemic antifungal therapy without canal debridement

items.prompt: A 22-year-old swimmer has 3 days of severe otalgia, pain with tragal pressure, and a swollen, debris-filled canal; the drum cannot be seen. He is not diabetic and has no cranial neuropathy. Why are topical drops preferred over oral antibiotics?
choices: They reach far higher drug levels in canal skin
Oral agents do not cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa
They prevent progression to skull-base osteomyelitis
Systemic therapy is unsafe when the drum is not seen

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Acquired cholesteatoma is keratinizing squamous epithelium within the middle ear/mastoid that accumulates keratin and causes progressive inflammation and bony erosion. Recognize pars-flaccida/attic or pars-tensa retraction pockets with keratin, chronic foul otorrhea, conductive hearing loss, granulation, or visible white debris. Primary acquired cholesteatoma develops behind an intact tympanic membrane, usually from a retraction pocket. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Definitive management is usually surgical because cholesteatoma is locally destructive and cannot be cured by topical therapy alone. Treat active infection/otorrhea enough to make surgery safer, but do not confuse temporary drying of the ear with eradication of disease. For congenital cholesteatoma, surgery is also the definitive treatment; the approach is tailored to extent. Small localized middle-ear lesions may be removed transcanally/endoscopically, whereas posterior, ossicular, or mastoid extension requires a broader tympanotomy/tympanomastoid approach. The goals are complete epithelial removal, a safe dry maintainable ear, preservation of the facial nerve/labyrinth, and hearing rehabilitation when it can be done without compromising disease control.

items.prompt: A 34-year-old has years of painless, foul otorrhea that returns after every course of drops. A pars flaccida retraction pocket is filled with white keratin. What mechanism makes this lesion progressively erode bone?
choices: Granulation tissue maturing into fibrous scar

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Treat a sudden unilateral sensorineural change as time-sensitive even when the patient describes fullness or a blocked ear. First distinguish SNHL from conductive loss with otoscopy, bedside tuning forks, and prompt audiometry. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Counsel that many cases remain idiopathic and that spontaneous recovery can occur, but treatment is time sensitive. Corticosteroids may be offered as initial therapy within 2 weeks of onset. Hyperbaric oxygen with steroids may be offered within 2 weeks initially or within 1 month as salvage in selected patients. Offer intratympanic steroid salvage for incomplete recovery approximately 2–6 weeks after onset. Do not routinely prescribe antivirals, thrombolytics, vasodilators, or vasoactive drugs. Treat an identified secondary cause specifically when one is found, and address residual hearing loss/tinnitus with rehabilitation.

items.prompt: A 48-year-old wakes with right-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. Otoscopy is normal, Weber lateralizes left, and Rinne is positive bilaterally. Which anatomic fact best explains the cochlea's vulnerability under the vascular theory?
choices: It is supplied by both carotid systems
Its hair cells depend on endolymph capillaries
Its labyrinthine artery is an end artery
Its spiral ganglion lies outside the otic capsule

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Progressive conductive or mixed hearing loss with normal otoscopy, absent acoustic reflexes and a characteristic audiogram suggests stapes fixation; a Carhart notch supports but does not prove otosclerosis. Stapes fixation causes conductive mechanics with normal TM; cochlear involvement can add SN loss. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Observation, hearing aids and stapes surgery are all reasonable depending on functional burden, cochlear reserve and patient goals. Counsel that surgery targets the conductive component and does not stop age-related/cochlear hearing decline. Observation, hearing aid or stapedotomy based on burden, anatomy and preference.

items.prompt: A 32-year-old woman has progressive left hearing loss that worsened during pregnancy. The drum is normal, there is a 30 dB air-bone gap with a bone-conduction dip at 2000 Hz, and acoustic reflexes are absent. What explains the 2000 Hz dip?
choices: Cochlear hair-cell loss at the 2 kHz place
A mechanical bone-conduction artifact of fixation

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Asymmetric SNHL, unilateral tinnitus or disproportionate word-recognition loss should prompt retrocochlear thinking; larger tumors may cause imbalance, facial/trigeminal symptoms or brainstem/cerebellar effects. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Observation, stereotactic radiation and microsurgery are all valid in selected patients. Decide from age/comorbidity, size/growth, symptoms, hearing, brainstem effect and patient preference rather than tumor diameter alone.

items.prompt: A 55-year-old has slowly progressive left hearing loss and tinnitus. Thresholds are mildly asymmetric, but left word recognition is only 40 percent. He has no vertigo. Why is vertigo uncommon despite a tumor of the vestibular nerve?
choices: Central compensation keeps pace with slow vestibular loss
The tumor usually arises from the cochlear nerve instead
Schwann-cell tumors secrete factors that stabilize firing
The dense otic capsule shields the vestibular nerve

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the otolaryngology service. During a cortical mastoidectomy, the resident becomes disoriented after opening the antrum and asks which boundaries should be re-established before further drilling. How do you organize temporal-bone anatomy spatially, which landmarks protect the facial nerve/labyrinth/dura/sigmoid, and what findings should make you stop and reassess?
items.answer_text: Re-establish known boundaries rather than drilling toward a memorized depth. Think from the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane into the epitympanum/antrum and mastoid while continuously identifying the tegmen superiorly, sigmoid sinus posteriorly, posterior canal wall and facial recess region anteriorly, and labyrinthine structures medially. The lateral semicircular canal is a key antral landmark; the facial nerve's tympanic and mastoid segments, second genu, digastric ridge and short process of the incus help orient deeper work. CT should be reviewed preoperatively for tegmen height, sigmoid position, mastoid aeration, labyrinth, facial-nerve anomalies and carotid/jugular variants. If anatomy is no longer trustworthy, stop drilling, irrigate, improve exposure and re-identify multiple fixed landmarks before proceeding. Unexpected facial stimulation/weakness, blue-lined labyrinth, CSF leak, brisk venous bleeding or suspected carotid injury requires complication-specific rescue rather than blind packing or continued drilling. The safe mastoidectomy is a boundary-based three-dimensional operation.

items.prompt: During a canal-wall-up mastoidectomy the resident has identified the lateral semicircular canal. Which structure lies just inferior to it and is most at risk while opening the facial recess?

An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. You are considering Audiogram Interpretation. First decide reliability, then air vs bone thresholds, conductive vs SN vs mixed pattern, symmetry, configuration, speech reception/word recognition and whether results fit the exam. When is Audiogram Interpretation the right test or evaluation, what information does it provide, and what limitation or pitfall should you remember when interpreting it?
items.answer_text: Pair pure tones with speech testing and tympanometry; asymmetric SN loss or unexpectedly poor speech performance can trigger retrocochlear evaluation.

items.prompt: A 40-year-old has right air-conduction thresholds of 50 dB HL with bone conduction of 5 dB HL; the left ear is normal. The right tympanogram is flat with normal canal volume. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Right sensorineural loss with unreliable bone scores
Right mixed loss with cochlear involvement
Right conductive loss from middle-ear fluid
Normal hearing with a collapsing ear canal

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. You are considering Tympanometry / Acoustic Reflexes. Type A tympanogram reflects near-normal middle-ear pressure/compliance; type B is flat and requires ear-canal volume interpretation; type C indicates negative middle-ear pressure. Acoustic reflex presence/absence adds information about the conductive pathway, cochlea, CN VIII, brainstem and CN VII. When is Tympanometry / Acoustic Reflexes the right test or evaluation, what information does it provide, and what limitation or pitfall should you remember when interpreting it?
items.answer_text: Interpret tympanometry with otoscopy and audiogram. For a type B tracing, normal canal volume suggests middle-ear effusion while large volume suggests a patent tube/perforation; small volume suggests probe obstruction or canal occlusion.

items.prompt: A child has a flat (type B) tympanogram in the right ear. Measured canal volume is 2.5 mL, versus 0.8 mL on the left. What does this combination indicate?
choices: An open perforation or patent tube

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. You are considering Eustachian Tube Dysfunction. OBSTRUCTIVE/DILATORY this condition as failure of middle-ear pressure equalization, not as a synonym for any sensation of ear fullness. Typical symptoms are pressure/fullness, popping, muffled hearing, otalgia or difficulty clearing the ear; chronic disease may produce tympanic-membrane retraction or effusion. Baro-challenge ETD can be symptomatic only during descent/ascent, with a normal ear between exposures. When is Eustachian Tube Dysfunction the right test or evaluation, what information does it provide, and what limitation or pitfall should you remember when interpreting it?
items.answer_text: Pair symptoms with objective evidence whenever possible. Perform pneumatic otoscopy/otomicroscopy, tympanometry and audiometry; chronic dilatory ETD is supported by tympanic-membrane retraction and/or negative middle-ear pressure, while effusion may create a flat tympanogram. Nasal endoscopy assesses the ET orifice and excludes inflammatory, scar-related or mass lesions. ETDQ-7 can quantify symptom burden but is not sufficiently specific to diagnose OETD by itself. A normal office tympanogram does not exclude baro-challenge ETD when the history is classic. Routine CT is not required unless alternate pathology or specific procedural/anatomic concern is suspected.

items.prompt: A 58-year-old with no prior ear disease has a persistent unilateral middle-ear effusion for 2 months. Which evaluation is mandatory?

An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Characterize acute vs chronic, size/site, edge, infection, hearing loss and ossicular/inner-ear clues. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Keep ear dry, treat infection when present, observe many acute perforations; tympanoplasty for persistent symptomatic/performance-limiting perforation when appropriate.

items.prompt: A 25-year-old has a small central perforation 2 weeks after a slap injury, with a 15 dB conductive loss and no vertigo. Which feature most predicts healing without surgery?
choices: Extension of the defect to the annulus
A small defect with healthy, intact edges
Vertigo with sensorineural loss after injury

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Large conductive air-bone gap after trauma, chronic ear disease or surgery with relatively normal TM/pressure suggests this condition; hypercompliant tympanometry can support but does not prove it. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Observe or amplify if functional burden is acceptable; reconstruct when hearing benefit is expected and the middle ear is safe/aerated enough for durable mechanics.

items.prompt: After a head injury, a patient has a 55 dB conductive loss in an ear with a normal-appearing drum. Tympanometry shows an unusually tall peak. What is the most likely cause?

An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Sound- or pressure-induced vertigo/oscillopsia, autophony, internal body-sound amplification and an apparent low-frequency conductive gap with intact middle ear suggest a third-window syndrome. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Observe mild symptoms and counsel trigger avoidance; consider surgical plugging/resurfacing for disabling, physiologically confirmed syndrome after excluding mimics such as patulous ET and ossicular disease.

items.prompt: A 45-year-old hears her own footsteps and eye movements, and loud sounds make the room tilt. Audiometry shows a low-frequency air-bone gap with bone conduction better than 0 dB, and acoustic reflexes are present. What is the mechanism?
choices: Stapes fixation at the oval window
A third window that shunts acoustic energy

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Episodic spontaneous vertigo with fluctuating unilateral sensorineural hearing symptoms, tinnitus and aural pressure suggests this condition; duration and audiometric documentation matter. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Educate about episodic disease, hearing rehabilitation and trigger/lifestyle measures; use vestibular suppressants only for acute attacks. Escalate from medical prevention to intratympanic therapy and, in disabling refractory disease, ablative options based on hearing status and goals.

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Recurrent vertigo, motion sensitivity or visually induced dizziness with migraine history/features can represent this condition even when headache is absent during some attacks. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Use migraine education, sleep/exercise/trigger management and preventive or acute migraine therapy tailored to attack frequency and comorbidity. Vestibular rehabilitation can help persistent motion/visual sensitivity.

items.prompt: A 36-year-old with lifelong migraine has recurrent attacks of vertigo lasting 2-6 hours, with photophobia during most attacks. Serial audiograms are normal. Which feature best separates this from Ménière disease?

An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Acute prolonged spontaneous vertigo lasting days with nausea, gait imbalance and no new hearing loss or focal neurologic deficit suggests this condition, but posterior-circulation stroke is the dangerous mimic. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Short-course vestibular suppressants/antiemetics are for the severe initial period only; begin early mobilization and vestibular rehabilitation. Prolonged suppressants delay central compensation.

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Brief vertigo triggered by position change with reproducible canal-specific positional nystagmus is a mechanical otolith disorder. Persistent spontaneous vertigo or atypical neurologic nystagmus should trigger a different differential. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Use the canal-appropriate repositioning maneuver and avoid chronic vestibular suppressants. Reassess persistent symptoms for wrong-canal localization, recurrence, cupulolithiasis or a central mimic.

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. First distinguish upper from lower motor-neuron weakness, complete from incomplete paralysis, immediate from delayed onset, and flaccid paralysis from synkinesis. Ear vesicles, trauma, tumor signs, recurrent episodes or progressive weakness are not routine Bell palsy. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Eye protection is immediate. Treat idiopathic acute palsy promptly with corticosteroids; manage Ramsay Hunt, infection, trauma or neoplasm according to cause. Persistent weakness evolves into rehabilitation, synkinesis treatment and reanimation planning.

items.prompt: A 30-year-old develops right facial weakness over 24 hours and cannot raise the right brow, close the right eye, or smile on the right. Why does forehead involvement indicate a peripheral lesion?
choices: The frontal branch leaves the skull separately
Upper-face neurons get bilateral cortical input
Trigeminal fibers supply the forehead centrally
Central lesions affect only eye closure

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. After head trauma, hemotympanum, otorrhea, hearing loss, vertigo or facial weakness should prompt temporal-bone injury assessment. Modern management is driven by functional complications rather than memorizing longitudinal versus transverse labels alone. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Most fractures are observed with treatment of specific complications. Persistent conductive loss suggests ossicular injury; CSF leak, complete facial paralysis or vascular injury require dedicated pathways.

items.prompt: A motorcyclist with an occipital blow has profound right sensorineural loss, spontaneous nystagmus, and immediate complete right facial paralysis. Which fracture pattern best explains this?

An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Cochlear Implant Candidacy is being considered. This card owns REFERRAL AND SELECTION, not the mastoidectomy. Refer patients whose sensorineural hearing loss is not adequately managed by optimized hearing aids rather than waiting for 'profound deafness.' In adults, evaluate each ear independently; the American Cochlear Implant Alliance revised 60/60 benchmark (PTA >=60 dB HL and unaided monosyllabic word recognition <=60% in the ear being considered) is a referral screen, not an exclusion rule. When is Cochlear Implant Candidacy indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: The operative decision in this card is WHICH EAR / WHETHER TO IMPLANT, not how to perform the facial recess. Choose the ear by integrating aided performance, residual hearing, anatomic feasibility, duration of deprivation, vestibular considerations, prior surgery and the plan for bilateral/bimodal hearing. Address active middle-ear infection or unsafe chronic ear disease before or as part of a staged implant strategy. Patients with cochlear ossification, inner-ear malformation or cochlear-nerve abnormality need individualized counseling because anatomy may alter electrode choice, insertion depth, CSF-leak risk and expected performance. Once the patient is selected and the side chosen, transition to the separate COCHLEAR IMPLANT SURGERY framework.

items.prompt: A 2-year-old became profoundly deaf after pneumococcal meningitis 3 weeks ago. Why are urgent imaging and early implantation planned?
choices: The cochlear nerve degenerates within days
Implants are approved only before age 3
New bone may fill the scala tympani

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Cochlear Implant Surgery is being considered. This card owns the OPERATION. Standard implantation places the receiver-stimulator securely and introduces an electrode array into the scala tympani through a round-window, extended-round-window or selected cochleostomy approach. The classic route is cortical mastoidectomy plus posterior tympanotomy/facial recess between the facial nerve and chorda tympani. When is Cochlear Implant Surgery indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Boards sequence: expose a safe receiver-stimulator bed/pocket -> cortical mastoidectomy -> identify incus/facial nerve/chorda -> open the facial recess -> visualize the round window -> create the planned cochlear opening -> insert the electrode atraumatically to the intended depth -> secure lead/device -> confirm impedance/neural responses -> close without pressure over the implant. Do not force an array against resistance: stop and reassess for ossification, false passage, fold-over or altered anatomy. In a gusher, obtain electrode placement and seal the cochleostomy/round-window region with appropriate soft tissue rather than abandoning implantation reflexively.

items.prompt: During implantation through the facial recess in a patient with residual low-frequency hearing, why is a slow, atraumatic round-window insertion preferred?
choices: It eliminates any risk to the facial nerve
A cochleostomy always enters scala vestibuli
The round window regrows to seal the array

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Classify this condition as pulsatile versus nonpulsatile, unilateral versus bilateral and bothersome versus incidental. Unilateral pulsatile this condition, objective bruit, asymmetric hearing loss or focal neurologic findings deserve focused evaluation. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat remediable ear/hearing disease, provide hearing aids when indicated, refer for cochlear implant evaluation when hearing loss qualifies, and use education/sound strategies/cognitive-behavioral therapy for bothersome chronic tinnitus. Do not routinely use medications, supplements, or rTMS (2026 AAO-HNSF update); bimodal neuromodulation is an emerging option. Schedule follow-up to track bother and treatment response.

items.prompt: A 62-year-old has bilateral high-pitched tinnitus that matches a bilateral 4-8 kHz sensorineural loss. Why does the tinnitus pitch match the hearing-loss region?
choices: Damaged hair cells emit audible tones
Central gain rises in deafferented channels
The stapedius muscle is in tonic spasm
Turbulent cochlear blood flow is heard

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Match rehabilitation to conductive, sensorineural or mixed deficit, ear anatomy and speech needs; conventional air-conduction aids require usable ear-canal/middle-ear conditions. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Counsel on realistic speech/hearing goals and choose technology from anatomy plus functional deficit.

items.prompt: A patient has single-sided deafness after vestibular schwannoma surgery. A bone-conduction device improves hearing of speakers on his deaf side. What can it not restore?
choices: Hearing for sounds on the deaf side

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Vestibular testing should answer a localization/functional question rather than be ordered as a fixed panel for every dizzy patient. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Use results to guide rehabilitation, document unilateral/bilateral loss, support third-window/otolith diagnoses or decide whether destructive vestibular treatment is safe.

items.prompt: A patient with suspected Ménière disease has a 45 percent caloric weakness on the affected side but a normal video head impulse test. What explains the dissociation?
choices: The caloric water temperature was wrong
Head impulses assess the otolith organs
The lesion must be in the brainstem
The tests sample different frequency ranges

items.prompt: An adult receiving a potentially ototoxic medication reports new bilateral tinnitus and difficulty understanding speech in noise. Another worker has chronic occupational noise exposure. How should you distinguish and monitor ototoxic injury from noise-induced loss, and what findings require a change in exposure or treatment rather than routine reassurance?
items.answer_text: Establish a detailed medication and acoustic-exposure timeline and compare current audiometry with a reliable baseline when available. Ototoxic injury often begins in the high frequencies and may progress with cumulative exposure; monitoring programs may use extended high-frequency audiometry and/or otoacoustic emissions when appropriate. Noise injury classically produces a high-frequency sensorineural pattern, but the individual audiogram, exposure history, asymmetry, and competing causes must be considered rather than relying on a single textbook notch. New threshold shift, worsening tinnitus with objective change, vestibular symptoms, or functional decline during ototoxic therapy should prompt coordination with the treating team to reduce dose, alter schedule, substitute therapy when medically feasible, and strengthen hearing-conservation/rehabilitation measures. Marked asymmetry, unilateral neurologic signs, or a pattern inconsistent with the exposure should trigger evaluation for another cause.

items.prompt: A patient receiving cisplatin develops bilateral tinnitus. Why do the first audiometric changes usually appear at the highest frequencies?
choices: Basal outer hair cells are injured first
Apical inner hair cells encode high pitch
Cisplatin targets the auditory nerve first
High tones are tested at louder levels

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Rapidly progressive or fluctuating often bilateral SNHL raises an immune-mediated hypothesis but has no single diagnostic biomarker. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Specialist-directed corticosteroid/immunologic treatment may be considered while preserving hearing rehabilitation options.

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Clear middle-ear fluid, recurrent meningitis or persistent unilateral effusion can reflect tegmen defect/encephalocele. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Repair symptomatic/persistent leaks using transmastoid, middle-fossa or combined strategy based on site/size/anatomy.

items.prompt: An obese 52-year-old woman with a persistent unilateral effusion has continuous clear watery drainage after tube placement. What is the most likely underlying mechanism?
choices: Perilymph leak at the round window
Allergic reaction to the tube material

items.prompt: A 72-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has persistent otorrhea and deep nocturnal otalgia despite topical therapy. Examination shows granulation tissue in the external auditory canal, and the pain is disproportionate to the visible inflammation. What is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Evaluate urgently for necrotizing external otitis/skull-base osteomyelitis with microbiology and cross-sectional imaging, then institute culture-directed systemic therapy
Reassure him that severe pain is expected in uncomplicated swimmer's ear and continue the same drops alone
Treat empirically as isolated otomycosis with topical antifungal therapy only
Schedule elective canalplasty for chronic canal stenosis before further diagnostic evaluation

items.prompt: A 74-year-old diabetic has 6 weeks of severe night-time otalgia, granulation at the floor of the bony-cartilaginous junction, and new facial weakness. Why is the facial nerve often the first cranial nerve involved?
choices: It runs within the canal skin itself
Pseudomonas toxin selectively hits motor neurons
Spread reaches the stylomastoid foramen first

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Localize expansile petrous-apex disease by CT density/bone behavior and MRI signal; cholesterol granuloma, cholesteatoma and neoplasm behave differently. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Observe stable incidental lesions or drain/resect according to diagnosis, symptoms, growth and access corridor.

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Progressive bilateral hearing difficulty—often speech-in-noise first—in an older adult should trigger formal hearing evaluation rather than being dismissed as normal aging. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Counsel on communication strategies and hearing-assistive technology; offer or refer for hearing aids when appropriate. Reassess benefit and escalate to cochlear-implant evaluation when appropriately fitted amplification does not provide adequate speech understanding.

items.prompt: A 78-year-old has a flat, moderate bilateral sensorineural loss with surprisingly good word recognition. Which presbycusis type best fits?

An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Postauricular erythema/swelling, auricular protrusion, persistent fever/otalgia or toxic appearance after AOM suggests mastoid complication; deep facial pain or cranial neuropathy raises concern for petrous apical extension. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Admit complicated disease, start appropriate IV antibiotics, obtain source control and monitor for intracranial/venous complications. Myringotomy/tube and mastoid surgery depend on abscess, coalescence, complications and response.

items.prompt: A 3-year-old with AOM develops postauricular swelling that pushes the pinna forward and outward. CT shows coalescence and a subperiosteal collection. What produced the collection?
choices: Pus eroding through the mastoid cortex

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Chronic nonspinning dizziness/unsteadiness present most days for months and worsened by upright posture, motion, complex visual environments or busy stores/screens suggests PPPD, often after a vestibular, migraine, anxiety or medical trigger. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Education, graded vestibular rehabilitation, treatment of comorbid migraine/anxiety and selected serotonergic medication are commonly combined. Avoid chronic vestibular suppressants, which can reinforce compensation failure.

items.prompt: A 44-year-old had vestibular neuritis 6 months ago. Testing is now compensated, but she has daily unsteadiness worse in supermarkets and when scrolling her phone. What best explains her symptoms?

An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. You are considering Patulous Eustachian Tube Dysfunction. this condition by AUTOPHONY—especially hearing one's own breathing and voice abnormally loudly—often with aural fullness. Symptoms commonly fluctuate, may worsen with exercise or dehydration, and may improve when supine or during an upper-respiratory infection as mucosal congestion narrows the lumen. Weight loss and habitual sniffing are useful clues but are not required. When is Patulous Eustachian Tube Dysfunction the right test or evaluation, what information does it provide, and what limitation or pitfall should you remember when interpreting it?
items.answer_text: Try to reproduce and objectively confirm the open-tube physiology while the patient is symptomatic. Examine the tympanic membrane for breathing-synchronous excursion during nasal respiration; long time-base tympanometry can demonstrate respiratory pressure fluctuations, while sonotubometry or tubo-tympano-aerodynamic testing can support abnormal patency where available. Note whether symptoms improve with supine positioning or temporary obstruction of the pharyngeal ET orifice. The Japan Otological Society framework requires characteristic symptoms plus symptom improvement with tubal obstruction maneuvers and/or objective evidence of patency for definite disease. If autophony is dominated by internal body sounds or vestibular sound/pressure phenomena, evaluate for a third-window lesion rather than forcing a PET diagnosis.

items.prompt: A 25-year-old who lost 20 kg hears her own breathing and an echo of her voice; symptoms vanish when she lies down. What explains relief when supine?
choices: Peritubal venous congestion closes the tube

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Sudden or fluctuating hearing loss, vertigo or disequilibrium after barotrauma, penetrating trauma, surgery or major pressure event can suggest a perilymph leak, but symptoms are nonspecific. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Activity/pressure precautions and observation are reasonable in selected stable cases; urgent surgical exploration is considered for compelling traumatic leaks, progressive SNHL or severe persistent symptoms.

items.prompt: A scuba diver develops sudden hearing loss and vertigo after a difficult descent with forceful Valsalva. What mechanism describes an implosive window rupture?
choices: Middle-ear pressure surge pushing the window inward
CSF pressure surge via the cochlear aqueduct
Fracture of an otosclerotic stapes footplate

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Cochlear Implant Failure / Revision is being considered. After a previously implanted cochlear implant system declines in performance, do not collapse every decline into 'device failure.' HARD failure means demonstrable loss of device function/integrity; SOFT failure is a clinical syndrome of declining performance, intermittent function, aversive auditory or nonauditory symptoms despite no definitive integrity-test abnormality and is therefore a diagnosis of exclusion. When is Cochlear Implant Failure / Revision indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Plan revision from the FAILURE MECHANISM. Review the original operative report, device model/electrode, imaging and recipient anatomy. Re-enter with facial-nerve and wound-scar risk in mind; preserve a usable cochlear lumen during explantation and avoid unnecessary traction on an intracochlear array. Replace or reposition the device/electrode when indicated and choose an alternate receiver bed or surgical strategy if migration, infection or soft-tissue compromise caused the failure. Fibrosis/neo-ossification can prevent full reinsertion, so have an electrode/approach contingency. After reimplantation confirm objective function and return the patient to audiologic activation/remapping and performance follow-up.

items.prompt: A 20-year-old implant user has gradually declining performance and painful sensations. Integrity testing is normal and reprogramming does not help. What is the working diagnosis?

An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Congenital SNHL with characteristic CT/MRI abnormalities may reflect cochlear, vestibular, semicircular-canal, IAC or cochlear-nerve malformation; syndromic clues and CSF-gusher risk matter. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Amplification, CI or auditory brainstem implantation depends on residual hearing, cochlear anatomy and nerve presence. Early language access remains the functional priority.

items.prompt: A child with progressive hearing loss has stepwise drops after minor head bumps. CT shows an enlarged vestibular aqueduct. Why does minor trauma worsen hearing?
choices: A missing modiolus lets the cochlea fracture
Perilymph drains into the middle ear
Pressure surges reach the inner ear via the aqueduct

items.prompt: In the clinical or operative context of Auditory Neuroanatomy / Cochlear Physiology, Sound becomes neural code through middle-ear transmission, cochlear traveling-wave mechanics, hair-cell transduction and tonotopic auditory pathways. For Auditory Neuroanatomy / Cochlear Physiology, what structures, relationships, or physiologic mechanisms must you be able to map, and why do they matter clinically?
items.answer_text: Localize from outer/middle ear to cochlea, spiral ganglion/CN VIII, cochlear nuclei, superior olivary complex, lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate and auditory cortex.

items.prompt: A drug abolishes outer hair cell electromotility but spares inner hair cells. Which audiologic change is expected?
choices: Normal thresholds with an absent ABR

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. You are considering Audiologic Electrophysiology / ABR-OAE-ECoG. OAEs test outer-hair-cell/cochlear function; ABR tests synchronized neural transmission through the auditory nerve/brainstem; ECoG interrogates cochlear/auditory-nerve potentials near the cochlea. When is Audiologic Electrophysiology / ABR-OAE-ECoG the right test or evaluation, what information does it provide, and what limitation or pitfall should you remember when interpreting it?
items.answer_text: Interpret thresholds, waveform presence/latency/interaural asymmetry and technical factors in context. Present OAEs with absent/abnormal ABR suggests auditory-neural dyssynchrony when the clinical setting fits.

items.prompt: A NICU graduate has present otoacoustic emissions but an absent ABR with a visible cochlear microphonic. What is the diagnosis?

An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Auditory deprivation changes central processing; duration and developmental timing influence how effectively restored peripheral input can be used. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Provide timely hearing access in children and avoid unnecessary prolonged deprivation in implant candidates; pair devices with auditory/language rehabilitation.

items.prompt: Why do children born deaf who are implanted before about age 3.5 develop more typical spoken language than those implanted after age 7?
choices: Older children have more cochlear ossification
Auditory cortex has a sensitive period
Implant arrays do not fit older cochleae
Spiral ganglion cells vanish by age 7

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Systemic autoimmune, infectious, metabolic, hematologic and skeletal disease can present with hearing loss, vestibular symptoms, middle-ear disease or temporal-bone findings. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat the systemic driver with the relevant team plus symptom-specific hearing/vestibular rehabilitation; urgent sudden or rapidly progressive deficits keep their time-sensitive pathways.

items.prompt: A 50-year-old has bilateral serous otitis media unresponsive to tubes, a saddle nose, and hematuria. Which test is most likely to confirm the unifying diagnosis?

An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Hyperacusis is abnormal intolerance of ordinary sound and differs from loudness recruitment, misophonia and phonophobia despite overlap. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Education, gradual sound desensitization and treatment of comorbid tinnitus/migraine/anxiety mechanisms are more useful than excessive sound avoidance in many patients.

items.prompt: A 29-year-old developed sensitivity to everyday sounds after a concert and now wears earplugs whenever she leaves home. Her symptoms are steadily worsening. Why does constant ear protection make hyperacusis worse?
choices: It promotes canal infection and pain
It damages outer hair cells over time
It further raises central auditory gain

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Acute vestibular syndrome with hearing loss suggests labyrinthine involvement rather than isolated vestibular neuritis; bacterial extension from otitis/mastoid disease can be destructive. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat the underlying infection/inflammation urgently when bacterial disease is possible, manage vertigo briefly when needed and begin hearing/vestibular rehabilitation as the acute phase resolves.

items.prompt: A 40-year-old with untreated cholesteatoma develops acute vertigo and complete hearing loss in that ear, with fever. CT shows a lateral semicircular canal fistula. What distinguishes suppurative from serous labyrinthitis?
choices: Bacterial invasion causing permanent sensory loss
Viral injury limited to the vestibular nerve

items.prompt: An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus, skew, impaired smooth pursuit/saccades, severe truncal ataxia or neurologic deficits push dizziness toward a central process. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat the underlying neurologic disease and use vestibular rehabilitation selectively; chronic central compensation may still improve with therapy.

items.prompt: A 68-year-old has acute continuous vertigo and nystagmus. The head impulse test is normal, nystagmus changes direction with gaze, and there is vertical skew. What is the most likely diagnosis?

An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. Persistent imbalance after unilateral or bilateral vestibular loss often reflects incomplete compensation rather than persistent dangerous disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Use adaptation, habituation, substitution and balance/gait training tailored to the deficit; prolonged vestibular suppressants can impede compensation in many chronic peripheral cases.

items.prompt: Five days after vestibular neuritis, a 50-year-old is improving but still takes meclizine three times daily and avoids moving her head. Why should the suppressant be tapered and head movement encouraged?
choices: Meclizine is toxic to vestibular hair cells

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the otolaryngology service. During a hearing-preservation vestibular schwannoma case, facial EMG has been robust but the auditory brainstem response deteriorates during internal-auditory-canal work; shortly afterward the facial response also becomes less reliable. As the senior resident, explain how neurotologic cranial-nerve monitoring is selected and baselined, what facial free-running/triggered EMG and auditory ABR/BAEP or near-field cochlear responses can and cannot tell you, how anesthesia and technical factors confound each modality, how you troubleshoot a sudden change before declaring neural injury, and when persistent deterioration should change the surgical maneuver or objective?
items.answer_text:
Foundation — neurotologic intraoperative cranial-nerve monitoring is a set of modality-specific adjuncts to anatomy and microsurgical technique, not a single alarm system. The nerve at risk and the function being preserved determine what is monitored. Facial motor function is commonly followed with free-running EMG plus direct electrical stimulation and evoked compound muscle responses. Hearing-preservation surgery may use far-field auditory brainstem response/brainstem auditory evoked potentials (ABR/BAEP), near-field cochlear nerve action potentials (CNAP), electrocochleographic techniques, or selected combinations. Lower cranial motor nerves can be monitored with appropriately placed muscle electrodes when the approach or lesion puts them at meaningful risk. The durable rule is that a waveform is useful only if you know what neural segment and end organ it samples, how quickly it updates, and what non-neural factors can change it.

BASELINE AND TEAM SETUP — before danger-zone dissection, establish that the selected modalities are technically reproducible. Confirm the intended nerves, recording muscles or auditory transducers, electrode integrity/impedance, stimulation hardware, laterality, and a baseline under the anesthetic conditions that will be used for critical dissection. Discuss neuromuscular blockade explicitly with anesthesia whenever motor EMG is needed. For auditory monitoring, confirm adequate stimulus delivery and a stable baseline before drilling/manipulation near the cochlea, labyrinth, internal auditory canal or cochlear nerve. A monitor that was never proven functional cannot later distinguish technical failure from injury.

FACIAL MOTOR MONITORING — free-running EMG is a warning channel. Brief spikes or bursts may reflect mechanical contact, whereas repetitive or sustained neurotonic activity during traction, drilling, cautery or tumor dissection should trigger immediate correlation with the surgical maneuver. Triggered stimulation helps identify or map the facial nerve and tests whether applied current evokes a distal muscle response. Neither modality proves complete anatomic continuity, guarantees normal postoperative function, or licenses blind dissection. A response depends on the stimulated site, current spread, distance/tissue between probe and nerve, electrode quality, muscle selection, anesthetic state and device characteristics.

ANESTHESIA AND MOTOR CONFOUNDERS — facial EMG records downstream muscle activity, so neuromuscular blockade can suppress or abolish a response even when the nerve is intact. Partial blockade can raise the stimulation current needed to obtain a response and alter amplitude. Therefore a rising threshold or falling amplitude is not automatically neural injury if the anesthetic state changed. Correlate with train-of-four or the anesthesia team's assessment, recent paralytic administration, temperature and relevant physiologic changes. Do not memorize a single mA threshold or amplitude-loss percentage as a universal cross-platform injury cutoff.

AUDITORY MONITORING — ABR/BAEP is a far-field averaged response with characteristic waves generated along the auditory pathway. In hearing-preservation vestibular schwannoma surgery, changes in wave morphology, amplitude and latency are interpreted as trends relative to a reproducible baseline. Because far-field responses require averaging, they are not instantaneous; surgical injury can occur faster than a slowly updating averaged waveform. Near-field CNAP/DNAP-type techniques can provide larger/faster responses in selected settings but require different electrodes/exposure and are not interchangeable with ABR. The current literature does not justify treating one absolute latency shift, amplitude percentage or waveform rule as a universal rescue threshold across every device, approach and baseline hearing level.

AUDITORY TECHNICAL DIFFERENTIAL — when ABR worsens, STOP the provoking maneuver first, then consider both biologic and technical causes. Verify the acoustic stimulus and ear insert/transducer, recording leads and impedance, masking/noise assumptions, electrical interference and whether drilling artifact or irrigation conditions are degrading the tracing. Check blood pressure, temperature and other systemic changes that can affect neural conduction. In otologic surgery, also think specifically about cochlear perfusion, labyrinthine trauma, excessive traction on CN VIII, thermal/mechanical injury during internal-auditory-canal drilling, and local fluid/blood effects. A deteriorating auditory signal is not automatically cochlear-nerve transection, but it is not something to ignore while continuing the same maneuver.

SUDDEN FACIAL SIGNAL LOSS — treat unexpected loss as a rescue problem before labeling it transection. First STOP traction, drilling, cautery or dissection. Keep the field stable and identify whether the change was temporally linked to a specific maneuver. Then troubleshoot the system: power/mute/settings, recording and reference electrodes, impedance, lead connections, stimulating probe/cable, current shunting through fluid, and whether the probe is contacting the intended tissue. Ask anesthesia immediately about neuromuscular blockade. Stimulate a known intact accessible segment or appropriate control point when safe. If nothing responds anywhere after a previously robust baseline, technical/anesthetic failure rises on the differential; if responses are preserved distally but fail across a newly manipulated segment, focal neural compromise becomes more concerning.

LOCALIZE, RESCUE, DECIDE — once technical and anesthetic causes have been addressed, inspect the operative danger zone. Release traction or compression, stop thermal/mechanical stress, irrigate when appropriate, and avoid blind cautery near a threatened nerve. In skull-base surgery, compare proximal/distal facial responses when anatomy safely permits. For hearing deterioration, stop the causative maneuver, reassess drilling/traction/irrigation and hemodynamic conditions, and allow the signal an opportunity to recover rather than repeatedly reproducing the insult. Monitoring has value only if its warning changes behavior.

If the nerve is visibly divided, the problem is no longer one of waveform interpretation: protect the ends and proceed to the appropriate immediate repair/reconstruction strategy when feasible. If anatomy appears intact but monitoring remains meaningfully degraded, the senior decision may be to alter the dissection plane, leave adherent tumor, accept subtotal/near-total resection, stage, or otherwise change the surgical objective when functional preservation outweighs additional tumor removal. The 2026 CNS vestibular-schwannoma guideline update supports intraoperative cranial-nerve monitoring in all vestibular schwannoma cases and emphasizes functional preservation; it also notes that no single facial or hearing monitoring strategy has emerged as universally superior and that the evidence base remains largely lower-level comparative evidence.

HEARING-VERSUS-FACIAL DISAGREEMENT — signals can disagree because they sample different nerves/functions and have different temporal resolution. A stable facial EMG does not reassure you about cochlear-nerve or cochlear injury. Conversely, an ABR change does not establish facial injury. When both deteriorate during the same maneuver, consider a common mechanical, vascular, thermal or technical event but still troubleshoot each channel independently. The mistake is collapsing all monitoring into one binary 'monitor is good/bad' interpretation.

LOWER CRANIAL NERVES — in selected jugular-foramen, lower-skull-base or CPA operations, motor EMG/stimulation of IX/X/XI/XII-related targets may be used when the nerve and end-organ recording strategy are appropriate. These modalities require procedure-specific setup and have their own anesthesia/technical constraints. The resident-level principle is to know why a nerve is being monitored, what muscle or physiologic output represents it, and what change would make the surgeon stop or alter the maneuver; do not extrapolate facial-nerve numeric thresholds to another cranial nerve.

NUMERIC PARAMETERS — record baseline and within-case trend rather than worshiping an isolated number. Facial monitoring commonly follows stimulation current/threshold and evoked amplitude; ABR follows waveform presence, morphology, amplitude and latency; near-field auditory techniques follow their own response characteristics. Published series use different devices, electrode sites, averaging schemes, muscles, stimulation techniques, tumor sizes and outcome definitions. Directional changes can be clinically useful, but a single universal stimulation threshold, amplitude-drop percentage, latency shift or alarm cutoff across neurotologic procedures is not supported. Manufacturer presets and device labeling are not universal physiologic laws.

EVIDENCE BOUNDARY — AAO-HNS guidance and its task-force consensus support strategic cranial-nerve monitoring as an adjunct to anatomy, with emphasis on setup, anesthesia, troubleshooting and documentation. Current CNS evidence-based guidance for vestibular schwannoma specifically recommends intraoperative cranial-nerve monitoring and recognizes combined strategies for facial and hearing preservation while acknowledging uncertainty over the optimal modality. A 2026 systematic review of auditory monitoring (PMID 42036522) separates diagnostic/predictive threshold performance from proof that an intervention triggered by the monitor improves hearing; those are not the same evidence question. Heterogeneous facial-monitoring parameter studies likewise do not create a universal predictive cutoff.

RETRACTION HYGIENE — a 2026 parotid facial-monitoring meta-analysis, PMID 41353726, was formally retracted July 28, 2026; the retraction notice is PMID 42520282. Its pooled benefit estimates must not be taught as affirmative evidence. This matters because a superficially impressive effect estimate can persist in notes after the underlying paper has been withdrawn. Current teaching should rely on non-retracted sources and explicitly label procedure-specific evidence strength.

FDA/SOCIETY BOUNDARY — intraoperative monitoring systems are regulated devices with manufacturer-specific indications, warnings, electrode configurations and settings. There is no single FDA indication or major society statement that converts one stimulation current, amplitude percentage or latency value into a universal alarm criterion for all neurotologic cranial nerves and operations. Society recommendations define appropriate use and evidence boundaries; anatomy, procedure, baseline function, modality and device instructions determine implementation.

Senior synthesis — use NERVE, BASELINE, CHANGE, STOP, SYSTEM, PHYSIOLOGY, LOCALIZE, RESCUE, DECIDE. NERVE: identify the function at risk and choose the matching modality. BASELINE: prove the channel is reproducible before danger-zone work. CHANGE: correlate a trend with the exact maneuver and modality. STOP: halt traction/drilling/cautery before troubleshooting. SYSTEM: check electrodes, transducers, leads, probe, impedance, noise and current shunting. PHYSIOLOGY: assess neuromuscular blockade for motor channels and systemic/hemodynamic/temperature factors for all channels. LOCALIZE: use known facial segments or modality-specific controls when safe. RESCUE: release mechanical/thermal stress and correct reversible causes. DECIDE: if meaningful deterioration persists, change the operative maneuver or objective rather than trusting the monitor to protect a function you continue to endanger.

items.prompt: At the end of a vestibular schwannoma resection, the facial nerve responds to 0.05 mA stimulation at the brainstem. What does this predict?

An adult is evaluated in otology clinic. A lateral skull-base mass is approached by epicenter, hearing status, cranial-nerve deficits, vascularity and growth—not by a single generic 'skull-base tumor' algorithm. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Observation, radiation and surgery depend on natural history, size/growth, symptoms, age, hearing and morbidity of the involved cranial nerves.

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. conventional this condition (AR) as an IgE-mediated nasal syndrome in which exposure to a clinically relevant allergen produces sneezing, nasal itching, watery rhinorrhea and/or congestion, often with ocular itching or tearing. The history should establish timing, seasonality or perennial exposure, trigger correlation, severity and quality-of-life impact rather than relying on pale turbinates alone. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Match therapy to the dominant symptom and disease burden. Intranasal corticosteroid is preferred monotherapy for persistent or quality-of-life-limiting AR; correct spray technique and adherence before declaring failure. Second-generation oral antihistamines are useful when itching and sneezing dominate, while an intranasal antihistamine is an effective topical option. For inadequate control, combined intranasal corticosteroid plus intranasal antihistamine has additive efficacy. Saline irrigation and targeted exposure reduction can be adjuncts when a relevant trigger is known. Do not use montelukast as routine first-line AR monotherapy, avoid depot systemic corticosteroid injections, and limit topical decongestants because of rebound congestion risk.

items.prompt: A 26-year-old with seasonal sneezing and nasal itch controls those symptoms with a second-generation antihistamine, but daily nasal congestion persists through the season. Which single therapy best treats both the early- and late-phase allergic response?

A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. CRS requires ≥12 weeks of compatible symptoms plus objective inflammation; phenotyping by polyps, eosinophilic/type-2 features, asthma/AERD, fungal disease and other modifiers is more useful than treating all CRS as one infection. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Saline and topical intranasal corticosteroid therapy are foundational. Add short systemic therapy, biologics or surgery according to phenotype, severity and prior response rather than requiring a rigid 'maximal medical therapy' checklist.

items.prompt: A 45-year-old with CRS with nasal polyps has asthma, blood eosinophils of 650/µL, and anosmia, and her polyps recurred within 18 months of complete endoscopic sinus surgery. Which biological feature best explains the early recurrence?

A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Adult-onset asthma, CRSwNP and respiratory reactions to COX-1 inhibitors form this condition. Severe recurrent polyposis and anosmia may precede a clearly recognized NSAID reaction history. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Use topical sinonasal therapy, guideline-based asthma care and appropriately selected biologic therapy. Aspirin desensitization followed by maintenance therapy is an option in selected patients; FESS is often coordinated to improve sinus access and disease control.

items.prompt: A 40-year-old with nasal polyps and asthma develops nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and wheezing 45 minutes after taking ibuprofen. She tolerates acetaminophen at usual doses. What is the core mechanism of this reaction?

A patient with unilateral frontal sinus disease is being considered for endoscopic frontal surgery. The coronal and sagittal CT show a narrow frontal drainage pathway with multiple frontal cells near the orbit and anterior skull base. How should you read this anatomy before operating, how do you choose surgical extent, and what findings require urgent escalation rather than routine elective treatment?
items.answer_text: Operate only for an appropriate disease burden after the diagnosis and medical strategy are clear; surgical extent should match the pathology and anatomy. Before entering the frontal recess, trace the drainage pathway in more than one CT plane and identify the agger nasi/frontal cells, frontal beak, lamina papyracea, anterior ethmoidal artery region and skull-base contour. The objective is a durable, mucosa-preserving drainage pathway, not indiscriminate superior dissection. Cell partitions are removed according to how they obstruct the true frontal outflow; distorted postoperative anatomy, osteitis, tumor or a very narrow pathway may justify a more extended approach. Stop and re-orient when landmarks are lost. Visual loss, an afferent pupillary defect, orbital hematoma, suspected invasive fungal disease, CSF leak/intracranial complication or uncontrolled hemorrhage changes the problem from routine frontal sinusitis to an urgent rescue pathway.

items.prompt: A patient with persistent frontal sinusitis is scheduled for revision endoscopic surgery. CT shows prior partial ethmoidectomy, residual frontal recess cells, a low skull base, and an anterior ethmoid artery close to the skull base. How should the CT drive the frontal recess dissection, and which findings should make you stop or change the planned extent rather than continue a routine frontal sinusotomy?
items.answer_text: Review thin-cut multiplanar CT systematically to reconstruct the true frontal drainage pathway, residual agger/frontal cells, frontal beak, orbit, skull-base contour, anterior ethmoid artery, and prior surgical defects. In revision surgery, preserve orientation by working from known landmarks and removing the specific partitions obstructing the pathway rather than blindly enlarging superiorly. The chosen frontal procedure should match disease, anatomy, and prior failure; more extensive drill-out is not automatically better. Orbital fat exposure, suspected CSF leak, loss of a reliable skull-base boundary, significant bleeding near the anterior ethmoid artery, or anatomy that no longer matches the preoperative map should stop routine progression and trigger direct complication assessment or a revised approach.

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. CSF Rhinorrhea is being considered. Suspect this condition when clear unilateral watery drainage is positional, salty/metallic, increases with straining, follows skull-base trauma/surgery, or occurs with recurrent meningitis. Spontaneous leaks are strongly associated with elevated intracranial pressure phenotypes, particularly obesity/IIH, and may coexist with empty sella or multiple skull-base defects. When is CSF Rhinorrhea indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text:
Endoscopic endonasal repair is first-line for most accessible anterior-skull-base defects. Choose exposure according to site, remove mucosa around the true defect, reduce/ablate nonfunctional herniated tissue when appropriate, and create a durable multilayer closure using free graft, fascia, cartilage/bone and/or vascularized flap according to defect size/flow and prior treatment. High-flow defects, large dural openings, irradiated fields and recurrent leaks increase the value of vascularized reconstruction. Lumbar drainage is selective rather than mandatory for every leak. Preserve olfaction and avoid unnecessary bilateral skull-base dissection when a unilateral site is well localized.

If CSF is encountered during ESS: stop powered instrumentation and avoid blind suction, cautery, or traction at the defect; maintain orientation; define the bony/dural margins; preserve viable mucosa and reconstructive options; and repair according to size, location, and flow. Small defects may be closed with appropriately supported free grafts, while larger/high-flow defects often require multilayer reconstruction and/or a vascularized flap such as a nasoseptal flap when anatomy and prior surgery permit. Do not enlarge an uncertain superior defect simply to 'see better' until intracranial and orbital boundaries are understood. Postoperatively, counsel on leak precautions, monitor for recurrent rhinorrhea, meningitis, and pneumocephalus, and coordinate management of elevated intracranial pressure in spontaneous disease.

items.prompt: In the clinical or operative context of Nasal Anatomy for Endoscopy, Use inferior turbinate/floor, middle turbinate, uncinate, bulla, basal lamella, sphenoethmoidal recess and choana as sequential orientation landmarks. For Nasal Anatomy for Endoscopy, what structures, relationships, or physiologic mechanisms must you be able to map, and why do they matter clinically?
items.answer_text: Use inferior turbinate/floor, middle turbinate, uncinate, bulla, basal lamella, sphenoethmoidal recess and choana as sequential orientation landmarks.

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Distinguish reversible mucosal congestion from fixed soft-tissue/bony enlargement and from nasal-valve/septal obstruction. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Optimize rhinitis therapy first; reduction is for persistent symptomatic hypertrophy and should preserve mucosal function.

items.prompt: A 34-year-old with chronic nasal obstruction from inferior turbinate hypertrophy that persists despite steroid sprays asks the surgeon to remove both turbinates completely. Why is mucosa-sparing submucosal reduction preferred?
choices: Turbinate mucosa senses and conditions airflow
The turbinate bone regrows after resection
The turbinate supports the nasal sidewall

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. A crooked septum matters only if it contributes meaningfully to the symptomatic airflow bottleneck. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Septoplasty when symptoms persist and septal anatomy is causal; combine with other functional treatment only when indicated.

items.prompt: A 28-year-old has a deviated septum causing nasal obstruction and undergoes septoplasty. During cartilage resection, why must at least about 1 cm of dorsal and caudal septal cartilage be preserved?
choices: It carries the septal blood supply
It supports the nasal dorsum and tip

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Discrete bacterial-pattern episodes with symptom-free intervals are different from chronic daily symptoms. this condition is generally defined as four or more distinct episodes of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in a year, each meeting criteria for acute disease with resolution of symptoms between episodes — the symptom-free interval is what separates this from chronic rhinosinusitis with exacerbations. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat individual bacterial episodes appropriately; prevention/surgery depends on documented pattern and anatomy rather than symptom count alone.

items.prompt: A 30-year-old has 5 episodes per year of acute bacterial sinusitis, with a clear CT between episodes. The CT shows a large Haller (infraorbital ethmoid) cell narrowing the maxillary infundibulum. Why does this anatomy matter?
choices: Haller cells erode the orbital floor
Ordinary viral swelling closes a narrow outflow
Haller cells block the nasolacrimal duct

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. CRSsNP is being considered. CHRONIC RHINOSINUSITIS WITHOUT NASAL POLYPS (this condition) as inflammatory sinonasal disease lasting at least 12 weeks with compatible symptoms AND objective evidence of inflammation, but without endoscopically visible nasal polyps. When is CRSsNP indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Offer ENDOSCOPIC SINUS SURGERY when appropriately selected CRSsNP remains symptomatic with objective disease despite reasonable disease-specific medical therapy, or when anatomy/secondary pathology creates a clear surgical indication. The operative objective is not simply to remove mucosa: open the diseased sinus pathways, restore ventilation/drainage, obtain access for postoperative topical therapy, preserve functional mucosa when possible and correct a focal driver such as obstructed odontogenic disease. Extent should match disease distribution and prior anatomy rather than applying the same operation to every CT. Postoperative saline, topical corticosteroid therapy and endoscopic debridement/follow-up remain part of the treatment—not evidence that surgery 'failed.'

items.prompt: A 50-year-old has 4 months of facial pressure, congestion, and discolored drainage despite saline. Endoscopy shows purulence in the middle meatus without polyps, and CT shows mucosal thickening with thickened bony septa. Which tissue pattern is typical of this phenotype?

A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. CRSwNP is being considered. CHRONIC RHINOSINUSITIS WITH NASAL POLYPS (this condition) as chronic inflammatory sinonasal disease with objective BILATERAL inflammatory polyposis in the usual phenotype. Patients often emphasize nasal obstruction and loss of smell more than pain, and recurrent polyps, asthma and NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD/N-ERD) should immediately suggest a strong type-2 inflammatory phenotype. When is CRSwNP indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: ESS in CRSwNP is both DISEASE CLEARANCE and DRUG-DELIVERY surgery: remove obstructing polyps, open involved sinuses widely enough for ventilation and topical access, preserve healthy mucosa and create a postoperative cavity that can be medically maintained. Counsel that surgery does not erase the inflammatory endotype and recurrence is common, especially with severe type-2 disease/AERD, so topical anti-inflammatory maintenance is mandatory. In severe recurrent disease, the decision is not 'surgery OR biologic' in the abstract: compare symptom burden, prior ESS quality and durability, systemic-steroid dependence, asthma/AERD, biologic eligibility, cost/access and the likelihood that revision surgery will improve topical access. Steroid-eluting implants are an option for selected postoperative recurrent polyp disease.

items.prompt: A 48-year-old with bilateral nasal polyps has a biopsy showing edematous, sparsely cellular stroma with abundant eosinophils. What mechanism explains why the polyps are soft, edematous masses?
choices: Fibrin deposits trap fluid in the stroma

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis is a noninvasive, usually type-2/eosinophilic inflammatory phenotype occurring in immunocompetent patients, often with nasal polyposis, thick eosinophilic mucin, asthma/atopy, heterogeneous sinus opacification and bony expansion/remodeling. The dramatic CT appearance can mimic invasive fungal disease, but this condition does not require fungal tissue invasion. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treatment combines complete surgical clearance of obstructing allergic mucin with durable sinus access plus postoperative anti-inflammatory therapy, especially topical corticosteroid irrigations and selected systemic steroids. Long-term endoscopic surveillance matters because recurrence is common. Antifungal drugs are not the central treatment for classic noninvasive AFRS, and a positive fungal culture should not trigger an invasive-fungal regimen without tissue invasion or the appropriate host/clinical syndrome.

items.prompt: A 19-year-old from Louisiana with allergic rhinitis has unilateral polyps, mild proptosis, and CT showing expansile opacification with heterogeneous hyperdensity. Surgery reveals thick, peanut-butter-like mucin. What is the mechanism?
choices: Fungal ball in a poorly draining sinus

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Acute this condition is an angioinvasive emergency, classically in neutropenia, hematologic malignancy, transplantation, profound immunosuppression, or poorly controlled diabetes/ketoacidosis. Early disease may look deceptively mild: severe or focal facial pain, fever, nasal crusting, pallor or anesthesia, facial numbness, orbital symptoms, or cranial neuropathy are more important than waiting for a black eschar, which is a late finding. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Management is simultaneous rather than sequential: urgent surgical source control, prompt systemic antifungal therapy chosen for organism/host context, and aggressive reversal of predisposing immunosuppression or metabolic derangement when feasible. Liposomal amphotericin B is a classic initial agent for mucormycosis; azoles such as isavuconazole or posaconazole have important roles depending on organism and treatment phase. New necrosis, neurologic progression, or persistent invasive tissue after the first debridement should trigger urgent reassessment rather than passive observation.

items.prompt: A neutropenic patient with leukemia has fever and facial pain. Endoscopy shows a pale, insensate middle turbinate without black eschar yet. What is the most important next step?

A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Expansile obstructed sinus lesion causing pressure, proptosis, diplopia, frontal headache or bony remodeling suggests this condition, often after prior surgery/trauma or chronic frontal disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Symptomatic/expansile mucoceles are generally treated by surgical marsupialization and restoration of drainage rather than complete stripping of sinus mucosa.

items.prompt: A 60-year-old who had frontal sinus fracture repair 20 years ago now has slowly progressive proptosis and diplopia. CT shows an expanded frontoethmoid sinus with thinned, remodeled bone. What drives the expansion?
choices: Mucus secretion into an obstructed sinus

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Inverted papilloma is a benign but locally aggressive Schneiderian epithelial tumor, classically presenting as a unilateral nasal mass with obstruction, epistaxis, or recurrent unilateral sinus disease. It matters because recurrence can be substantial if the attachment is not cleared and because synchronous or metachronous squamous cell carcinoma can occur. Unilateral polyposis in an adult should therefore not be presumed inflammatory until neoplasm is excluded. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Definitive therapy is complete surgical excision with treatment of the attachment site rather than simple debulking. Endoscopic resection is preferred for most accessible disease, with open or combined approaches reserved for anatomy/extension that cannot be safely controlled endonasally. Long-term endoscopic surveillance is required because recurrence may be delayed. If SCC is present, treatment follows sinonasal cancer principles and may require wider resection and adjuvant therapy rather than the benign-tumor pathway.

items.prompt: A 55-year-old has a unilateral lobulated nasal mass. CT shows opacification of the maxillary sinus with a focal cone of hyperostosis on its anterolateral wall. Why is that finding surgically useful?
choices: It marks the tumor's attachment site

items.prompt: A 58-year-old patient presents with progressive unilateral nasal obstruction, recurrent epistaxis, facial pressure and new diplopia. Nasal endoscopy shows a friable superior nasal-cavity mass; MRI demonstrates ethmoid/superior nasal-cavity disease abutting the anterior skull base with focal periorbital involvement, while CT is being reviewed for bone destruction. As the senior resident planning biopsy and definitive management, explain how you would work up and localize a suspected sinonasal malignancy, identify the orbit/skull-base/carotid and hemorrhage danger zones, decide whether an endoscopic, open, combined, radiation-based or induction-response-adapted strategy is appropriate, and show how histology changes treatment. Include explicit rescue/bailout decisions when the orbit, dura, optic apparatus, cavernous/skull-base region or major vessels make the planned operation unsafe?
items.answer_text:
Foundation — treat “sinonasal malignancy” as an anatomic problem plus a histologic family, not as one generic cancer. Persistent unilateral obstruction, epistaxis, facial numbness or pain, diplopia, proptosis, cranial neuropathy, a unilateral middle-meatal mass, or unilateral sinus opacification with destructive or infiltrative features should lower the threshold for neoplasm. Endoscopy defines the mucosal epicenter and supplies tissue, but cross-sectional imaging defines dangerous deep extent. Contrast-enhanced MRI is particularly important for orbit, dura, brain, perineural spread, cavernous/skull-base soft tissue and marrow; thin-cut CT complements MRI for bone remodeling or destruction, lamina papyracea, cribriform/fovea, frontal recess and pterygoid/maxillary architecture. Image the neck and chest/systemic sites according to histology and stage. Biopsy should be planned, not reflexive: review vascularity and skull-base relationships first, correct reversible bleeding risk, choose a site that will not create an avoidable CSF leak or orbital injury, and obtain enough tissue for expert classification and molecular testing when indicated.

Anatomic map — the roof is not a flat plate. The cribriform plate, lateral lamella and fovea ethmoidalis create a variable anterior skull-base boundary; the lateral lamella can be exceptionally thin. Superior/posterior disease can involve dura, olfactory bulbs, planum or sphenoid and intracranial structures. The medial orbital boundary includes lamina papyracea and periorbita, but oncologic orbital assessment must distinguish bone or periorbita contact from invasion of extraconal fat, extraocular muscles, globe, intraconal contents, optic nerve or apex. Posterior disease can enter the pterygopalatine and infratemporal fossae, follow V2 and other nerves, reach the vidian region or foramen rotundum, and approach the cavernous sinus and petrous/paraclival internal carotid artery. The sphenopalatine/internal-maxillary arterial system can generate major hemorrhage. These compartments determine both oncologic margins and whether the next millimeter of dissection is routine, reconstructive, vascular, neuro-ophthalmic or potentially catastrophic.

Workup and histology — first establish histology because sinonasal squamous cell carcinoma (SNSCC), intestinal and nonintestinal adenocarcinoma, olfactory neuroblastoma (ONB), sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma (SNUC), neuroendocrine carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, NUT carcinoma, SWI/SNF-deficient tumors and other entities do not share one treatment algorithm.
