items.topic: Endoscopic CSF Leak Repair / Nasoseptal Flap
items.canonical_topic: Endoscopic CSF Leak Repair / Nasoseptal Flap
items.prompt: A patient has persistent unilateral clear rhinorrhea confirmed to be CSF. Thin-cut CT suggests a small cribriform defect, MRI shows an associated meningocele, and the patient has imaging features that raise concern for idiopathic intracranial hypertension. In the OR, how should the resident localize the defect, choose between free-graft/multilayer versus vascularized nasoseptal-flap reconstruction, protect the flap pedicle, and respond if the defect proves larger or higher-flow than expected?
items.answer_text:
Foundation — separate three questions that are often collapsed into one: is the fluid truly CSF, where is the skull-base defect, and why did the leak occur? Beta-2 transferrin or beta-trace protein can confirm suspicious nasal drainage when the diagnosis is uncertain. Once a leak is established, high-resolution thin-cut CT defines bony defects and skull-base anatomy; MRI is complementary for meningocele/encephalocele, soft tissue and indirect signs of elevated intracranial pressure. A normal office examination does not exclude an intermittent leak. Spontaneous CSF rhinorrhea should trigger explicit assessment for idiopathic intracranial hypertension because repairing the hole without recognizing the pressure disorder leaves the mechanism of recurrence untreated.

Preoperative map — read the skull base in coronal, sagittal and axial planes. Identify whether the defect is cribriform, ethmoid roof, planum/sphenoid or another site; define the size and number of defects, meningoencephalocele, septal anatomy, prior surgery, sphenoid pneumatization, carotid/optic relationships and the anticipated reconstructive corridor. Plan the reconstruction before raising a flap. If a vascularized nasoseptal flap may be needed, avoid injuring its posterior septal vascular pedicle during the approach and do not casually cauterize or transect posterior septal blood supply before the reconstruction requirement is known.

Localization — expose only enough skull base to identify healthy margins around the true defect. Remove obstructing mucosa at the repair interface so graft material sits on a stable bed rather than on mobile mucosa, but do not convert a focal leak into an unnecessarily broad skull-base dissection. Encephalocele tissue that prevents closure may require controlled reduction after its relationship to functional neural/vascular structures is defined. Image guidance is useful when anatomy is distorted or the suspected site is close to high-consequence structures, but navigation confirms a map; it does not replace direct anatomic identification. Intrathecal fluorescein can help in selected difficult occult or multifocal leaks, but it is not a routine substitute for preoperative localization and requires institution-specific, informed, carefully dosed use because intrathecal administration is off-label and neurologic toxicity has been reported with inappropriate dosing.

Reconstruction choice — match the repair to defect size, location, tissue quality and CSF flow. A small, well-localized low-flow anterior skull-base defect may be closed successfully with a free mucosal graft, fascia or other appropriately supported graft, sometimes in a single layer. Larger defects, meningoencephaloceles, revision beds, radiated tissue, broad dural openings or high-flow leaks increasingly favor multilayer reconstruction and vascularized tissue. The board trap is treating 'nasoseptal flap' as synonymous with every CSF-leak repair. The contemporary principle is escalation to the least complex reconstruction that gives a durable, watertight separation for that defect.

Nasoseptal flap — the pedicled nasoseptal flap is based posteriorly on the posterior septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery. Its power is vascularized surface area and reliable reach, not simply thickness. Before harvest, estimate whether the flap will cover the defect without tension and whether prior septal surgery or vascular injury has compromised the pedicle. Preserve the posterior pedicle during sphenoidotomy, posterior septectomy and cautery. When the flap is not initially required but an expanded approach could create a high-flow leak, a rescue-flap strategy can preserve reconstructive options without committing every patient to full harvest. At inset, the vascularized surface must contact a prepared recipient bed broadly without twisting, folding, pedicle compression or a hidden channel beneath it.

Multilayer reasoning — 'multilayer' is not a fixed recipe. Depending on the defect, an inlay or underlay layer may buttress dura, an onlay may span bony margins, and a vascularized flap may provide external biologic coverage. Rigid buttress is useful selectively when needed to resist displacement, but overpacking against the orbit, optic apparatus, carotid or intracranial contents creates its own danger. Sealants and packing are adjuncts; they do not rescue poor defect exposure, inadequate graft overlap or a compromised vascular pedicle.

Unexpected high-flow leak — if the defect opens widely into a cistern or ventricle, the operative goal changes. Stop enlarging the defect merely to improve visualization, communicate the change to the skull-base/anesthesia team, define the full dural margins, and escalate the planned reconstruction. Confirm that vascularized tissue is viable and large enough; if the planned ipsilateral nasoseptal flap is unavailable, deliberately assess contralateral or alternate vascularized options rather than improvising a marginal free graft. A repair that looks adequate under dry conditions but lifts or channels with CSF pulsation is not adequate.

IIH distinction — classic textbooks correctly emphasize closing the anatomic defect; modern spontaneous-leak literature adds that durable success also requires attention to the pressure disorder. The international consensus states that ICP-lowering measures are supplementary and do not substitute for surgical closure. Conversely, closure alone is incomplete management when spontaneous leakage coexists with probable IIH. After closure, coordinate weight/IIH assessment, ophthalmologic evaluation when indicated, and individualized medical, CSF-diversion or venous-sinus evaluation rather than reflexively placing a shunt in every patient.

Lumbar-drain trap — a lumbar drain is not a universal component of endoscopic CSF-leak repair. It can provide selected perioperative pressure control or aid management of particular large/high-flow defects, but it adds infection, overdrainage, pneumocephalus and immobility risks. The resident should be able to state the specific reason for a drain in this patient rather than invoking it as ritual.

Postoperative rescue — recurrent clear drainage, severe positional headache, fever/meningismus, pneumocephalus symptoms or neurologic change after repair requires prompt reassessment rather than routine observation. Suspected recurrent leak should trigger endoscopic evaluation and targeted imaging/laboratory confirmation as appropriate; tension pneumocephalus or meningitis is an emergency. Persistent or recurrent spontaneous leakage should also reopen the IIH question and the integrity of the reconstruction rather than being labeled simply a 'failed graft.'

Senior synthesis — use five checks: CONFIRM asks whether the drainage is CSF; LOCALIZE asks exactly where the defect and any encephalocele are; MECHANISM asks traumatic/iatrogenic versus spontaneous/pressure-related disease; RECONSTRUCT asks what level of graft/flap complexity the size and flow actually require; PRESSURE asks what must be done after closure to reduce recurrence. The dangerous errors are blind exploration of an unlocalized leak, sacrificing the nasoseptal pedicle before knowing reconstruction needs, using a free graft for an unexpectedly high-flow defect without reassessing, using a nasoseptal flap reflexively for every tiny leak, routine lumbar drainage without an indication, and treating IIH therapy as either a substitute for closure or an irrelevant afterthought.

items.topic: Endoscopic CSF Leak Repair / Nasoseptal Flap
items.canonical_topic: Endoscopic CSF Leak Repair / Nasoseptal Flap
items.prompt: After endoscopic resection of a large pituitary macroadenoma, the surgeon finds a high-flow CSF leak from an opened suprasellar cistern. Why is a pedicled nasoseptal flap preferred over a free mucosal graft for the reconstruction?
choices: It is harvested without any donor-site morbidity
It removes the need to control raised ICP
Its own blood supply heals faster and resists pressure
It can be raised after the sphenoidotomy is widened

items.prompt: An adolescent boy has recurrent brisk epistaxis and unilateral obstruction; MRI/CTA show a markedly enhancing nasopharyngeal mass extending through the sphenopalatine foramen toward the pterygopalatine fossa. How do you establish the diagnosis safely, stage vascular/skull-base extension, and plan embolization and resection without creating avoidable hemorrhage?
items.answer_text: A classic juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is primarily an imaging diagnosis; routine office biopsy should be avoided because the tumor is highly vascular. Contrast CT/MRI defines the nasopharyngeal origin, bony remodeling and skull-base/intracranial extension, while angiographic evaluation clarifies dominant arterial supply and dangerous anastomoses when embolization is planned. Stage and map extension into the pterygopalatine/infratemporal fossae, sphenoid and skull base because these relationships determine exposure and control. Preoperative embolization can reduce blood loss in appropriately selected cases, but timing, embolic agent and vascular anatomy require experienced interventional planning, particularly when supply approaches ophthalmic or intracranial circulations. Endoscopic resection is feasible for many tumors; more extensive disease may require combined/open strategies or selected nonsurgical management. The OR plan should include large-bore access, blood availability, proximal vascular-control strategy and clear stop/escalation points for uncontrolled hemorrhage. Acute hemodynamic instability from epistaxis is treated as hemorrhage first, before definitive tumor surgery.

items.prompt: A 15-year-old boy has unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent severe epistaxis. CT shows a mass centered at the sphenopalatine foramen with anterior bowing of the posterior maxillary wall. Why should biopsy not be performed in clinic?
choices: The mass is cystic and collapses

items.prompt: An adult reports six months of persistent smell loss after a viral illness. Nasal endoscopy shows no obstructing polyps or mass, but the patient also describes intermittent parosmia. How should you localize and evaluate the olfactory deficit, and which findings would justify imaging or broader neurologic/skull-base evaluation rather than routine postviral counseling?
items.answer_text: First separate conductive loss from sensorineural/postviral, traumatic, medication-related, or neurodegenerative dysfunction using focused history, nasal endoscopy, and validated smell testing when it will affect counseling or follow-up. Routine imaging is not required for every otherwise typical postviral loss, but unilateral findings, epistaxis or a nasal mass, cranial neuropathy, significant head trauma, progressive unexplained loss, or other focal neurologic/skull-base features should redirect evaluation toward targeted CT or MRI and the relevant specialty workup. Counsel on smoke/gas/food-safety precautions and olfactory training when appropriate.

items.prompt: A 40-year-old lost her sense of smell after a viral infection 4 months ago. She now reports that coffee and onions smell like garbage. What best explains the distortion?

A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Chronic congestion/rhinorrhea without a convincing IgE-mediated pattern suggests nonallergic rhinitis; escalating topical decongestant use with rebound obstruction suggests rhinitis medicamentosa. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Remove triggers, use saline and phenotype-directed intranasal therapy; stop the offending topical decongestant in rhinitis medicamentosa and support withdrawal with anti-inflammatory therapy as appropriate.

items.prompt: A 32-year-old has used oxymetazoline spray several times daily for 2 months. Each dose works for a shorter time, and her congestion is now worse than before she started. What is the mechanism?

A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Unilateral obstruction, bleeding, unilateral polyposis, facial numbness, orbital symptoms or unilateral sinus opacification deserves a different differential than routine bilateral inflammatory CRS. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat the cause: odontogenic/inflammatory disease, fungal disease, benign neoplasm or malignancy each requires a different pathway. Red flags should accelerate tissue diagnosis and multidisciplinary planning.

items.prompt: A 55-year-old has 3 months of right nasal obstruction and blood-tinged discharge. CT shows unilateral opacification of the right maxillary and ethmoid sinuses with erosion of the medial orbital wall. What is the most important next step?
choices: Antibiotics and a repeat CT in 6 weeks

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Persistent nasal obstruction/discharge and cough in a child for ≥12 weeks with objective disease suggests pediatric CRS; adenoid disease, allergy, asthma, reflux symptoms and recurrent viral illness commonly overlap. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Saline and intranasal anti-inflammatory therapy are foundational; prolonged or repeated antibiotics should be phenotype-driven rather than automatic. Adenoidectomy is often the first surgical step in appropriate younger children before full FESS.

items.prompt: A 5-year-old has 4 months of purulent rhinorrhea, cough, and congestion despite saline, nasal steroids, and a 3-week antibiotic course. What is usually the first surgical step?

items.topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
items.canonical_topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Early severe CRS, nasal polyposis, chronic wet cough, bronchiectasis, recurrent otitis or neonatal respiratory history should raise CF or PCD rather than isolated idiopathic CRS. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Use aggressive saline/topical therapy and disease-specific pulmonary management. Antibiotics are culture/phenotype driven. Surgery may improve drainage/topical access but cannot correct the underlying clearance defect.

items.topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
items.canonical_topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
items.prompt: A 9-year-old has bilateral nasal polyps, chronic purulent rhinorrhea, and poor weight gain. What should be excluded first?

A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Frequent bacterial sinus infections, pneumonia, unusual organisms, poor vaccine response or refractory CRS despite appropriate therapy should raise humoral or broader immune deficiency. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Optimize topical CRS therapy, culture-directed antibiotics and immune-specific treatment such as vaccination strategy or immunoglobulin replacement when indicated by immunology.

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Nasal obstruction is subjective; objective tests measure different components of airflow/geometry and do not perfectly substitute for symptoms. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat the identified mechanism and use objective testing when it resolves a real question rather than as a routine prerequisite for every obstructed patient.

items.prompt: A 45-year-old reports severe nasal obstruction 3 years after bilateral total inferior turbinectomy. Acoustic rhinometry shows a very large nasal cross-sectional area. What explains the mismatch?

items.topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
items.canonical_topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Most facial pressure/headache is not automatically sinus disease. Migraine and other primary headache disorders commonly mimic 'sinus headache.'. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat proven sinonasal inflammation when present and route primary headache/TMJ/neuralgia to the correct pathway. Avoid antibiotics or ESS for imaging findings that do not fit the syndrome.

items.topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
items.canonical_topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
items.prompt: A 38-year-old has monthly episodes of facial pressure with nasal congestion, worse with weather changes. Endoscopy is normal and a CT obtained during an episode is clear. What is the most likely cause?

A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Unilateral mass, recurrent epistaxis, remodeling/erosion, cranial neuropathy or atypical 'polyps' should trigger a tumor framework rather than routine CRS assumptions. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Management ranges from surveillance to endoscopic/open resection based on histology, growth, attachment, symptoms and skull-base/orbital involvement. Use the staging above to set expectations: higher Krouse stage IP and higher Fisch stage JNA both carry higher recurrence/incomplete-resection risk and more often need a combined or open approach and closer surveillance, even though the operative principles (attachment-oriented resection for IP; vascular control and embolization planning for JNA) stay the same across stages.

items.prompt: A 20-year-old has painless left cheek fullness. CT shows expansion of the maxilla with a ground-glass matrix and indistinct margins; serial imaging shows growth stopped after puberty. What is the most likely diagnosis?

items.topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
items.canonical_topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
items.prompt: A patient is evaluated in rhinology clinic. Crusting, septal perforation, destructive lesions, refractory inflammation or multisystem symptoms can reflect vasculitis, granulomatous, autoimmune, infectious or toxic disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat the systemic driver with the appropriate specialty while controlling local infection, crusting, bleeding and structural complications.

items.topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
items.canonical_topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
items.prompt: A 35-year-old has nasal crusting, a large septal perforation, and early saddle deformity. Biopsies are nondiagnostic, ANCA is positive, and he admits to regular cocaine use. Why must the ANCA result be interpreted cautiously?
choices: ANCA is never positive in GPA

items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. HPV-associated OPSCC commonly arises in palatine or lingual tonsillar crypt epithelium and often presents with a small/occult primary but bulky or cystic cervical nodes. p16 immunohistochemistry is the standard surrogate used for staging in appropriate oropharyngeal SCC, but p16 positivity outside the oropharynx does not automatically confer HPV-mediated staging. Tobacco exposure and comorbidity still matter prognostically even within HPV-associated disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Early and selected intermediate disease may be treated with transoral surgery plus neck management or definitive radiation-based therapy; the best choice balances oncologic control against swallowing, speech, xerostomia, aspiration, and treatment burden. Pathology after surgery determines whether observation, radiation, or chemoradiation is needed. Positive margins and extranodal extension are major adverse features that can drive concurrent chemoradiation; other risk features may support postoperative radiation. De-intensification strategies should not be improvised outside evidence-based protocols simply because the tumor is HPV-positive.

items.prompt: A 46-year-old nonsmoker has a painless cystic level II neck mass. FNA shows squamous cell carcinoma with strong, diffuse p16 staining. Why is p16 overexpression a reliable surrogate for an HPV-driven tumor?
choices: Viral E6 directly switches on p16
p16 is encoded by the HPV genome

items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. Persistent dysphonia, odynophagia, dysphagia, hemoptysis, otalgia or airway symptoms require laryngeal visualization; glottic cancers often present earlier with voice change than supraglottic disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Early disease can often be treated with single-modality transoral surgery or radiation; advanced disease requires larynx-preservation CRT versus total laryngectomy/surgery based on resectability, cartilage/function and patient factors.

items.prompt: A 64-year-old smoker has 4 months of hoarseness. Laryngoscopy shows an exophytic lesion of the left true vocal fold extending into the ventricle, and the left fold is fixed. CT shows no cartilage destruction. Which finding makes this T3 disease?
choices: A tumor diameter greater than 2 cm

items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. Unknown Primary with Cervical Metastasis is being considered. In an adult, a persistent cystic or solid cervical node should be considered metastatic carcinoma until proven otherwise, especially at level II/III. HPV-associated oropharyngeal SCC frequently presents as a cystic neck mass with a small or occult tonsil/base-of-tongue primary; EBV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma has a different mucosal home and testing pathway. When is Unknown Primary with Cervical Metastasis indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: During operative workup, systematic bilateral palatine tonsil evaluation and lingual tonsil/base-of-tongue assessment are favored over random biopsies of normal mucosa. Transoral robotic/laser lingual tonsillectomy can identify an otherwise occult HPV-associated primary. Neck dissection extent follows nodal burden and oncologic principles rather than the desire to 'find the primary.' Preserve CN XI, internal jugular vein, and SCM when oncologically safe; sacrifice is dictated by gross involvement, not by the label 'unknown primary.'

items.prompt: A 52-year-old has a p16-positive SCC metastasis in a left level IIA node. Office exam, flexible laryngoscopy, and PET-CT show no primary. Which procedure is most likely to identify the primary tumor?
choices: Excisional biopsy of the neck node

items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. Neck Dissection is being considered. this condition as regional oncologic surgery whose indication and extent are determined by the PRIMARY SITE, clinical nodal status, expected lymphatic drainage, prior treatment, and whether the neck is being treated electively or therapeutically. Do not reduce the operation to memorizing levels I-V. When is Neck Dissection indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Operate by preserving normal function WITHOUT compromising clearance. Raise appropriately vascularized flaps, identify the boundaries of the selected nodal levels, and remove the fibrofatty lymphatic packet in a controlled fashion while deliberately identifying or protecting key structures: marginal mandibular nerve and facial vessels around level IB; hypoglossal and lingual nerves; carotid artery/vagus/IJV; spinal accessory nerve as it crosses level II and enters the posterior triangle; phrenic nerve and brachial plexus deep to level IV/V; and the thoracic duct at the low LEFT neck. Preserve CN XI, IJV, and SCM when not grossly involved; sacrifice is an oncologic decision, not a requirement of every comprehensive dissection. For transoral oropharyngeal surgery performed with neck dissection, ASCO recommends ligating at-risk feeding vessels to reduce severity/incidence of postoperative hemorrhage. Before closure, obtain hemostasis, inspect the low neck for lymphatic leakage when relevant, and document the exact levels and structures removed/preserved.

items.prompt: A 60-year-old with a T2 supraglottic cancer and a clinically N0 neck undergoes bilateral selective neck dissection of levels II-IV. Why is level V usually omitted?
choices: Level V dissection endangers the phrenic nerve
Laryngeal primaries rarely involve it alone
Level V drains only the scalp
Level V contains no lymph nodes

items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. Oral Tongue SCC is being considered. this condition as an ORAL-CAVITY cancer of the mobile anterior two thirds of the tongue, classically presenting with a persistent ulcer, indurated lesion, pain, dysarthria, bleeding, or referred otalgia. Do not confuse it with base-of-tongue/oropharyngeal SCC. Tobacco/alcohol exposure remains relevant, but p16 is not used as the site-defining staging surrogate that it is for HPV-mediated oropharyngeal SCC. When is Oral Tongue SCC indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Plan the glossectomy from three-dimensional extent, not surface diameter alone. Achieve an oncologically adequate deep margin while protecting residual tongue mobility when feasible. Decide whether primary closure, local tissue, or free-flap reconstruction best restores bulk and mobility; a larger defect may need radial forearm or anterolateral-thigh-type reconstruction depending on volume and goals. Coordinate neck dissection in the same oncologic plan. For advanced lesions involving floor of mouth/mandible, escalate to composite resection only when invasion requires it rather than removing mandible prophylactically. Frozen sections can help margin assessment but do not replace correct initial resection geometry.

items.prompt: A 58-year-old has a 2.5 cm lateral oral tongue SCC with a 6 mm depth of invasion on biopsy and imaging, and a clinically N0 neck. Why is elective neck dissection recommended?
choices: Lateral tongue cancers usually spread bilaterally
Radiation cannot treat oral cavity disease
Depth of invasion predicts occult nodes

items.prompt: A patient with tobacco and alcohol exposure has a painful ulcerative floor-of-mouth lesion, tongue numbness, and a palpable ipsilateral level I node. Examination suggests fixation near the mandibular periosteum. What must be defined before treatment, and which anatomic findings most strongly change the resection, neck, and reconstruction plan?
items.answer_text: Confirm squamous cell carcinoma with biopsy and define the full oral-cavity primary by inspection and bimanual palpation, including depth, relationship to the mandible, tongue musculature, Wharton ducts, lingual nerve, and crossing of midline. Cross-sectional imaging should assess deep soft-tissue and mandibular invasion and characterize the neck; staging should include nodal and distant evaluation appropriate to disease burden. Mandibular cortical or medullary invasion changes marginal-versus-segmental mandibulectomy planning, while deep tongue/floor involvement changes functional resection and reconstructive requirements. A clinically involved neck requires therapeutic nodal management, and even a cN0 neck may require elective treatment based on pathologic risk such as depth of invasion. Reconstruction should restore tongue mobility, oral competence, and separation from the neck rather than simply close the defect.

items.prompt: A 66-year-old edentulous man has a floor-of-mouth SCC abutting the mandible. CT shows tumor reaching the alveolar ridge without medullary invasion. Why is the edentulous mandible at higher risk of direct tumor invasion?
choices: Dental roots normally block tumor spread
The inferior alveolar nerve is absent
Resorbed alveolar bone exposes the ridge

items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. HPV-associated disease may present as a cystic neck node with subtle tonsil primary. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Transoral surgery + neck management or radiation-based treatment depending on stage/anatomy/function.

items.prompt: A 50-year-old has a p16-positive left tonsil SCC. CT shows tumor extending through the superior constrictor into the medial pterygoid muscle, and he has new trismus. Why does this finding matter?
choices: It means the tumor is radioresistant

items.prompt: A patient presents with an HPV-associated level II neck node and subtle asymmetry of the lingual tonsil/base of tongue without an obvious oral cavity primary. How do you establish and stage the primary, choose between transoral surgery and radiation-based treatment, and what anatomic or functional findings should change the plan?
items.answer_text: Treat this as an oropharyngeal cancer problem, not as an isolated neck mass. Complete flexible endoscopic examination and contrast cross-sectional imaging, obtain tissue diagnosis with appropriate HPV/p16 characterization, and evaluate nodal and distant disease according to stage and risk. If the primary remains occult, directed examination under anesthesia with tonsillar and lingual-tonsil evaluation may localize a small tumor. Treatment selection depends on tumor extent, nodal burden, exposure, anticipated margins and expected swallowing toxicity. Transoral resection is reasonable only when exposure permits an oncologically complete resection with acceptable functional cost; the surgeon must understand the relationship of the deep tongue-base resection to the lingual artery and neurovascular structures. Extensive deep invasion, poor exposure, inability to obtain adequate margins without major morbidity, or a disease pattern better served by definitive radiation/chemoradiation should redirect treatment. Neck management and adjuvant therapy are determined by pathology and stage rather than by the technical success of removing the primary alone. When adverse features make postoperative chemoradiation highly likely, avoid a transoral operation that creates predictable trimodality therapy without a compensating oncologic or functional benefit.

items.prompt: A 57-year-old has 3 months of right ear pain. Otoscopy and tympanometry are normal. Flexible laryngoscopy shows a firm base-of-tongue mass. Which nerve explains the referred otalgia?
choices: Facial nerve via the chorda tympani

items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. supraglottic SCC as a LYMPHATIC + SWALLOWING cancer phenotype, not simply glottic cancer located higher. It arises from the suprahyoid/infrahyoid epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids, false cords, or ventricular surface. Presenting symptoms may be throat pain, odynophagia, referred otalgia, dysphagia, muffled voice, hemoptysis, neck mass, or later airway symptoms; hoarseness can be late unless the tumor approaches the ventricle/glottis. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat early T1-T2 supraglottic cancer with a single definitive modality when appropriate: radiation or transoral/open supraglottic resection can both be curative, with selection driven by exposure, subsite/deep extension, swallowing reserve, voice/swallow goals and institutional expertise. Unlike early glottic cancer, management must usually include the at-risk cervical lymphatics—elective nodal irradiation or appropriately selected neck dissection, often bilateral depending on primary location. Locally advanced but larynx-preservable disease may be treated with concurrent chemoradiation; extensive cartilage destruction, major extralaryngeal invasion, a nonfunctional larynx, or disease poorly suited to conservation can favor total laryngectomy with pathology-directed adjuvant therapy.

items.prompt: A 60-year-old has a T2 lateral supraglottic carcinoma of the aryepiglottic fold and a clinically N0 neck. Why are both sides of the neck treated electively?
choices: The glottis drains to the opposite neck
The thyroid gland is routinely involved

items.prompt: A smoker has persistent dysphonia and biopsy-proven glottic squamous cell carcinoma. Endoscopy shows a lesion approaching the anterior commissure with reduced but not absent vocal-fold mobility. What must be defined for staging and treatment selection, and how do mobility, subglottic extension, cartilage involvement, and baseline laryngeal function change the plan?
items.answer_text: Define the exact vocal-fold and commissure extent endoscopically and with imaging when deeper spread or cartilage involvement is a concern, and document true vocal-fold mobility before treatment. Early superficial disease with preserved function may be treated with appropriately selected transoral surgery or radiation, with modality choice based on exposure, expected voice, extent, and patient preference. Impaired or fixed mobility, meaningful subglottic or paraglottic extension, cartilage invasion, bulky disease, or a nonfunctional larynx moves the problem beyond a simple early-glottic paradigm and may require more extensive surgery or nonsurgical organ-preservation therapy according to stage and function. The neck is generally lower risk in truly early glottic disease than in supraglottic disease, but nodal management follows actual stage and extension rather than the subsite label alone.

items.prompt: A 62-year-old has a T1a glottic SCC limited to the middle third of one mobile vocal fold. Why is elective treatment of the neck not recommended?
choices: Glottic tumors are usually carcinoma in situ
Radiation fields always include the neck
Occult neck nodes regress after treatment
Vocal fold submucosa has few lymphatics

items.prompt: A patient with progressive dysphagia, weight loss, referred otalgia, and a pyriform-sinus lesion has biopsy-proven squamous cell carcinoma with ipsilateral cervical adenopathy. What must be defined before choosing definitive therapy, and which findings most strongly change whether organ-preservation treatment or primary surgery is reasonable?
items.answer_text: Complete endoscopic examination and cross-sectional staging should define subsite extent, laryngeal function, cartilage/prevertebral or major-vessel involvement, nodal burden, distant disease risk, nutrition, pulmonary reserve, and baseline swallowing. Treatment is stage- and function-dependent: potentially functional organs may be treated with appropriately selected chemoradiation or surgery, while grossly destructive disease, nonfunctional larynx, major structural invasion, salvage setting, or inability to tolerate organ-preservation therapy can favor primary surgery with planned reconstruction and swallowing rehabilitation.

items.prompt: A 63-year-old smoker has a pyriform sinus SCC and a 3 cm ipsilateral neck node at presentation. Why does hypopharyngeal cancer have the poorest prognosis among laryngopharyngeal sites?
choices: It does not respond to radiation
It occurs mainly in young adults

items.prompt: A 46-year-old adult presents with a painless level II neck mass, persistent unilateral middle-ear effusion, intermittent epistaxis, and new diplopia. Nasopharyngoscopy shows a lateral nasopharyngeal mass and biopsy confirms non-keratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma. As the senior resident, build the case from anatomy and EBV biology through current AJCC/UICC staging, imaging, definitive radiation/systemic therapy, plasma EBV-DNA interpretation, and surveillance. Then explain when induction chemotherapy is favored but not universal, what current FDA-approved immunotherapy applies in recurrent/metastatic disease, when salvage nasopharyngectomy or neck dissection is reasonable, and what carotid/re-irradiation danger zones should make you stop or change the salvage plan?
items.answer_text:
Foundation — nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is not managed like a routine mucosal head-and-neck squamous cell carcinoma. Start with the anatomy. The primary commonly arises in the lateral nasopharynx around the pharyngeal recess/fossa of Rosenmüller, immediately adjacent to the Eustachian-tube cushion. That relationship explains why an adult with a new persistent unilateral serous middle-ear effusion, especially with a neck mass, nasal obstruction, epistaxis, headache, or cranial neuropathy, needs visualization of the nasopharynx rather than repeated treatment for isolated otitis media. The nasopharynx also has rich retropharyngeal and bilateral cervical lymphatic drainage, so nodal disease can be the first obvious manifestation and can be bilateral even when the mucosal primary is small.

Pathology and biology — distinguish keratinizing squamous carcinoma from non-keratinizing NPC. Endemic non-keratinizing NPC is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), whereas nonendemic biology is more heterogeneous and a subset can be HPV-associated. Plasma EBV DNA is a highly useful biomarker in EBV-associated disease for prognosis, baseline risk assessment, response assessment and surveillance, but it is not a substitute for histologic diagnosis, endoscopy, or imaging. Assay platforms and treatment-adaptation thresholds are not perfectly interchangeable across centers, so a detectable or rising result should trigger clinical evaluation rather than an automatic treatment change without localization of disease.

Diagnostic workup — perform complete head-and-neck examination, flexible nasopharyngoscopy and biopsy of the primary when feasible. Image the nasopharynx and skull base with contrast-enhanced MRI because deep parapharyngeal extension, skull-base invasion, cavernous-sinus involvement and perineural/cranial-nerve spread may be underappreciated by surface examination alone. PET/CT or appropriate whole-body staging is important for nodal and distant disease. Document cranial nerves carefully; abducens dysfunction, trigeminal sensory changes, lower-cranial-neuropathy findings or Horner syndrome can localize advanced skull-base/parapharyngeal disease. A cervical node can be sampled when needed, but finding a metastatic node should not end the search for the nasopharyngeal primary.

Current staging — use the current AJCC/UICC ninth-version NPC framework rather than reflexively applying older stage-group memory. TNM-9 entered global use in January 2025. Important changes include advanced radiologic extranodal extension as an N3 feature, regrouping of nonmetastatic disease into stages I-III, and subdivision of metastatic disease into M1a/IVA for three or fewer metastatic lesions versus M1b/IVB for more than three lesions. The resident-level principle is not merely memorizing labels: stage must reflect the primary's skull-base/deep extension, bilateral/retropharyngeal nodal burden and metastatic burden because those features change systemic-therapy and radiation decisions.

Definitive treatment — NPC is predominantly a radiation-treated disease. Modern intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) is central because the primary sits near the brainstem, temporal lobes, optic apparatus, cochleae, salivary glands and cranial nerves while the at-risk retropharyngeal and cervical nodal basins often require treatment. Surgery is not the routine primary treatment for newly diagnosed conventional NPC. For genuinely early disease, radiation alone can be appropriate in selected low-risk presentations. As locoregional risk rises, concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiation becomes central, and modern evidence strongly supports induction chemotherapy before chemoradiation for many patients with locoregionally advanced/high-risk disease.

Induction-chemotherapy nuance — do not convert the modern preference for induction therapy into the false rule that every NPC patient receives identical induction chemotherapy. Contemporary guideline and ASCO syntheses favor induction chemotherapy, commonly gemcitabine plus cisplatin in evidence-based regimens, followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy for many locoregionally advanced patients. However, exact thresholds vary with the staging version, nodal burden, EBV-DNA risk, endemic versus nonendemic evidence base, comorbidity and institutional protocol. Some lower-risk stage groups can be managed without induction, and the value/tolerability of adjuvant chemotherapy after definitive chemoradiation is not interchangeable with the evidence supporting induction. Teach the direction of evidence and the reasons for selection, not a one-line universal sequence.

EBV-DNA application — obtain a pretreatment plasma EBV-DNA level when an appropriate validated assay is available in EBV-associated NPC. A high baseline level, slow clearance during induction, or persistent post-treatment detectability is prognostically adverse and may identify patients who deserve intensified evaluation. Yet biomarker-directed changes in the exact number of induction cycles or post-treatment therapy remain an evolving precision-oncology area. Do not cancel curative local therapy because the number falls quickly, and do not start salvage therapy from an isolated low-level result without confirming disease.

Response and surveillance — after treatment, assess the nasopharynx and neck clinically and endoscopically and use imaging at an appropriate interval; contemporary guidance commonly places the first major response assessment around three months. MRI is particularly useful for the nasopharynx and skull base; PET can help distinguish viable tumor from post-radiation change in the correct time window. Follow cranial-nerve function, hearing, swallowing, endocrine and other late-radiation effects. Persistent unilateral symptoms, a new neck mass, progressive neuropathy, recurrent epistaxis or rising EBV DNA deserves directed workup rather than attribution to radiation alone.

Senior recurrent/metastatic decision — separate potentially salvageable locoregional recurrence from disseminated disease. Selected small local recurrences can be treated with salvage nasopharyngectomy at experienced centers; contemporary guideline evidence includes a randomized comparison in carefully selected small local recurrences showing an endoscopic nasopharyngectomy advantage over re-irradiation. Carotid or intracranial invasion can make nasopharyngectomy inappropriate. Persistent or recurrent nodal disease can require selective or radical neck dissection depending on extent. Re-irradiation can control selected disease but carries major risks including temporal-lobe injury, cranial neuropathy, osteoradionecrosis and catastrophic carotid hemorrhage; prior dose, recurrence volume, disease-free interval, carotid involvement and performance status must be reviewed before committing.

Recurrent/metastatic systemic therapy — checkpoint inhibition is no longer merely experimental in the United States. FDA approved toripalimab-tpzi with cisplatin and gemcitabine in October 2023 for first-line adults with metastatic or recurrent locally advanced NPC, and toripalimab monotherapy after platinum progression in recurrent unresectable/metastatic disease. In April 2025 FDA also approved penpulimab-kcqx with cisplatin or carboplatin plus gemcitabine first-line for recurrent/metastatic non-keratinizing NPC, with a later-line monotherapy indication after platinum and at least one additional line. Those approvals do not mean PD-1 therapy should be inserted automatically into every curative localized case; integration of immunotherapy into definitive locoregionally advanced therapy continues to evolve and should follow current disease-setting evidence, regulatory labeling and multidisciplinary guidance.

OR/salvage danger zones — salvage surgery after radiation is not a routine primary-nasopharynx dissection. Expect scarred planes, altered vascularity and proximity to the parapharyngeal/internal carotid artery and skull base. Before nasopharyngectomy, define carotid relationship and intracranial extension and ensure that an endoscopic approach can achieve exposure and oncologic margins. Before neck dissection for irradiated nodal recurrence, anticipate fibrosis around the carotid sheath, cranial nerves and prior treatment fields. Do not pursue a deep margin blindly when the carotid is not controlled or the skull-base plane is uncertain; stop, reorient, obtain vascular/skull-base help when necessary, and change the salvage plan rather than converting uncertainty into exsanguination or cranial-nerve injury.

Bleeding rescue — recurrent epistaxis in an irradiated NPC patient is not always benign mucosal bleeding. A sentinel hemorrhage can precede carotid blowout, particularly after re-irradiation, skull-base necrosis or recurrent tumor near the carotid. Prioritize airway and hemodynamic resuscitation, avoid uncontrolled blind instrumentation, obtain urgent vascular imaging/interventional support when carotid injury is plausible, and coordinate endovascular or operative control according to anatomy. The senior bailout is to recognize when 'epistaxis' has become a vascular emergency.

Synthesis — the board and OR framework is: suspect NPC from the presentation; visualize and biopsy; map skull base, cranial nerves, retropharyngeal/bilateral nodes and distant disease; stage with the current TNM system; use radiation-based definitive therapy with stage/risk-appropriate systemic treatment; use EBV DNA as a powerful adjunct rather than an oracle; reserve surgery for selected salvage and neck disease; and in the recurrent irradiated patient respect carotid, skull-base and re-irradiation danger. Durable textbook anatomy remains stable, while systemic therapy, staging and biomarker use must be updated to contemporary evidence.

items.prompt: A 40-year-old man of Southern Chinese descent has a new unilateral middle-ear effusion and a level V neck node. Biopsy shows nonkeratinizing carcinoma of the fossa of Rosenmüller. Which blood test best tracks his tumor burden?

A patient is evaluated by the otolaryngology service. A 64-year-old with advanced laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma has a technically resectable tumor but severe pretreatment aspiration, poor pulmonary reserve, weight loss, and a largely nonfunctional larynx. How should you decide between nonsurgical organ preservation and total laryngectomy, and which pretreatment findings should outweigh the desire to preserve the anatomic larynx?
items.answer_text: Laryngeal preservation should mean preservation of useful laryngeal function, not simply avoidance of laryngectomy. I would define tumor extent with endoscopy and contrast imaging, assess vocal-fold mobility, cartilage and extralaryngeal invasion, and obtain tissue diagnosis and appropriate chest/distant staging. Just as important, document baseline airway, swallowing and aspiration, pulmonary reserve, nutrition, performance status, renal function and hearing if cisplatin is being considered, and the patient's ability to complete radiation and systemic therapy. A patient can be anatomically eligible for organ-preservation therapy yet be a poor functional candidate if the larynx is already severely dysfunctional, aspiration is clinically important, airway protection is poor, pulmonary reserve is limited, or treatment completion is doubtful. Major cartilage destruction or extensive extralaryngeal disease may also favor surgery depending on stage and resectability. Total laryngectomy can provide superior functional separation of airway and alimentary tract in selected patients with a nonfunctional larynx. Conversely, a functional larynx with appropriate disease burden and adequate reserve may justify nonsurgical preservation. The senior decision explicitly weighs oncologic control, baseline function, treatment toxicity, salvage options, and patient priorities rather than treating 'organ preservation' as an automatic endpoint.

items.prompt: A 60-year-old with glottic SCC and a fixed vocal fold is choosing between total laryngectomy and chemoradiation. Which additional finding most strongly favors primary laryngectomy?
choices: Vocal fold fixation alone, with normal swallowing
A single ipsilateral neck node under 3 cm
Thyroid cartilage destruction (T4a) or a poorly functioning larynx with aspiration
A strong wish to preserve voice and avoid a stoma

items.prompt: A patient with advanced laryngeal cancer is being considered for total laryngectomy after multidisciplinary review. The patient asks what changes permanently after surgery and what must be planned before the operation. What preoperative assessment and counseling are essential, and which postoperative complications require immediate escalation?
items.answer_text: Confirm oncologic extent and resectability while assessing nutrition, pulmonary reserve, swallowing, thyroid status when relevant, prior radiation, dental and reconstructive needs, and the patient's ability to participate in rehabilitation. Counsel explicitly that the airway becomes permanently separated from the mouth and nose: the patient will breathe only through the neck stoma and requires a new communication strategy such as TEP, electrolarynx, or esophageal speech with speech-language pathology involvement. Plan pharyngeal closure/reconstruction according to defect and tissue quality and protect major vessels in high-risk salvage settings. Postoperatively, airway problems are managed through the stoma—not by oral or nasal intubation. Neck swelling or bleeding, salivary leak/pharyngocutaneous fistula, wound breakdown, hypocalcemia when thyroid/parathyroid tissue is affected, or signs of carotid exposure/infection require prompt evaluation and source-specific rescue.

items.prompt: A 65-year-old is scheduled for salvage total laryngectomy after failed chemoradiation. Preoperative labs show a TSH of 14 mIU/L. Why should this be addressed before surgery?
choices: It prevents use of a voice prosthesis

items.prompt: An adult has a slowly enlarging parapharyngeal-space mass causing medial tonsillar displacement. MRI shows a well-circumscribed lesion, but the relationship to the carotid space and deep-lobe parotid is not yet clear. How should you localize the tumor before biopsy or surgery, and which imaging features change the differential and operative risk?
items.answer_text: Use cross-sectional imaging to determine whether the lesion is prestyloid or poststyloid and to define its relationship to the deep parotid, carotid artery, internal jugular vein, sympathetic chain, and lower cranial nerves. Direction of fat displacement, carotid/jugular displacement, continuity with the parotid, and vascular flow characteristics help distinguish salivary tumors, nerve-sheath tumors, and paragangliomas. A hypervascular lesion should not undergo routine transoral needle manipulation without appropriate vascular consideration, and encasement or major-vessel displacement changes surgical planning. Approach selection should provide safe neurovascular control and adequate exposure for the tumor's size and origin; the apparent oropharyngeal bulge alone is not sufficient reason to choose a transoral approach.

items.prompt: MRI shows a well-circumscribed parapharyngeal mass that displaces the internal carotid artery anteriorly and contains flow voids. Which compartment and tumor are most likely?

A healthy adult has a slowly enlarging pulsatile carotid-bifurcation mass that splays the internal and external carotid arteries on imaging. How do you confirm the diagnosis without creating bleeding risk, assess hereditary/multifocal disease, and choose observation, radiation or surgery while counseling about vascular and cranial-nerve morbidity?
items.answer_text: A classic hypervascular carotid-bifurcation lesion should be characterized radiographically rather than routinely biopsied. MRI/MRA or CTA defines vascularity, carotid displacement/encasement, skull-base extension and surgical complexity; functional imaging can be useful for multifocal/metastatic evaluation in selected patients. History should address catecholamine symptoms and family history, and biochemical testing plus genetic counseling/testing should be considered according to paraganglioma phenotype, age, multiplicity and contemporary hereditary-risk practice. Treatment is individualized by age, growth, symptoms, cranial neuropathy, tumor size/complexity, comorbidity and patient priorities. Observation with serial imaging is reasonable for selected indolent tumors; radiation can provide durable control when operative morbidity is unattractive; surgery offers removal but carries increasing carotid and lower-cranial-nerve risk with larger/encasing lesions. Operative planning must anticipate proximal/distal vascular control, vagal/hypoglossal/sympathetic injury and possible vascular-reconstruction needs. Rapid growth, new cranial neuropathy, concerning secretory symptoms or threatened vascular/skull-base structures changes urgency and workup.

items.prompt: A 45-year-old has a painless, pulsatile neck mass. Imaging shows a hypervascular tumor splaying the internal and external carotid arteries. Why is germline genetic testing recommended?
choices: Most of these tumors are malignant
SDH mutations are common and multifocal
Testing replaces the need for imaging

items.prompt: A 61-year-old undergoes curative-intent resection of an oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma with neck dissection. Final pathology shows a negative but close primary margin, pT3 disease, perineural invasion, three metastatic cervical nodes, and extranodal extension in one node. How should the tumor board translate the operative and pathologic findings into postoperative observation versus radiation versus concurrent chemoradiation, which findings carry the strongest evidence for adding concurrent systemic therapy, and what patient or treatment factors can change the plan?
items.answer_text: Postoperative treatment is driven by the recurrence risk demonstrated by the resection specimen, not simply by the preoperative clinical stage. First separate the classic high-risk features from intermediate-risk features. A microscopically positive surgical margin means invasive tumor remains at the cut edge, and extranodal extension (ENE) means metastatic tumor has extended beyond the lymph-node capsule into surrounding soft tissue. In a patient with resected mucosal head-and-neck squamous cell carcinoma who can tolerate treatment, either finding classically supports postoperative radiation with concurrent cisplatin-based systemic therapy rather than radiation alone. Before accepting a positive margin as immutable, the surgeon and tumor board should determine whether a clearly oriented, oncologically meaningful re-resection can safely clear it; a vague additional specimen or an anatomically impossible re-resection should not create false reassurance. Intermediate adverse features—including pT3-4 primary disease, multiple involved nodes or greater nodal burden, perineural invasion, lymphovascular invasion, and a close but negative margin—commonly support postoperative radiation according to site-specific risk. They do not automatically carry the same evidence-based indication for concurrent chemotherapy as positive margin or ENE, so avoid adding chemotherapy merely because several intermediate features are present without considering the disease site, guideline context, and patient fitness. Margin interpretation must remain site- and specimen-specific: orientation, the exact involved surface, separately submitted margins, bone versus soft-tissue involvement, and whether the 'close' distance is meaningful for that anatomic site can change the discussion. The tumor board should also review HPV/p16 status when relevant, pathologic T/N stage, number and laterality of nodes, ENE extent, PNI/LVI, prior radiation, wound healing, nutrition, performance status, renal function, baseline hearing and neuropathy before selecting concurrent cisplatin. If cisplatin is contraindicated, do not casually substitute another radiosensitizer as though it has identical postoperative evidence; radiation alone or an alternative regimen requires multidisciplinary, disease-specific judgment. Finally, adjuvant therapy is time-sensitive: healing and dental/nutritional preparation should be coordinated so postoperative radiation is not unnecessarily delayed, with initiation within roughly six weeks after surgery used as an important quality target when feasible. The senior decision is therefore not 'bad pathology equals more treatment'; it is to identify which pathologic feature changes modality, confirm that the pathology actually represents residual or extracapsular disease, and balance oncologic benefit against treatment toxicity without losing the postoperative treatment window.

items.prompt: After resection and neck dissection for a pT2 oral tongue SCC, pathology shows a 2.5 cm node with extranodal extension; margins are clear. What adjuvant treatment is recommended?

A long-term head-and-neck cancer survivor develops progressive dysphagia, xerostomia, neck fibrosis, dental deterioration and new mandibular pain years after chemoradiation. How do you separate expected late toxicity from recurrence or osteoradionecrosis, what surveillance and rehabilitation are required, and which findings need urgent escalation?
items.answer_text: Late radiation effects are longitudinal syndromes, but new focal or progressive symptoms still require evaluation for recurrence. I would assess weight and nutrition, aspiration/pneumonia history, cranial nerve and mucosal examination, dental status, thyroid function, neck mobility and the tempo/localization of pain or dysphagia. Instrumental swallowing assessment guides rehabilitation when aspiration or pharyngeal dysfunction is suspected; dental prevention, fluoride, saliva strategies, jaw range-of-motion work and thyroid surveillance should be built into survivorship rather than added after complications occur. New exposed mandibular bone, fistula, pathologic fracture, progressive focal pain or imaging concern requires evaluation for osteoradionecrosis and recurrent tumor, with biopsy when oncologically appropriate. New neurologic deficit, threatened airway, significant bleeding, severe aspiration-related pulmonary compromise or suspected carotid/major-vessel complication requires urgent escalation. Management should distinguish reversible focal problems from diffuse fibrosis and use multidisciplinary swallowing, dental, nutrition, endocrine, rehabilitation and oncologic follow-up.

items.prompt: Two years after chemoradiation for oropharyngeal cancer, a patient develops rapidly progressive dental caries along the gum line despite brushing. What is the main mechanism?
choices: Loss of saliva from acinar cell injury

items.prompt: A total-laryngectomy patient is considering tracheoesophageal puncture for voice rehabilitation. The stoma is well healed, but the patient has limited hand dexterity and intermittent dysphagia. What factors determine candidacy for TEP speech, and how should new leakage or loss of previously effective voice be evaluated rather than automatically replacing the prosthesis?
items.answer_text: Assess motivation, cognition, vision and dexterity, caregiver support when needed, stoma access, pulmonary reserve for airflow, pharyngoesophageal segment function, swallowing, and the ability to maintain the prosthesis with speech-language pathology. For dysfunction, distinguish leakage through the prosthesis from leakage around it and separate prosthesis failure from tract enlargement, candidal biofilm, poor pulmonary airflow, pharyngoesophageal spasm/stenosis, recurrent tumor, or other structural disease. New dysphagia, progressive loss of voice, bleeding, pain, or unexplained tract change should trigger endoscopic or imaging evaluation as indicated rather than repeated blind prosthesis exchange.

items.prompt: A laryngectomy patient with a well-fitted voice prosthesis can produce only strained, interrupted voice. Insufflation testing shows high pharyngoesophageal segment pressure. Which treatment helps most?
choices: Botulinum toxin to the PE segment

items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. Persistent lymphadenopathy with systemic symptoms or atypical nodal pattern may require lymphoma-specific tissue handling. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Hematologic therapy dominates; surgery is diagnostic or for selected complications rather than routine nodal clearance.

items.prompt: A 22-year-old has painless matted cervical lymphadenopathy, drenching night sweats, and 6 kg weight loss. FNA shows atypical lymphoid cells. Why is core or excisional biopsy still needed?
choices: FNA seeds lymphoma along the tract
Excision of the node is curative

items.topic: Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
items.canonical_topic: Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. HEAD-AND-NECK CUTANEOUS SCC (cSCC) as a keratinocyte carcinoma whose key resident-level question is not merely whether the lesion can be excised, but whether it has biologic features that predict recurrence, perineural spread, parotid/neck metastasis, or skull-base progression. Typical lesions are keratotic, ulcerated, indurated, tender, bleeding, or rapidly enlarging, but biopsy establishes diagnosis. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Surgery is the curative backbone for most resectable cSCC. Use margin-controlled surgery such as Mohs when exhaustive margin assessment and tissue preservation are especially valuable, or wide excision when oncologic geometry/reconstruction makes that preferable. High-risk disease may require multidisciplinary postoperative radiation based on margin, PNI, recurrence, nodal disease, bone invasion and other adverse features. Established parotid or cervical metastasis requires therapeutic regional management rather than a BCC-style local excision alone, with adjuvant RT commonly considered according to burden/pathology. For disease not curable by surgery or radiation, immune-checkpoint therapy is a major systemic option. Current U.S. therapy also includes adjuvant cemiplimab for selected adults at high risk of recurrence after surgery and radiation; do not teach immunotherapy only as end-stage salvage.

items.prompt: A kidney transplant recipient on tacrolimus has developed five aggressive cutaneous SCCs of the scalp in 2 years, one with perineural invasion. Why is her risk so high?
choices: Transplant patients get more sun exposure
Renal failure itself causes skin cancer

items.topic: Basal Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
items.canonical_topic: Basal Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. HEAD-AND-NECK BASAL CELL CARCINOMA (BCC) as the most common cutaneous malignancy and, in contrast with cSCC, primarily a problem of LOCAL DESTRUCTION, MARGIN CONTROL, and preservation of facial tissue/function. Classic morphology includes a pearly or translucent papule/plaque, telangiectasia, rolled border, ulceration, or a scar-like morpheaform lesion, but biopsy is required before definitive planning when diagnosis or subtype is uncertain. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Surgery remains the cornerstone. Favor Mohs or another complete margin-control strategy for recurrent, poorly defined, aggressive-histology or tissue-critical facial BCCs; standard excision is appropriate for selected lower-risk lesions when reliable margins and reconstruction are straightforward. Topical or destructive approaches belong to carefully selected superficial/low-risk disease and generally trade lower cure certainty for less invasive treatment. Radiation is an option when surgery is unsuitable or in selected advanced settings. For unresectable/locally advanced or metastatic BCC, Hedgehog-pathway inhibition (for example vismodegib/sonidegib according to indication) is disease-specific systemic therapy; cemiplimab is FDA-indicated after prior Hedgehog inhibitor or when a Hedgehog inhibitor is not appropriate. That systemic pathway is different from advanced cSCC.
