items.prompt: A 70-year-old has a slowly enlarging pearly nodule on the nasal ala that has been present for 2 years. Biopsy shows basal cell carcinoma. Why does this tumor almost never metastasize?
choices: It is always found while small
It depends on its specific stroma

items.topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
items.canonical_topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. HEAD-AND-NECK CUTANEOUS MELANOMA as a melanocytic malignancy whose first resident-level questions are Breslow depth, ulceration, nodal status and stage—not the cSCC checklist of perineural invasion and parotid-risk features. Suspicious lesions may follow ABCDE change (asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter/evolution), but nodular melanoma may present as a rapidly growing relatively symmetric papule or nodule. Biopsy establishes diagnosis. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Definitive local therapy is WIDE LOCAL EXCISION with margins based on Breslow thickness rather than a single head-and-neck skin-cancer margin: melanoma in situ generally 0.5-1 cm; invasive melanoma <=1 mm uses 1 cm; >1-2 mm uses 1-2 cm; and >2 mm uses 2 cm when anatomy permits. Coordinate SLNB at the time of wide excision when indicated because prior rearrangement can disrupt lymphatic mapping. A positive SLN does not automatically mandate completion neck/parotid dissection; modern management commonly uses active nodal-basin ultrasound surveillance with multidisciplinary systemic-therapy planning. Resected stage IIB/IIC and stage III disease may merit adjuvant anti-PD-1 therapy; BRAF V600-mutant stage III disease may also have a BRAF/MEK targeted option. Unresectable/metastatic disease is managed by melanoma stage, immune-therapy strategy and actionable biology—not by the advanced-cSCC cemiplimab pathway.

items.topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
items.canonical_topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
items.prompt: A 1.2 mm thick, nonulcerated melanoma of the posterior scalp is excised. Why is lymphoscintigraphy with sentinel node biopsy especially useful in this location?
choices: Head and neck drainage is unpredictable
Scalp melanoma drains only to level I
Melanoma does not spread to the parotid
Sentinel node biopsy cures most patients

items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. MCC is an aggressive cutaneous neuroendocrine carcinoma that may look like a rapidly enlarging painless red-violet dermal nodule. Small primary size does not imply low biologic risk, and immunosuppression increases concern. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Local-regional management commonly combines margin-negative excision with consideration of radiation because MCC is radiosensitive and recurrence-prone. Nodal disease requires definitive regional treatment. For advanced/metastatic disease, immune checkpoint therapy is generally favored over historical chemotherapy because responses can be more durable.

items.prompt: A 78-year-old has a rapidly enlarging, painless violet nodule on the cheek. Biopsy shows small round blue cells with perinuclear dot-like CK20 staining. Which virus drives most of these tumors?

A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. Recurrence may be local, regional or distant and can present with pain, dysphagia, weight loss, cranial neuropathy, new neck mass or subtle post-treatment imaging change. Distinguish recurrence from treatment effect before committing to salvage. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Potentially curable isolated recurrence may be treated with salvage surgery and/or carefully selected re-irradiation strategies. Unresectable or metastatic disease shifts toward systemic therapy, trials and symptom-directed care, with immunotherapy now central for many patients. FIRST-LINE SYSTEMIC THERAPY (KEYNOTE-048 framework): for unresectable recurrent/metastatic disease, pembrolizumab monotherapy is preferred for PD-L1 CPS >=1; pembrolizumab plus platinum/5-FU chemotherapy is used regardless of CPS status (including CPS <1) when a faster response is needed or CPS is low/unknown. For disease that progresses after platinum-based therapy, nivolumab or pembrolizumab monotherapy (CheckMate 141 / KEYNOTE-040) is standard second-line therapy. Re-irradiation with or without systemic therapy is reserved for selected unresectable local/regional recurrence beyond the interval above, in patients fit enough to tolerate it.

items.prompt: A 62-year-old has recurrent oral cavity SCC with lung metastases that is not amenable to surgery or reirradiation. Tumor PD-L1 combined positive score is 20. What is the preferred first-line systemic therapy?

A 61-year-old patient with HNSCC is reviewed at multidisciplinary tumor board. The team is considering checkpoint inhibition, but the correct role depends on whether disease is newly diagnosed and resectable, recurrent/metastatic and incurable with local therapy, or progressing after prior platinum exposure. How should PD-L1 CPS, resectability, disease tempo, prior treatment, performance status, and immune-related risk change the systemic plan, and which findings should prevent the team from using immunotherapy as a substitute for urgent airway control, definitive local therapy, or treatment of immediately threatening disease?
items.answer_text:
Start by defining the treatment setting before interpreting a biomarker. Checkpoint inhibition is not one generic HNSCC treatment. Confirm histology and stage, HPV/p16 status when appropriate, sites and burden of disease, prior platinum and radiation exposure, performance status, organ function, symptoms, resectability, and whether salvage surgery or radiation could still provide meaningful local control. Obtain PD-L1 testing reported as combined positive score (CPS) when it is relevant to regimen selection, but do not let CPS replace the clinical assessment.

For recurrent or metastatic HNSCC that is not curable with local therapy, pembrolizumab-based first-line therapy is selected according to the approved clinical setting, PD-L1 expression, disease tempo, comorbidity and the need for rapid cytoreduction. Pembrolizumab monotherapy is an important option for PD-L1-positive disease when a slower response trajectory is clinically acceptable and avoiding chemotherapy toxicity matters. When tumor burden is high, symptoms are substantial, or a faster and more reliable response is needed, pembrolizumab plus platinum-based chemotherapy is generally favored over choosing monotherapy simply because CPS is positive. Prior platinum exposure, timing of recurrence and prior checkpoint therapy also change subsequent-line choices; do not recycle a first-line algorithm without reviewing what the patient has already received.

For newly diagnosed resectable locally advanced HNSCC, immunotherapy must be integrated with—not substituted for—definitive surgery and pathology-directed adjuvant treatment. A current perioperative pembrolizumab pathway exists for appropriately selected adults with PD-L1 CPS at least 1: neoadjuvant pembrolizumab is followed by surgery, then adjuvant pembrolizumab with radiation with or without cisplatin according to pathologic risk, followed by pembrolizumab maintenance. Positive margins and extranodal extension still matter because they drive the need for concurrent cisplatin with postoperative radiation when the patient is eligible. The senior mistake is to hear 'immunotherapy' and relax the surgical margin, neck-management, or adjuvant-risk framework.

Before treatment, screen for factors that may make immune checkpoint therapy hazardous or require specialist input, including active or severe autoimmune disease, solid-organ transplant, prior serious immune-related toxicity, and other major comorbidity. During therapy, new diarrhea, hepatitis, pneumonitis, endocrinopathy, nephritis, severe rash, neurologic symptoms, or myocarditis-type symptoms should trigger an immune-related adverse-event evaluation rather than being dismissed as routine chemotherapy toxicity. Significant suspected immune toxicity may require holding checkpoint therapy and prompt organ-specific workup and immunosuppression according to severity.

Finally, immunotherapy does not rescue an unstable airway or an immediately threatening local problem on the timetable of an emergency. Stridor, impending obstruction, major hemorrhage, threatened carotid involvement, spinal or cranial neurologic compromise, uncontrolled infection, or rapidly progressive symptomatic disease demands immediate airway, procedural, radiation, surgical, or other multidisciplinary stabilization as appropriate. Likewise, a technically resectable recurrence with a meaningful chance of salvage should not be declared systemic-only merely because a checkpoint agent is available. The senior decision is to match immunotherapy to the disease setting while preserving curative local options and recognizing problems that cannot safely wait for a systemic response.

items.prompt: Ten weeks after starting pembrolizumab for recurrent HNSCC, a patient reports fatigue and cold intolerance. TSH is 25 mIU/L with a low free T4. What is the mechanism?
choices: Tumor invasion of the thyroid gland

items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. SALVAGE SURGERY as potentially curative resection of persistent, recurrent, or second-primary head-and-neck cancer in a field previously treated with radiation and/or chemoradiation. The key resident-level distinction is that salvage is not simply 'repeat the original operation later': prior treatment changes tissue vascularity, fibrosis, wound healing, airway exposure, vessel quality, swallowing reserve, reconstructive options, and the expected complication profile…. What are your immediate priorities, what is the first definitive management step, and which finding should trigger escalation?
items.answer_text:
Select salvage surgery when an R0/R1-intent resection with acceptable morbidity is realistically achievable and the patient understands the trade-off between cure probability and functional cost. Favor surgery for technically resectable isolated locoregional recurrence when durable control is plausible, especially after prior full-dose radiation limits further radiotherapy options. Do not equate 'technically operable' with 'appropriate': short disease-free interval, major comorbidity, poor performance status, carotid/prevertebral/skull-base fixation, extensive distant disease, or an operation that cannot deliver meaningful control may shift the recommendation toward nonsurgical therapy or symptom-focused care. Prehabilitate nutrition, tobacco/alcohol cessation, pulmonary status, and swallowing when time permits, and plan reconstruction before incision rather than after the defect appears.

POST-CRT RESPONSE-DIRECTED MANAGEMENT: Manage according to RESPONSE. Complete clinical/metabolic nodal response after definitive CRT: observe with surveillance rather than performing a routine planned neck dissection. Confirmed resectable residual or recurrent primary-site disease: discuss salvage resection appropriate to the involved subsite and functional cost. Confirmed persistent/recurrent nodal disease without distant progression: salvage neck dissection may provide regional control when complete resection is achievable. Equivocal early imaging should not automatically trigger surgery; use targeted reassessment because inflammatory uptake can resolve. Unresectable recurrence, distant disease, or prohibitive morbidity shifts management toward systemic therapy, reirradiation in selected patients, clinical trial, or palliative care.

items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. The clinically N0 neck can still harbor occult metastasis; treatment depends on primary site, T stage, depth/biology and expected nodal drainage rather than a universal elective neck dissection. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Elective neck treatment may be surgical or radiation-based depending on the primary strategy. Therapeutic neck dissection addresses clinically involved nodal basins; postoperative RT/CRT depends on adverse pathology such as extranodal extension and margins.

items.prompt: A 55-year-old has a T2 oral tongue SCC and a clinically N0 neck. The plan includes elective neck dissection of levels I-III, with level IV often added. Why are lower levels included?
choices: Tongue cancers can skip to lower levels
Tongue lymphatics drain only to level IV
Level III contains the thyroid gland
Level IV is involved in every case

items.topic: Reconstruction Selection After Head & Neck Ablation
items.canonical_topic: Reconstruction Selection After Head & Neck Ablation
items.prompt: A patient will undergo composite oral cavity resection with a through-and-through soft-tissue defect and segmental mandibular loss after prior radiation. At the preoperative conference, how do you translate the anticipated defect into reconstructive requirements, choose local/regional versus free tissue, and plan for recipient vessels, airway, nutrition and failure rescue before the ablative operation begins?
items.answer_text: Choose the simplest reconstruction that reliably restores function and withstands the oncologic environment. Start with the defect requirements: mucosal lining, external skin, dead-space fill, mandibular continuity, tongue mobility, separation of contaminated spaces and the volume needed for swallowing/speech. Small favorable defects may accept local or regional tissue, but a through-and-through irradiated defect with segmental bone loss generally needs robust vascularized free tissue, often with vascularized bone when mandibular continuity must be restored. Plan the flap around pedicle reach and recipient-vessel availability rather than choosing a donor site in isolation; prior radiation, neck dissection or vessel sacrifice should trigger a recipient-vessel and backup plan. Coordinate tracheostomy/airway strategy, enteral access, anticoagulation/VTE strategy and postoperative flap monitoring. Senior planning includes a second reconstructive option and a salvage pathway for venous congestion, thrombosis or flap loss, because reconstruction begins before the oncologic incision and cannot depend on an idealized defect.

items.topic: Reconstruction Selection After Head & Neck Ablation
items.canonical_topic: Reconstruction Selection After Head & Neck Ablation
items.prompt: After segmental mandibulectomy from parasymphysis to angle for oral cancer, the patient wants dental implants. Which reconstruction best meets this goal?

A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. Osteoradionecrosis of the Jaw is being considered. Osteoradionecrosis (ORN) is devitalized irradiated bone that fails to heal, most often mandible, and may present with exposed bone, pain, drainage, fracture, fistula, trismus or secondary infection. It is not simply osteomyelitis after radiation: radiation creates hypovascular, hypocellular, fibrotic tissue with impaired remodeling, and infection may be secondary. When is Osteoradionecrosis of the Jaw indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Debridement/sequestrectomy is appropriate when limited necrotic bone can be removed back to bleeding viable margins. Segmental mandibulectomy is required for advanced structural disease/pathologic fracture or diffuse full-thickness necrosis; reconstruction generally needs well-vascularized tissue, commonly osseous free flap when continuity is lost. In an irradiated field, durable soft-tissue coverage is as important as bone fixation. Do not perform repeated small debridements indefinitely when the mandible has structurally failed.

items.prompt: Eighteen months after 70 Gy to the oral cavity, a patient has a lower molar extracted. The socket never heals and bone remains exposed 4 months later. Why did the extraction trigger this?
choices: Extraction severed the inferior alveolar nerve
Irradiated bone cannot repair the injury

items.topic: Nonfunctional Larynx / Chronic Aspiration After Cancer Therapy
items.canonical_topic: Nonfunctional Larynx / Chronic Aspiration After Cancer Therapy
items.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the otolaryngology service. A disease-free head-and-neck cancer survivor has severe radiation fibrosis, silent aspiration of secretions and oral intake, three pneumonias in a year, feeding-tube dependence, and profound dysphagia despite expert rehabilitation. How should you determine whether additional rehabilitation or targeted endoscopic treatment is still worthwhile and when to discuss aspiration-prevention surgery or functional total laryngectomy despite the absence of recurrent cancer?
items.answer_text: First confirm that the larynx is oncologically disease-free and define why it is functionally failing. Instrumental swallowing evaluation should characterize secretion burden, timing and volume of aspiration, pharyngeal propulsion, residue, airway sensation, UES opening, and whether compensatory strategies meaningfully reduce risk. Treat reversible contributors when present—stenosis, focal UES dysfunction, poor dentition, xerostomia-related bolus problems, or a discrete structural lesion—but recognize when global fibrosis, neuropathy, and sensory loss make further local procedures unlikely to restore safe swallowing. Feeding-tube dependence does not eliminate aspiration of saliva or refluxate. Recurrent aspiration pneumonia, inability to handle secretions, progressive pulmonary injury, major quality-of-life loss, and failure of high-quality rehabilitation justify discussion of aspiration-prevention procedures. Options can include laryngotracheal separation or, in selected cancer survivors, functional total laryngectomy; these sacrifice normal laryngeal airflow and natural voice but can provide durable separation of the airway and alimentary tract. The senior decision is goals-based: compare the burden of irreversible loss of laryngeal function with the ongoing morbidity of a larynx that is anatomically preserved but no longer safely functional.

items.topic: Nonfunctional Larynx / Chronic Aspiration After Cancer Therapy
items.canonical_topic: Nonfunctional Larynx / Chronic Aspiration After Cancer Therapy
items.prompt: Three years after chemoradiation for supraglottic cancer, a patient with no evidence of tumor has had four aspiration pneumonias despite a gastrostomy tube and swallowing therapy. Why might total laryngectomy be offered?

items.topic: Head & Neck Cancer Surveillance / Second Primaries
items.canonical_topic: Head & Neck Cancer Surveillance / Second Primaries
items.prompt: A tobacco-exposed survivor of treated oral cavity SCC returns two years later with new unilateral otalgia and weight loss but a normal routine oral examination. How should surveillance distinguish recurrence, treatment toxicity and a second primary, and what symptoms should trigger targeted imaging or endoscopic evaluation rather than routine follow-up?
items.answer_text: Surveillance combines symptom-driven examination with risk-based follow-up rather than repetitive imaging by habit. Review the original site, stage, treatment and recurrence pattern; perform complete head-and-neck examination including flexible endoscopy when appropriate, assess neck nodes and treatment-related function, and address tobacco/alcohol cessation, dental care, nutrition, swallowing, thyroid or other treatment-specific late effects. New focal pain, referred otalgia, unexplained weight loss, bleeding, dysphagia, new mass, cranial neuropathy or progressive voice/airway change requires targeted investigation even when the routine surface examination is unrevealing. Choose CT, MRI, PET/CT or directed endoscopy/biopsy according to the suspected site and clinical question rather than ordering every modality. Tobacco-exposed patients remain at risk for second primaries in the upper aerodigestive tract and lung, so a new symptom is not automatically local recurrence. Surveillance should also detect functional morbidity that is treatable. The key is to establish a new diagnosis promptly while avoiding low-yield indefinite imaging in an asymptomatic stable survivor.

items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. Unilateral obstruction, epistaxis, facial numbness, orbital symptoms, cranial neuropathy or destructive unilateral imaging should raise malignancy rather than routine CRS. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Most resectable epithelial sinonasal cancers require multidisciplinary surgery and radiation consideration; some histologies favor different systemic/radiation strategies. Orbital preservation depends on true soft-tissue/apical invasion rather than proximity alone.

items.prompt: An adult with months of progressive wheeze unresponsive to asthma therapy is found to have a proximal tracheal mass causing critical fixed narrowing. How do you secure the airway without converting partial obstruction into complete obstruction, stage resectability and decide endoscopic temporization versus definitive tracheal resection or nonsurgical therapy?
items.answer_text: First treat the airway physiology. A critically narrowed fixed trachea can collapse with sedation, paralysis or poorly planned instrumentation, so define the level and severity from awake examination/imaging and coordinate an airway strategy with anesthesia and thoracic/head-and-neck expertise before induction. CT of the neck/chest characterizes length, extraluminal invasion, nodal/distant disease and relationship to major vessels/esophagus; bronchoscopy provides tissue and precise endoluminal mapping when it can be performed safely. Endoscopic debulking, dilation or stenting can restore lumen or obtain tissue in selected unstable/obstructed patients, but it is temporizing when an oncologic resection is feasible and can also complicate later surgery. Definitive segmental tracheal resection depends on histology, tumor length, margin feasibility, laryngeal/cricoid involvement, mediastinal mobility and whether a tension-free anastomosis is possible. Unresectable or medically inoperable disease may require radiation/systemic therapy according to histology. Stridor, increasing work of breathing, inability to lie flat or rapidly worsening obstruction mandates urgent controlled-airway planning rather than routine elective bronchoscopy.

items.prompt: A 45-year-old has 2 years of progressive exertional dyspnea and wheeze treated as asthma without improvement. CT shows a smooth mass narrowing the trachea by 70 percent; biopsy shows adenoid cystic carcinoma. Why was diagnosis delayed?
choices: It is obvious on plain chest X-ray

items.topic: Palliative / Goals-of-Care Decision-Making in Head & Neck Cancer
items.canonical_topic: Palliative / Goals-of-Care Decision-Making in Head & Neck Cancer
items.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the otolaryngology service. A 67-year-old with unresectable recurrent oropharyngeal SCC has progressive dysphagia, fungating neck disease with intermittent bleeding, severe pain, increasing secretion burden, and a narrowing but currently stable airway. He values time at home and wants to avoid prolonged hospitalization. How should you prioritize symptom targets, discuss tracheostomy, feeding access, hemostatic or debulking procedures, and decide when a technically feasible intervention is more burdensome than beneficial?
items.answer_text: Start by defining the patient's goals and the specific symptom each proposed intervention is intended to relieve. Palliative care should run in parallel with disease-directed treatment and should address pain, dyspnea, bleeding risk, dysphagia, nutrition, secretions, communication, psychosocial distress, and caregiver burden. A tracheostomy may prevent catastrophic airway obstruction but can increase secretion-management needs, hospitalization, caregiver burden, and the possibility of surviving with a tube-dependent airway; it should therefore be discussed before a crisis when possible. Feeding access can support nutrition but does not necessarily prevent aspiration or improve quality of life in every patient. Focal bleeding may be addressed with packing, endovascular therapy, radiation, or selected surgery depending on source and expected durability. Debulking can be reasonable when a discrete obstructive or symptomatic target can be relieved with acceptable recovery, but major salvage surgery without realistic oncologic or functional benefit may consume much of the patient's remaining time. The senior decision is proportionality: choose interventions with a clear, patient-valued endpoint and avoid procedures whose recovery burden, complication risk, or loss of independence outweighs the symptom benefit the patient actually wants.

items.prompt: In the clinical or operative context of Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons, Radiation is a spatial dose treatment with acute and late toxicity; definitive, adjuvant and palliative intent answer different oncologic questions. For Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons, what structures, relationships, or physiologic mechanisms must you be able to map, and why do they matter clinically?
items.answer_text: Localize target volumes and organs at risk conceptually: primary bed, nodal basins, spinal cord/brainstem, salivary glands, mandible, larynx/pharyngeal constrictors and carotid/skin in salvage contexts.

What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Multidisciplinary selection follows disease state and current guidelines. Surgeons should understand why systemic therapy is chosen, major toxicities and what response/progression means for salvageability.

Cetuximab was equally effective and less toxic

items.prompt: A patient is reviewed by the head-and-neck team. FREE-FLAP COMPROMISE as a TIME-CRITICAL postoperative diagnosis. The resident should know the flap's baseline immediately after inset and again at handoff: color, temperature, capillary refill, turgor, pinprick character when used, and the expected arterial/venous Doppler signal. A healthy skin paddle is typically warm and appropriately colored with brisk but not instantaneous refill. What are your immediate priorities, what is the first definitive management step, and which finding should trigger escalation?
items.answer_text: Manage the first minutes with PARALLEL RESCUE: notify the microvascular team, stop external compression, place the head/neck in a neutral non-kinking position, correct significant hypotension/hypoxia/hypothermia, and prepare for urgent re-exploration. Do not repeatedly massage, needle, or observe a progressively abnormal flap while waiting for a better Doppler. A small superficial hematoma without flap effect is different from a tense neck or hematoma altering pedicle geometry; the latter requires rapid decompression and operative control. Monitoring intensity is greatest early after surgery because vascular complications cluster in the early postoperative period, and every handoff should state the flap's current exam and the specific trigger for escalation.

items.prompt: Twelve hours after a radial forearm free flap to the tongue, the skin paddle is purple and swollen, and pinprick produces rapid dark blood. What is the problem?

At tumor board, a patient with resectable laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma asks whether an open partial/conservation laryngectomy can preserve the organ. How do you decide whether conservation surgery is oncologically and functionally appropriate, what must the resection preserve, and which disease or patient factors should move the recommendation toward nonsurgical therapy or total laryngectomy?
items.answer_text: Select transoral, open partial, radiation-based or total-laryngectomy strategies by oncologic extent and expected function; functional preservation without a safe airway and swallow is not success. Conservation laryngectomy requires a tumor that can be removed with adequate margins while leaving enough functional laryngeal framework and at least one usable cricoarytenoid unit for airway protection and phonatory/swallow rehabilitation. I would review endoscopy, vocal-fold/arytenoid mobility and cross-sectional imaging for subglottic, pre-epiglottic/paraglottic, cartilage and extralaryngeal extension, then integrate pulmonary reserve, baseline aspiration/swallow function and rehabilitation capacity. Disease that cannot be cleared without sacrificing the functional unit, extensive framework/extralaryngeal involvement, or a patient unlikely to tolerate the expected aspiration burden argues against conservation surgery. The senior decision is not 'can I remove less larynx?' but whether the selected strategy preserves both cancer control and a usable organ.

items.prompt: A 68-year-old with supraglottic SCC and mobile vocal folds has severe COPD (FEV1 35 percent predicted). Why is supraglottic laryngectomy contraindicated?

items.topic: Transoral Laser Microsurgery for Laryngeal Cancer
items.canonical_topic: Transoral Laser Microsurgery for Laryngeal Cancer
items.prompt: A 64-year-old patient with a biopsy-proven glottic squamous cell carcinoma is being considered for transoral laser microsurgery. The lesion approaches the anterior commissure, exposure is borderline on suspension laryngoscopy, and the team wants a single-modality larynx-preservation treatment. As the senior resident, explain how you decide whether TLM is oncologically appropriate, how tumor anatomy and exposure determine the resection, how you manage margins and the neck, what functional tradeoffs must be anticipated, how laser/shared-airway safety changes the setup, and what intraoperative or pathologic finding should make you stop, re-resect, convert, or choose another treatment?
items.answer_text:
Foundation — transoral laser microsurgery (TLM/TOLMS) is an oncologic resection approach, not an indication by itself. The decision starts with tumor extent, laryngeal function, ability to obtain reliable endoscopic exposure, expected margin control, neck disease, patient comorbidity, and the functional tradeoff versus radiation or open surgery. For early glottic cancer, both endoscopic CO2 laser excision and radiation are established single-modality options; the best choice is multidisciplinary and patient-specific. The laser is a cutting/coagulating tool. It does not make a poorly selected tumor resectable and it does not compensate for inadequate exposure.

ANATOMIC FRAMEWORK — map the lesion in three dimensions before touching the laser. For glottic disease, define true-vocal-fold surface and depth, anterior commissure involvement, posterior extension toward the arytenoid/cricoarytenoid unit, subglottic extension, and whether mobility is impaired. Deep spread toward the paraglottic space or cartilage changes the oncologic problem. The anterior commissure deserves special attention because exposure can be difficult and recurrence risk is higher in several series. Broyles' tendon and the relationship of the anterior commissure to thyroid cartilage are durable anatomic concepts, but modern management should not reduce this region to a simplistic automatic-cartilage-invasion rule. For supraglottic lesions, understand pre-epiglottic/paraglottic spread and separately plan the clinically occult or involved neck.

SELECTION — classic high-value TLM candidates are selected Tis/T1 and favorable T2 glottic cancers in which the whole intended resection can be exposed and a functionally acceptable negative-margin operation is realistic. Selected supraglottic tumors can also be managed transorally in experienced hands. More advanced T3/T4a disease has been treated with TLM in specialized series, but current evidence does not justify presenting that as a routine default; advanced glottic tumors in particular have less favorable recurrence outcomes in pooled data. Impaired vocal-fold mobility, major cartilage invasion, substantial subglottic extension, bulky deep-space disease, inability to expose the tumor, or a resection whose functional cost defeats the larynx-preservation goal should push the team toward another strategy.

EXPOSURE IS AN ONCOLOGIC VARIABLE — perform suspension laryngoscopy and obtain a stable line of sight before committing to definitive laser resection. Dental anatomy, mandibular restriction, cervical extension, tongue-base bulk, tumor location and anterior-commissure access can make exposure inadequate. Prospective data associate suboptimal exposure with positive margins. The senior rule is simple: if you cannot see the intended peripheral and deep resection planes, do not solve the exposure problem by taking blind laser bites. Improve exposure, change the laryngoscope or positioning, stage or abort the transoral attempt, or choose radiation/open surgery as appropriate. Poor exposure is an oncologic reason to stop, not a technical inconvenience.

EXTENT OF RESECTION — the European Laryngological Society cordectomy framework is useful language for describing how much vocal-fold tissue is removed; it is not itself a cancer stage. Resection depth should match tumor depth. A superficial lesion should not automatically receive a function-destroying deep cordectomy, while suspected vocalis invasion cannot be treated as a mucosal stripping procedure. As excision becomes deeper and wider, voice morbidity generally increases. Discuss that tradeoff preoperatively rather than calling every larynx-preserving operation function-preserving.

MARGINS — orientation and communication with pathology matter as much as the laser. Label the specimen and/or directed margin biopsies so the team can distinguish superficial from deep risk. Thermal artifact, specimen shrinkage, piecemeal technique and different institutional definitions of close complicate interpretation, so there is no universal millimeter cutoff across every TLM series. Current evidence makes a positive deep margin or multiple concerning margins more worrisome than a trivial superficial/thermal-artifact question. A 2025 meta-analysis of 26 studies and 5,463 patients found positive margins associated with worse disease-free survival, while effects on local control and overall survival remained uncertain. A 2026 meta-analysis of T2-T3 transoral resections found a positive-margin rate around 22% with substantial heterogeneity and uncertain outcome effects. These data reinforce selection and margin discipline rather than a one-number rule.

WHAT TO DO WITH A CLOSE OR POSITIVE MARGIN — first determine what the margin means: superficial versus deep, focal versus multiple, interpretable versus thermally distorted, and whether visible residual tumor remains. Obvious residual disease is not a surveillance problem. When a meaningful deep or multiple positive margin is suspected, options include prompt endoscopic re-resection/enlargement when exposure and function remain acceptable, radiation in selected settings, or conversion to a more definitive surgical strategy. Some early-glottic series support close surveillance for selected superficial or close margins because disease-specific survival and laryngeal preservation can remain high, but other data show worse recurrence-free survival and especially higher recurrence risk with close/deep or positive/deep margins. Therefore positive margin equals automatic total laryngectomy and positive margin equals observe everyone are both wrong.

AIRWAY AND LASER SAFETY — shared-airway planning is part of the operation. Before activation, surgeon and anesthesia team should explicitly agree on airway device/ventilation technique, laser mode, oxidizer strategy, protection of combustible materials, and what will happen if fire occurs. FDA guidance classifies ENT microsurgical CO2 lasers as devices intended for surgical excision of ENT tissue, including lesions/tumors of the vocal cords and adjacent areas; individual devices have manufacturer-specific cleared indications and instructions. Device clearance does not decide which laryngeal cancer should receive TLM. For laser airway work, use the institution's laser-safe airway strategy when an endotracheal tube is present, minimize oxidizer concentration to the lowest level compatible with safe oxygenation, avoid nitrous oxide, protect cuffs/adjacent combustible material according to device and institutional protocols, and keep saline immediately available. APSF fire-prevention guidance emphasizes the oxidizer–ignition–fuel triad and the particular risk of airway laser surgery.

AIRWAY FIRE RESCUE — if an airway fire is suspected, STOP laser energy and the procedure, stop/disconnect oxidizer flow, remove the burning airway device and other burning material from the airway, extinguish with saline/water, then re-establish ventilation with a safe device and assess the airway, typically including bronchoscopy after stabilization. Do not continue lasing while debating whether a flash was really a fire. This must remain consistent with the repository's existing shared-airway fire rescue gate.

BLEEDING AND DEEP-DANGER DECISIONS — laser hemostasis can create false confidence. Know where the lesion sits relative to larger vessels, particularly in supraglottic work, and do not pursue uncontrolled deep bleeding blindly through a narrow laryngoscope. Stop, improve exposure, use appropriate endoscopic hemostatic tools, and escalate the airway or approach when necessary. Thermal injury near cartilage, cricoarytenoid structures and uninvolved mucosa can worsen edema, stenosis, aspiration or functional loss. The senior resident should be able to say when the safest oncologic choice is to stop the transoral operation rather than extend thermal injury into anatomy that cannot be safely controlled.

NECK MANAGEMENT — TLM treats the primary site; it does not erase regional metastatic risk. Early glottic lesions have relatively low occult nodal risk, but supraglottic cancers have richer lymphatic drainage and may require elective or therapeutic neck treatment according to subsite, T/N stage and the overall treatment plan. A technically perfect transoral primary resection with an ignored at-risk neck is not complete regional oncologic care.

FUNCTIONAL COUNSELING — compare the entire treatment package, not just the presence or absence of an external incision. TLM can offer short treatment, repeatability in selected recurrences and laryngeal preservation, but increasing cordectomy extent can worsen voice, supraglottic resection can affect swallow, and positive margins can convert intended single-modality surgery into additional treatment. Contemporary meta-analysis suggests patient-reported long-term voice and quality-of-life outcomes after TLM and radiation for T1-T2 glottic cancer are broadly comparable, with substantial heterogeneity. The right answer is not laser always preserves voice better.

SALVAGE SETTING — prior radiation changes the problem. The European Laryngological Society salvage consensus supports CO2 TOLMS only in carefully selected recurrent laryngeal SCC after radiotherapy/chemoradiotherapy, with strict attention to workup, exposure, extent and follow-up. Radiation fibrosis, impaired healing, submucosal spread and difficult margin interpretation lower the tolerance for casual re-resection. Salvage TLM should not be taught as equivalent to primary early-glottic TLM.

CURRENT TREATMENT BOUNDARY — current National Cancer Institute PDQ lists endoscopic CO2 laser excision among accepted options for selected stage I glottic cancer and laser surgery among stage II glottic options, alongside radiation and partial/total laryngeal operations as anatomically appropriate. This supports a choice framework, not a mandate for TLM. Recent long-term early-glottic data continue to show high laryngeal preservation with careful selection, while T2 disease, anterior-commissure involvement and margin status are recurrent risk factors. Current evidence for selected T3/T4a TLM remains mostly nonrandomized and heterogeneous.

Senior synthesis — use SELECT, EXPOSE, MAP, RESECT, ORIENT, MARGIN, NECK, FUNCTION, RESCUE. SELECT the patient and tumor rather than selecting the laser. EXPOSE the entire intended oncologic field before committing. MAP superficial, deep, anterior-commissure, subglottic, arytenoid and deep-space extent. RESECT only to planes you can see and control. ORIENT tissue so pathology can answer the clinical question. MARGIN interpretation is pattern-specific, especially deep versus superficial/thermal artifact, not a universal millimeter rule. NECK treatment follows subsite and nodal risk. FUNCTION includes voice, swallow, airway and the possibility of multimodality treatment. RESCUE means aborting or converting when exposure, bleeding, airway/fire risk, deep extension or margin control defeats a safe oncologic transoral operation.

items.prompt: Two days after left modified radical neck dissection, drain output becomes milky and rises from 80 mL to 600 mL per day after the patient starts eating. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Chyle leak from thoracic duct injury

items.prompt: A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. A this condition is a malignancy-risk and symptom problem, not an automatic surgical diagnosis. Suspicious nodes, hoarseness, rapid growth or fixation change urgency. Specific history should be taken for known malignancy risk factors: prior head/neck external-beam radiation exposure (including childhood radiation therapy), a family history of thyroid cancer or a hereditary syndrome such as MEN2 (RET-associated) or PTEN hamartoma syndrome, and — while most nodules oc…. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Observation, interval ultrasound, ablation in selected benign symptomatic nodules, lobectomy or total thyroidectomy depends on malignancy probability, symptoms, bilateral disease, patient preference and downstream treatment needs. Let sonographic findings, cytology, clinical factors and patient preference determine the pathway: Bethesda II generally receives risk-adapted clinical/ultrasound follow-up; Bethesda III allows repeat FNA, molecular testing, surveillance or diagnostic lobectomy; Bethesda IV commonly prompts molecular testing or diagnostic lobectomy rather than mandatory repeat FNA; Bethesda V/VI generally prompt surgery or appropriate cancer-specific management, with extent decided by tumor size, pathology, nodes and risk factors rather than Bethesda category alone. Thermal ablation may be considered for appropriately verified benign symptomatic/cosmetic nodules in experienced hands; ethanol ablation is particularly used for recurrent symptomatic cystic nodules. These options do not replace indicated biopsy or malignancy evaluation.

items.prompt: A 44-year-old has a 2.2 cm solid thyroid nodule found on a carotid ultrasound. She has mild palpitations and her TSH is 0.1 mIU/L. What is the most appropriate next step before deciding on fine-needle aspiration?

A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. Differentiated Thyroid Cancer is being considered. this condition (DTC) as the parent pathway encompassing papillary, follicular, and oncocytic-lineage carcinomas. Start by separating initial disease extent from biologic recurrence risk: tumor size, gross extrathyroidal extension, clinically apparent nodal/distant metastasis, aggressive histology, vascular invasion, and molecular features do not all answer the same question. When is Differentiated Thyroid Cancer indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Match the operation to the disease actually present. Preserve the recurrent laryngeal nerves and viable parathyroid tissue, avoid prophylactic sacrifice of uninvolved structures, and perform therapeutic compartment-oriented neck dissection for clinically involved nodes rather than berry-picking. Do not add completion thyroidectomy reflexively after an initial lobectomy: the 2025 ATA update shifts completion surgery toward a selective decision when persistent disease, RAI planning, or surveillance strategy provides a concrete benefit.

items.prompt: A 38-year-old has a 1.8 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma with two involved ipsilateral central neck nodes. Why does this cancer so often spread to nodes yet rarely cause death?
choices: Nodal metastases that regress on their own
Reliable cure by lobectomy in every case

items.prompt: A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. Primary Hyperparathyroidism is being considered. this condition (PHPT) as inappropriate PTH secretion for the calcium level: usually hypercalcemia with an elevated PTH, but an inappropriately normal PTH in a hypercalcemic patient is also abnormal. Classic complications are nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis, cortical bone loss or fragility fracture, and symptomatic hypercalcemia; many patients are now discovered biochemically. When is Primary Hyperparathyroidism indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Choose focused parathyroidectomy when biochemistry and localization support a single-gland process and bilateral exploration when localization is negative/discordant, multigland disease is suspected, or the clinical context demands it. Identify abnormal tissue while protecting the recurrent laryngeal nerves and preserving viable normal parathyroid tissue. Intraoperative PTH (ioPTH) is most useful during focused surgery: a >50% fall from an appropriate pre-excision reference at the protocol-specified time is a common cure criterion, but the absolute value and clinical context matter. Renal dysfunction can slow PTH clearance and produce delayed kinetics, so a failure to fall promptly should not automatically trigger indiscriminate exploration—repeat sampling and interpret the curve with the patient's renal function and operative findings. Anticipate postoperative hypocalcemia; patients with severe skeletal disease or very high preoperative PTH/alkaline phosphatase are at particular risk for hungry-bone syndrome.

items.prompt: A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. Salivary Gland Malignancy is being considered. Salivary malignancy should be suspected with rapid growth, pain, skin fixation, trismus, facial weakness, deep-lobe/parapharyngeal extension or cervical adenopathy, but low-grade tumors can be painless and mobile. Histology matters enormously: mucoepidermoid, acinic, adenoid cystic, salivary duct carcinoma, carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma and other entities differ in nodal propensity, perineural spread and distant-metastatic behavior. When is Salivary Gland Malignancy indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Identify the facial nerve using reliable landmarks and dissect it deliberately rather than 'staying away' from it. A nerve that is merely adherent but functioning should not be sacrificed without evidence of gross invasion; a nerve encased by tumor may need oncologic resection. If sacrificed, document proximal/distal ends and reconstruct immediately with cable graft or nerve transfer when possible, plus eye-protection planning. Deep-lobe/parapharyngeal tumors may require transcervical/transparotid exposure; mandibulotomy is reserved for selected access problems rather than routine use.

items.prompt: A 58-year-old has a firm, slowly enlarging 2 cm submandibular gland mass. Why is the chance that it is malignant higher than for a parotid mass of the same size?
choices: The submandibular gland has no myoepithelial cells
Smaller glands have a higher malignant fraction

items.prompt: A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and secretes calcitonin; it behaves differently from differentiated follicular-cell thyroid cancer and does not respond to radioactive iodine. Disease may be sporadic or hereditary through germline RET alterations/MEN2. Diarrhea/flushing can occur with advanced secretory disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Primary resectable MTC is treated surgically with total thyroidectomy; central-compartment nodal management and therapeutic lateral neck dissection are based on clinical nodal disease, tumor burden, calcitonin level, imaging, and guideline risk assessment. RAI has no role. Persistent biochemical disease after surgery is not automatically an indication for blind re-exploration; localize structural disease and balance likelihood of cure against morbidity. Advanced progressive unresectable/metastatic RET-altered disease may be treated with selective RET-targeted systemic therapy in appropriate oncology pathways.

items.prompt: A 40-year-old has medullary thyroid cancer confirmed by FNA and an elevated calcitonin. Why is radioactive iodine not part of treatment?
choices: C cells do not concentrate iodine
MTC is too slow-growing to need adjuvant therapy
MTC is treated only with external radiation

items.prompt: A 72-year-old patient develops a rapidly enlarging hard thyroid/neck mass with new hoarseness, dysphagia, stridor, and CT evidence of bulky invasive disease abutting the trachea and great vessels. Core biopsy is being expedited and the airway is currently tenuous but maintainable. How should an otolaryngology resident organize the first hours of management, determine resectability, use urgent molecular testing—especially BRAF V600E—to change treatment, and decide when surgery or tracheostomy helps versus creates avoidable morbidity?
items.answer_text:
Foundation: anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC) is an oncologic and airway emergency, not a routine differentiated-thyroid-cancer pathway. In an older adult with a rapidly enlarging fixed thyroid/neck mass, pain or pressure, dysphagia, hoarseness, vocal-fold dysfunction, stridor, or imaging showing invasion, compress the diagnostic timeline. Examine the larynx early, define present airway stability, obtain cross-sectional imaging of the neck/chest appropriate to the patient's stability, secure tissue rapidly, and involve endocrine/head-and-neck surgery, medical oncology, radiation oncology, pathology/molecular diagnostics, anesthesia/airway expertise, and palliative/supportive care early. ATC is stage IV by definition, but the clinically decisive questions are whether disease is grossly resectable, whether distant disease or performance status changes the goal of local therapy, and whether the airway is likely to fail before disease-directed treatment can work.

Application: resectability is not synonymous with 'can something be removed.' A useful operation should have a realistic path to gross complete (R0/R1) resection without disproportionate morbidity. Carefully assess encasement/invasion of carotid or other major vessels, prevertebral fascia, mediastinal structures, larynx/trachea/esophagus, recurrent laryngeal nerves and the extent of nodal/distant disease. Avoid heroic R2 debulking simply because the tumor is operatively accessible; incomplete high-morbidity surgery can delay systemic/radiation therapy without providing durable control. Conversely, do not permanently label a patient unresectable before the multidisciplinary team considers whether a rapid response to mutation-directed therapy could convert selected disease to a useful resection.

Molecular pivot: obtain rapid BRAF V600E testing at diagnosis and broader molecular profiling without allowing testing logistics to delay stabilization. BRAF V600E is immediately actionable: current FDA-linked testing identifies patients who may receive dabrafenib plus trametinib, and BRAF/MEK inhibition can produce rapid major responses. In a BRAF V600E-positive patient with initially unresectable locoregional disease, targeted therapy may be used to obtain disease control and, in selected responders, permit reassessment for surgery. Published neoadjuvant series support this conversion strategy, but they are not a license to promise resectability or to ignore complications of rapid tumor response. Re-image and re-discuss the patient rather than leaving 'unresectable' or 'operative' as permanent labels. BRAF-wild-type disease requires a different mutation- and trial-informed systemic strategy; do not empirically give BRAF-directed therapy without the target.

Senior decision: separate three clocks—airway, tumor biology, and treatment response. If the airway is stable enough, avoid reflex prophylactic tracheostomy solely because the tumor is ATC. Bulky invasive tumor can make tracheostomy technically difficult, bloody, poorly healing, and potentially tumor-contaminated, and a rapidly responding systemic regimen may avoid it in selected patients. But 'avoid tracheostomy' is not the same as 'allow airway catastrophe.' Progressive stridor, inability to handle secretions, worsening oxygenation/ventilation, or a trajectory suggesting imminent obstruction requires an explicit rescue plan with the most experienced airway and surgical teams. Awake techniques, rigid bronchoscopy, intubation, tracheostomy, cricothyrotomy, or an operative airway each have context-specific limitations when the anterior neck and trachea are distorted by tumor; the plan must be individualized from endoscopy and imaging rather than memorized.

Once immediate threats are controlled, treatment is multidisciplinary. Grossly resectable locoregional disease in a patient who can tolerate therapy may be managed with surgery as part of multimodality treatment; unresectable or metastatic disease shifts emphasis toward mutation-directed/systemic therapy, radiation when useful for local control, clinical trials, symptom management, and repeated reassessment. Early goals-of-care discussion is compatible with aggressive treatment—it prevents emergency decisions from being made without understanding the patient's priorities. For selected responders to targeted therapy, surgery should be reconsidered only if the response creates a meaningful complete-resection opportunity; treatment-related necrosis, bleeding or aerodigestive fistula can also occur, so a dramatic radiographic response does not eliminate airway and wound-risk surveillance.

Rescue rule: systemic therapy never substitutes for oxygenation and airway rescue in a patient who is actually decompensating. If the airway is deteriorating, stop treating BRAF testing, radiation scheduling, or the next scan as the emergency. Mobilize anesthesia, ENT/head-and-neck surgery, bronchoscopy and critical-care resources; preserve spontaneous ventilation when appropriate to the anatomy and planned technique; have backup strategies physically available; and choose the safest achievable airway based on the level of obstruction and tumor involvement. The senior-level goal is not 'operate versus do not operate.' It is to stabilize the airway, establish the diagnosis and actionable biology quickly, avoid futile morbidity, exploit rapid targeted responses when present, and repeatedly reassess whether a previously unresectable patient has become a candidate for meaningful local control.

items.prompt: A 72-year-old has a rapidly enlarging, hard thyroid mass over 3 weeks with new hoarseness and stridor. Core biopsy shows anaplastic carcinoma with a BRAF V600E mutation. Why is this mutation clinically important?

An adult with papillary thyroid carcinoma has suspicious ipsilateral level VI nodes on ultrasound and a separate patient with a small cN0 intrathyroidal cancer asks whether central neck dissection should be added routinely. How do you distinguish therapeutic from prophylactic central dissection, define the compartment and choose unilateral versus bilateral extent, protect the recurrent laryngeal nerves and parathyroid blood supply, handle tumor adherent to a nerve or scarred revision planes, and rescue bleeding, bilateral nerve dysfunction, or postoperative hypocalcemia/hematoma?
items.answer_text:
Foundation — start with indication, not with the fact that central nodes commonly contain microscopic disease. A therapeutic central neck dissection is performed for clinically apparent central nodal metastasis identified preoperatively, by imaging, or convincingly intraoperatively. A prophylactic/elective dissection is removal of a clinically negative central compartment. The durable ATA/AAO-HNS/AHNS/AAES terminology statement matters because a central neck dissection is compartment-oriented surgery, not removal of a few visible nodes. The classic nodal groups are prelaryngeal/Delphian, pretracheal, and right and left paratracheal basins, with the inferior central compartment extending into the upper mediastinal level VII territory that is safely accessible from the neck. Record whether the dissection is unilateral or bilateral and why. 'Berry picking' only abnormal nodes leaves the rest of the involved basin behind and is not a substitute for a therapeutic compartment dissection.

Current indication reasoning — clinically involved central nodes are a strong indication for therapeutic dissection when the disease is resectable. The controversial question is cN0 disease. Older teaching and some retrospective series favored routine prophylactic central dissection because occult nodal metastases are common and nodal yield improves pathologic staging. Contemporary practice is more selective. The 2025 ATA DTC guideline emphasizes individualized risk/benefit decisions and broader de-escalation for appropriately low-risk disease; a small intrathyroidal cN0 cancer should not trigger automatic bilateral central dissection merely to discover microscopic N1a disease. Potential benefits of prophylactic dissection—staging information, lower central recurrence in some series, and influence on adjuvant planning—must be weighed against added transient and permanent hypoparathyroidism and RLN morbidity. Advanced primary disease, suspicious lateral nodal disease, tumor biology, need for reliable staging, surgeon experience and whether the information would actually change management can shift that balance. Preserve the disagreement explicitly: therapeutic CND for evident N1a disease is accepted; routine prophylactic CND for every cN0 PTC remains controversial and should not be taught as mandatory.

Anatomic map — before dividing lymphatic tissue, mentally map both recurrent laryngeal nerves, the superior and inferior parathyroid glands with their vascular pedicles, trachea, esophagus, carotid sheath, inferior thyroid artery branches, thymic tongue and thoracic inlet. The right RLN usually approaches the larynx more obliquely and may be hidden by nodal tissue; the left typically ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove. Neither course should be assumed, particularly with large tumors, prior surgery, inflammation, a nonrecurrent nerve variant or distorted anatomy. The nerve is at particular risk where disease or dissection converges near the inferior thyroid artery and Berry ligament. The parathyroid objective is not simply 'identify four glands'; it is to preserve viable glands with intact perfusion. Skeletonizing every gland or devascularizing its terminal vessels in pursuit of a cleaner specimen defeats that goal.

Operative application — expose the central compartment enough to see the structures that define the dissection. In a therapeutic unilateral paratracheal dissection, identify the RLN in a reliable segment and maintain direct awareness of it while nodal tissue is mobilized away from the nerve. Remove the prelaryngeal and pretracheal tissue appropriate to the planned compartment and clear the involved paratracheal basin en bloc when feasible. Avoid traction that tents the nerve into clips or energy. Keep thermal devices away from the nerve even when it is visually intact. On the right, pay attention to tissue posterior to the RLN when oncologically relevant; on either side, the esophageal surface and thoracic inlet become increasingly unforgiving as the dissection deepens.

Parathyroid strategy — preserve arterial inflow and venous drainage whenever possible. If a gland can remain in situ with convincing perfusion, leave it attached to its blood supply rather than stripping it free. If a parathyroid is unavoidably removed or clearly devascularized, confirm tissue when appropriate and autotransplant viable parathyroid tissue according to the operative context. Bilateral central dissection raises the cumulative parathyroid-risk burden, so the indication for crossing to the contralateral side should be explicit rather than reflexive. Postoperative PTH and calcium strategy should anticipate the extent of thyroid and central-compartment surgery; symptoms of hypocalcemia require prompt recognition and treatment rather than waiting for severe tetany or arrhythmia.

Senior oncologic decision — gross tumor involving the RLN changes the problem from routine nerve preservation to oncologic judgment. Do not shave blindly until the anatomy and preoperative nerve function are known. A functioning nerve that is adherent but not clearly invaded may sometimes be preserved with careful dissection depending on disease biology and ability to achieve appropriate control. A nerve with gross invasion may require resection when that is necessary for oncologic clearance, but the decision should integrate preoperative vocal-fold function, contralateral nerve status, expected residual disease, adjuvant options and reconstructive/voice consequences. AHNS consensus principles support deliberate rather than automatic nerve sacrifice. If the contralateral nerve is at risk or its function is uncertain, bilateral paralysis is the catastrophic endpoint to avoid.

Revision central neck — scar removes the normal visual and tactile planes. Do not reproduce a primary operation by force. Use preoperative imaging to localize structural disease, obtain baseline laryngeal examination when indicated, enter through the safest available tissue plane, identify the nerve from an undisturbed segment when possible, and accept that parathyroids and nerve may be densely adherent to scar or tumor. Reoperation should target clinically meaningful structural disease, not biochemical anxiety alone. When a safe plane disappears, stop traction, restore landmarks, use magnification/nerve-monitoring information as adjuncts rather than substitutes for anatomy, and obtain senior help. A small-volume target that would require destructive dissection may justify a different risk-benefit discussion than bulky progressive disease.

Rescue — uncontrolled central-neck bleeding is managed by pressure, suction, exposure and controlled ligation; blind deep clamping beside an incompletely visualized RLN, esophagus or carotid sheath is a dangerous response. Loss of a nerve-monitoring signal is not itself proof of transection: stop, inspect the nerve, correct tube/electrode and anesthetic factors, stimulate proximally/distally and determine whether a true neural event occurred before committing to the opposite side. If the first side has a convincing functional RLN loss during an elective bilateral operation, staged completion may prevent bilateral vocal-fold paralysis unless oncologic circumstances demand otherwise. After surgery, an expanding neck hematoma with pressure, dysphagia, voice change, stridor or respiratory distress is an airway emergency—release a threatening wound and secure oxygenation/airway while arranging immediate definitive hemorrhage control. Symptomatic or biochemical hypocalcemia is treated promptly, and unexpectedly low PTH after extensive bilateral surgery should trigger an active calcium/calcitriol plan.

Senior synthesis — ask six questions. INDICATION: is the central disease clinically positive or am I proposing prophylactic surgery in cN0 disease? COMPARTMENT: am I performing a complete indicated basin rather than node plucking, and is unilateral or bilateral extent justified? NERVE: where is the RLN now, what was preoperative function, and is tumor merely adherent or grossly invasive? PARATHYROID: which glands remain perfused and what action is needed if one is devascularized? CONTRALATERAL COMMITMENT: after first-side nerve trouble, is it safe to proceed?
