The major traps are routine bilateral prophylactic dissection in low-risk cN0 disease, berry picking therapeutic nodes, assuming the RLN course, thermal or traction injury, devascularizing parathyroids while 'preserving' them anatomically, sacrificing a functioning nerve without an oncologic plan, forcing scarred revision planes, continuing contralaterally after a true first-side neural injury, blind clamping of central bleeding, and observing a compressive postoperative hematoma.

items.prompt: After total thyroidectomy with bilateral central neck dissection for papillary carcinoma, a patient develops perioral tingling and a positive Chvostek sign. Why is hypocalcemia more common after central neck dissection?
choices: The superior parathyroids are always removed
Central dissection removes the thymus only
Inferior parathyroid blood supply is disrupted
The recurrent laryngeal nerve controls calcium

items.prompt: A patient previously treated with total thyroidectomy now has biopsy-proven nodal recurrent papillary thyroid carcinoma in the central neck. Preoperative laryngoscopy shows one mobile and one mildly paretic vocal fold, and imaging suggests the target abuts the tracheoesophageal groove. How should you confirm the indication and exact target, plan recurrent-laryngeal-nerve and parathyroid protection, decide when nerve sacrifice is oncologically justified, and prepare for bilateral nerve or calcium complications?
items.answer_text: Reoperation should begin with proof that the expected oncologic benefit exceeds the substantially higher morbidity of scarred central-neck surgery. Confirm the structural target with high-quality ultrasound and cross-sectional imaging when needed, correlate suspicious nodes with cytology and thyroglobulin washout when appropriate, and map every compartment that will require treatment so the operation is not an exploratory reentry. Document baseline vocal-fold mobility because an unrecognized preexisting paresis dramatically changes the consequence of injury to the contralateral nerve. Review prior operative and pathology reports and anticipate distorted parathyroid blood supply. Intraoperatively, identify the recurrent laryngeal nerve using an approach through the least scarred expected segment, often inferiorly or near its laryngeal entry point, and use nerve monitoring as an adjunct rather than a substitute for anatomic identification. Preserve functioning parathyroid tissue and vascularity when possible and plan postoperative calcium/PTH surveillance. A functioning nerve should generally be preserved when disease can be completely dissected off it; deliberate sacrifice is reserved for direct gross invasion when oncologic control requires it and should trigger immediate counseling/reconstruction planning. If the contralateral fold is already weak, the threshold for staged or modified surgery rises because bilateral dysfunction can create an airway emergency.

items.prompt: A patient needs reoperation for recurrent papillary carcinoma in the right thyroid bed. Why do many surgeons use a lateral (back-door) approach between the strap muscles and the SCM?
choices: It avoids the recurrent laryngeal nerve entirely
It removes the need for nerve monitoring
It allows access to the contralateral lobe
It enters through less scarred tissue

items.prompt: A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. Secondary / Tertiary Hyperparathyroidism is being considered. SECONDARY hyperparathyroidism (SHPT) as an adaptive CKD-mineral/bone disorder rather than a solitary-gland surgical disease. Declining renal phosphate excretion, reduced calcitriol activity, hypocalcemic drive and altered FGF23/vitamin-D physiology chronically stimulate all parathyroid glands, producing diffuse/nodular multigland hyperplasia. When is Secondary / Tertiary Hyperparathyroidism indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Operate as a MULTIGLAND disease. Common renal-HPT strategies are subtotal parathyroidectomy (leaving a deliberately measured vascularized remnant) or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation; institutional practice and transplant status influence the choice. Perform a systematic four-gland exploration, search predictable ectopic/supernumerary sites when a gland is missing, and consider cervical thymectomy when indicated because supernumerary/intrathymic tissue can drive persistence. Mark/document the retained remnant or autograft so future recurrence can be approached rationally. The major immediate postoperative hazard is HUNGRY BONE SYNDROME: abrupt PTH withdrawal permits avid skeletal uptake of calcium, phosphate and magnesium after prolonged high-turnover bone disease. Anticipate frequent calcium monitoring and aggressive calcium plus active-vitamin-D replacement rather than treating postoperative hypocalcemia as an unexpected complication.

items.prompt: A dialysis patient has markedly elevated PTH despite optimized medical therapy and is referred for surgery; another patient with a functioning renal transplant remains hypercalcemic with persistently autonomous PTH secretion. How do you distinguish the operative physiology in these two scenarios, and what perioperative issue must be anticipated after successful surgery?
items.answer_text: Secondary hyperparathyroidism is usually diffuse multigland hyperplasia driven by chronic kidney disease, whereas tertiary disease is autonomous PTH secretion after prolonged stimulation and typically presents with hypercalcemia. Surgical planning therefore assumes multigland disease rather than a single adenoma and may use subtotal parathyroidectomy or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation according to the clinical context. After successful correction, anticipate profound calcium demand/hungry-bone physiology and monitor calcium closely with proactive replacement when indicated.

items.prompt: A patient with biochemically confirmed primary hyperparathyroidism has discordant/nonlocalizing localization studies and concern for multigland disease. During bilateral exploration, how should the surgeon systematically identify all four parathyroid glands, use embryology and the recurrent laryngeal nerve to search for ectopic glands, decide what to resect when multiple glands are enlarged, interpret an inadequate intraoperative PTH fall, and avoid trading persistent hyperparathyroidism for permanent hypoparathyroidism or recurrent-laryngeal-nerve injury?
items.answer_text:
Foundation — four-gland exploration is an anatomy-driven operation, not a hunt for the first brown nodule. Confirm that the patient truly has a surgical parathyroid disorder before entering the neck; localization studies are for operative planning, not for making the biochemical diagnosis. Modern PHPT care does not require bilateral exploration for every patient. A well-localized apparent single adenoma can be treated selectively in experienced hands, but known or suspected multigland disease, hereditary disease, lithium-associated disease, negative/nonlocalizing studies, discovery of multiple abnormal glands, inability to find the expected abnormal gland, or an inadequate intraoperative PTH response should lower the threshold for bilateral/four-gland exploration.

Build a reproducible map. Expose one side sufficiently to identify the thyroid lobe, tracheoesophageal groove, recurrent laryngeal nerve region, carotid sheath and thymic/thyrothymic tissue without devascularizing normal glands. Search expected superior and inferior positions systematically rather than repeatedly dissecting the same scar plane. The most durable anatomic rule from Cummings is the relationship to the recurrent laryngeal nerve: superior glands usually lie posterior/dorsal to the RLN plane, whereas inferior glands are usually anterior/ventral. This relationship is often more useful than asking whether a gland looks physically “high” or “low.”

Superior-gland search — the superior parathyroid develops from the fourth pouch and migrates less, so it is commonly found near the posterior upper/mid thyroid, around the cricothyroid junction or posterior to the recurrent nerve. When ectopic, follow its predictable posterior migration possibilities: paraesophageal, retroesophageal, paratracheal and occasionally retropharyngeal locations. A descended superior gland can sit deceptively low but typically remains posterior to the RLN plane; mistaking it for an inferior gland can leave the true inferior gland undiscovered.

Inferior-gland search — the inferior parathyroid develops with the thymus from the third pouch and has a wider migration path. Search the lower thyroid pole, thyrothymic ligament, thymic tongue and upper mediastinal trajectory. An apparently “missing” inferior gland may be intrathymic or descend toward the anterior superior mediastinum. Do not perform progressively dangerous blind central-neck dissection without first using embryology, prior imaging and the glands already identified to decide where the missing gland should be.

Identify normal before sacrificing normal. During true bilateral exploration, compare size, shape, color, texture and vascularity across glands. Fat, lymph nodes, thyroid nodules and brown fat can mimic parathyroid tissue, and a single enlarged gland does not prove single-gland disease when the preoperative picture suggests hyperplasia. Conversely, mildly asymmetric normal glands should not all be removed merely because they are visible. The goal is biochemical cure while preserving enough well-perfused parathyroid tissue to avoid permanent hypoparathyroidism.

Single adenoma versus multigland disease — if one clearly enlarged gland is found and the remaining explored glands are convincingly normal, remove the pathologic gland and use the entire clinical picture, exploration findings and intraoperative PTH protocol to decide whether exploration is complete. If multiple glands are enlarged, think hyperplasia or double adenoma rather than repeatedly labeling each new gland an incidental finding. Known four-gland hyperplasia is not treated by removing only the largest gland. Common operative strategies include subtotal parathyroidectomy, leaving a deliberately sized well-vascularized remnant of the most normal-appearing gland, or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation in selected settings. The exact strategy depends on sporadic versus hereditary disease, renal disease context, recurrence risk and surgeon/endocrine-surgery plan.

Protect perfusion and the RLN. Parathyroid viability depends on a delicate end-arterial supply. When preserving a remnant, avoid skeletonizing or crushing its vascular pedicle; if normal parathyroid tissue is inadvertently devascularized and clearly nonviable, current AAES guidance supports autotransplantation. At the same time, do not convert a search for a gland into a recurrent-laryngeal-nerve injury. Identify the nerve when the dissection requires it, stay oriented to the nerve/gland plane, and stop blind traction, cautery or deep clamping when anatomy is uncertain.

Intraoperative PTH is a physiologic adjunct, not a substitute for anatomy. PTH has a short half-life, and many protocols use an appropriate fall after excision to support biochemical success. If the level does not fall adequately, first verify timing, sampling and the assay protocol; then assume residual hyperfunctioning tissue until proved otherwise. During a focused operation, failure of an appropriate PTH decrease is a classic reason to convert to bilateral exploration. During an already bilateral exploration, reconsider whether one of the “identified” structures was actually parathyroid, whether a second adenoma or hyperplastic gland remains, or whether a fifth/supernumerary or ectopic gland is present.

Important nuance — a slow or incomplete intraoperative PTH fall is not interpreted in a vacuum. Renal dysfunction can alter PTH clearance and baseline elevation, so the trend must be interpreted with the assay protocol and the patient's physiology rather than forcing resection solely to make one number cross a threshold. The dangerous alternative is removing progressively normal-appearing glands because the curve is slower than expected without reconciling renal function, timing and operative findings.

Missing-gland algorithm — stop and account for what you know. Confirm which glands are truly identified and which side/embryologic class is missing. Re-review imaging if available. For an inferior gland, inspect thyrothymic ligament/thymic tissue and the anterior mediastinal path. For a superior gland, inspect posterior/paraesophageal/retroesophageal locations. Consider an intrathyroidal gland only after more common locations are excluded; thyroid resection solely as an undirected “search maneuver” is poor strategy. A supernumerary fifth gland becomes more plausible in persistent multigland disease after four credible glands have been addressed.

Hereditary/multigland context changes the endpoint. MEN1 and other hereditary syndromes have a different recurrence biology than a sporadic solitary adenoma, so the operation may require planned subtotal resection or total parathyroidectomy/autotransplantation and, in selected hereditary settings, cervical thymectomy. The senior mistake is applying a focused-adenoma mindset to a patient whose disease is biologically multiglandular.

Postoperative rescue — watch for neck hematoma, voice change, symptomatic hypocalcemia and hungry-bone physiology. Perioral numbness, paresthesias, carpopedal spasm or QT prolongation demand calcium assessment and treatment. Patients with marked preoperative bone disease may have substantial calcium uptake after cure and need proactive calcium/vitamin-D management. A new breathy voice or aspiration symptoms require laryngeal assessment rather than being dismissed as routine postoperative discomfort. Cure is not declared because the wound looks good; long-term biochemical follow-up confirms eucalcemia and detects persistence or recurrence.

Senior synthesis — use five questions. INDICATION: why is this a four-gland operation rather than a focused one? MAP: which glands are identified, and are they anterior or posterior to the RLN plane as expected? BIOLOGY: does the pattern fit single adenoma, double adenoma, sporadic hyperplasia, lithium-associated disease or hereditary multigland disease? PHYSIOLOGY: does intraoperative PTH support cure, and if not, have timing, renal clearance, ectopic/supernumerary tissue and missed multigland disease been considered? PRESERVATION: can you cure the patient while leaving a viable, perfused parathyroid remnant and an intact recurrent laryngeal nerve? The dangerous errors are stopping after the first enlarged gland in a multigland patient, searching randomly for a missing gland, mistaking a descended superior gland for an inferior gland, sacrificing the remnant's blood supply, chasing a slow PTH curve by removing normal tissue, and ending the case without a plan for hypocalcemia, hematoma, voice change or biochemical persistence.

Current-evidence reconciliation — do not teach bilateral exploration as either obsolete or automatically superior. The 2022 international surgical consensus retains bilateral neck exploration for nonlocalized or multigland disease and defines conversion from selective surgery when findings or physiology no longer support a single-gland endpoint. A 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis found comparable cure rates between minimally invasive parathyroidectomy and bilateral exploration in selected PHPT populations, with shorter operations/hospitalization and fewer temporary adverse events after minimally invasive surgery, while about 8.5% required conversion to bilateral exploration. The teaching implication is selection: concordant single-gland disease can appropriately remain focused, whereas negative/discordant localization, hereditary or lithium-associated biology, multiple abnormal glands, an absent expected gland, or an inadequate physiologically interpreted ioPTH response should trigger a systematic multigland strategy.

Intraoperative-PTH nuance — define which baseline your local protocol uses before interpreting the curve. A pre-incision sample can establish a true operating-room baseline before manipulation; a pre-excision/pre-resection sample may capture a manipulation-associated peak and can therefore change the denominator for a percent-drop criterion. Do not mix baselines casually. A >50% decline is commonly used in validated protocols, but the exact endpoint and sampling time must follow the institution's reliable protocol and be reconciled with the final absolute level and clinical setting. If the PTH does not fully fall as expected, first check draw timing, assay/sampling error, baseline choice and renal function. Poor renal function can slow PTH clearance and maintain a higher baseline, so a borderline curve should not provoke indiscriminate removal of normal glands. Conversely, renal dysfunction is not a blanket excuse for a persistently nonresponsive curve when operative findings still suggest residual hyperfunctioning tissue.

Senior bailout — when four credible glands have been accounted for yet physiology still suggests active disease, stop before converting uncertainty into injury. Reconstruct the gland map, specimen identity and ioPTH timeline; reconsider supernumerary/ectopic tissue, intrathymic disease and whether an apparent gland was actually fat/lymph node/thyroid. Use embryology and targeted adjuncts rather than blind deep dissection. If safe cervical exploration is exhausted and the suspected target is mediastinal or otherwise outside a controlled field, end the cervical operation with a documented localization/reoperative plan rather than injuring the RLN, esophagus, great vessels or a viable parathyroid remnant simply to declare that every possible location was searched.

items.prompt: A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. Submandibular Sialolithiasis is being considered. salivary duct obstruction from the history before reaching for imaging. The classic presentation is recurrent unilateral submandibular swelling and colicky pain that begins or worsens with meals as stimulated saliva backs up behind an obstruction. Examine the floor of mouth and Wharton duct for a palpable stone, reduced salivary flow, or turbid/purulent saliva. When is Submandibular Sialolithiasis indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Choose the operative corridor from stone location and duct anatomy. For transoral submandibular duct surgery, identify the duct and remember that the lingual nerve loops beneath/around Wharton duct in the posterior floor of mouth; proximal dissection therefore carries lingual-nerve risk. Sialendoscopy can dilate stenoses, retrieve selected stones, and guide combined approaches while preserving the gland. Submandibular gland excision is reserved for selected irretrievable intraparenchymal/proximal disease, severely damaged glands, or recurrent disease not amenable to gland-preserving care; its risks include marginal mandibular, lingual, and hypoglossal nerve injury.

items.prompt: A 45-year-old has recurrent painful swelling under the jaw at mealtimes. Why do salivary stones form most often in the submandibular gland?
choices: Long uphill duct with alkaline, calcium-rich saliva
Its saliva is mainly serous and watery
Its duct is the shortest of the major glands

items.prompt: A patient has recurrent meal-related submandibular swelling and imaging shows an obstructing ductal stone. Which features determine whether sialendoscopy is likely to be gland-preserving and successful, and when should you plan a combined or alternative approach?
items.answer_text: Use history, examination, ultrasound or other appropriate imaging to define stone size, mobility, depth/location, duct caliber/stricture, and gland condition. Small accessible intraductal stones and focal strictures are favorable for endoscopic treatment. A large impacted hilar or intraparenchymal stone, unfavorable duct anatomy, severe fixed stenosis, suspected tumor, or repeated failure may require a combined endoscopic-open approach or another operation rather than repeated traumatic endoscopic attempts.

items.prompt: A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. Sialendoscopy is being considered. this condition as a diagnostic and gland-preserving therapeutic platform for obstructive salivary disease, not simply a camera used after a stone is already proven. Appropriate problems include recurrent meal-related gland swelling from mobile duct stones, duct stenosis/scar, mucus/debris, and selected recurrent inflammatory obstruction. When is Sialendoscopy indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Cannulate and progressively dilate the papilla gently, maintain continuous irrigation for visualization, and advance under direct vision rather than forcing the scope against resistance. Protect the duct wall from perforation, false passage, basket entrapment, and avulsion. When combining endoscopy with an incision, use the illuminated/localized stone to minimize dissection and preserve the duct and nearby nerves. Counsel about postoperative edema, duct perforation/stenosis, infection, retained/recurrent stones, temporary tongue/floor-of-mouth symptoms, and the possibility that a second or combined procedure may be needed.

items.prompt: An adult has recurrent painful left submandibular swelling despite appropriate gland-preserving treatment, but imaging also shows a discrete intraglandular mass that requires oncologic exclusion. How should you decide whether whole-gland excision is appropriate, plan a safe transcervical operation around the marginal mandibular, lingual, and hypoglossal nerves, control the facial vessels and Wharton duct, change the dissection if tumor biology or scar makes the usual plane unsafe, and rescue bleeding or postoperative airway compromise?
items.answer_text:
Foundation — first decide why the gland is being removed. Submandibular gland excision is not the default treatment for every stone or episode of sialadenitis. Modern obstructive-salivary practice favors gland preservation when feasible: sialendoscopy, transoral stone removal, or a combined approach can treat many stones and stenoses while retaining gland function. Whole-gland excision remains appropriate for refractory obstructive/inflammatory disease when conservative and gland-preserving options have failed or are unsuitable, and for selected neoplasms when removal of the gland is part of an oncologically sound operation. A discrete mass changes the preoperative mindset: do not enter the neck assuming chronic sialadenitis when salivary malignancy remains possible. Obtain appropriate imaging and tissue diagnosis when indicated, stage suspected malignancy, and plan the operation around histology, extent, nerve involvement and neck-management needs rather than using a benign stone operation as the template.

Anatomic map — the submandibular gland has superficial and deep components that wrap around the posterior free edge of the mylohyoid. The superficial gland fills much of the submandibular triangle. The facial vein and facial artery are closely related to the gland and may need deliberate ligation or preservation depending on the operation. The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve is vulnerable in the superior flap near the mandibular border and facial vessels. Deep to the gland, the lingual nerve, submandibular ganglion, Wharton duct and hypoglossal nerve are the major structures that turn a routine dissection into a nerve-injury operation. The lingual nerve is intimately related to the duct in the floor of mouth; the hypoglossal nerve lies deeper and inferior/posterior to the operative field. Never treat a white cord as 'the duct' until the nerve-duct relationship is understood.

Exposure and marginal-mandibular protection — place the transcervical incision sufficiently below the mandibular border and raise the superior flap in a controlled plane. There are several accepted ways to protect the marginal mandibular nerve, including deliberate identification in selected cases or maintaining a protective fascial plane and manipulating the facial vessels/gland inferiorly. No single maneuver should be taught as universally mandatory; the durable rule is to know where the nerve is at risk, avoid blind superior traction and energy use, and keep the nerve with the protected flap rather than dissecting toward it unintentionally. A scarred inflammatory neck deserves slower layer-by-layer exposure because inflammation can erase the clean tissue planes described in textbooks.

Gland mobilization and vessel control — develop the inferior and posterior gland surfaces under direct vision. The facial vein may be encountered superficially and the facial artery may groove or traverse the posterior gland. Control vessels deliberately with adequate proximal/distal purchase rather than avulsing them from the gland. If brisk bleeding obscures the field, apply pressure, improve exposure and obtain controlled vascular ligation; blind clamping in the deep submandibular space risks the lingual or hypoglossal nerve. Hemostasis should improve the anatomy, not make it less visible.

Deep dissection — as the gland is mobilized, identify the posterior mylohyoid edge and understand when the deep lobe, duct and lingual-nerve complex come into view. Retracting the mylohyoid and gland can expose the floor-of-mouth relationships. Identify the lingual nerve before dividing structures attached to the gland. The submandibular ganglion/parasympathetic connections can be divided from the gland under direct vision while preserving the lingual nerve. Trace Wharton duct far enough to distinguish it confidently from neural tissue, then ligate/divide the duct without incorporating the lingual nerve. Protect the hypoglossal nerve during inferior/deep mobilization; avoid aggressive traction, blind clips and thermal spread in its expected plane. Remove the gland without unnecessary violation of adjacent floor-of-mouth structures.

Benign inflammation versus tumor — chronic sialadenitis may make the gland densely adherent, but fibrosis is not permission to sacrifice a nerve for an elective benign endpoint. When the expected plane disappears, stop, re-establish landmarks from a safer direction, obtain assistance if needed, and decide whether the benefit of completing elective excision justifies escalating nerve risk. Conversely, a suspected neoplasm should not be 'shelled out' through the gland. Preserve the tumor capsule when possible and avoid piecemeal violation. If an unexpected infiltrative process is encountered, reassess the oncologic plan rather than forcing completion of a benign dissection. For resectable salivary malignancy, contemporary ASCO guidance supports complete surgical resection when appropriate; neck management and adjuvant therapy depend on stage, grade, histology, margins, perineural disease and other risk features. The senior distinction is that nerve preservation is the default in benign disease, whereas proven gross malignant nerve invasion can change the oncologic balance and requires an explicit resection/reconstruction discussion.

Gland preservation is also evolving for selected benign tumors. A 2026 meta-analysis of four studies and 318 patients found better unstimulated salivary flow, cosmetic outcomes and a lower marginal-mandibular injury rate with gland-preserving surgery, without a detected recurrence penalty. That is promising but not a universal new standard: the evidence base is small and vulnerable to selection bias, and it applies to appropriately selected benign tumors, not lesions of uncertain or malignant biology. Preserve this disagreement explicitly: durable textbook total-gland excision remains a standard operation, while carefully selected benign disease may increasingly be managed with gland-preserving techniques at experienced centers.

Completion and postoperative plan — inspect the field with attention to the facial-vessel pedicles, floor of mouth and nerve courses before closing. A drain is selective rather than a substitute for hemostasis. Counsel about transient or permanent marginal mandibular weakness, tongue numbness/taste disturbance from lingual-nerve injury, tongue weakness from hypoglossal injury, scar/contour change and xerostomia. Unexpected tongue deviation, lower-lip asymmetry or sensory loss deserves an anatomic diagnosis rather than being dismissed as routine swelling.

Rescue — an expanding neck or floor-of-mouth hematoma with dysphagia, voice change, tongue elevation, stridor or respiratory distress is an airway emergency. Prioritize oxygenation and airway control, release a threatening wound when necessary, and return urgently for definitive hemorrhage control. For uncontrolled intraoperative facial-artery/vein bleeding, pressure and deliberate vascular exposure are safer than blind deep clamping. If the lingual nerve versus duct anatomy cannot be distinguished, stop before ligation and improve exposure. If dense benign scarring makes preservation of the lingual or hypoglossal nerve impossible to assure, the bailout is reorientation, senior help, or aborting an elective benign excision—not knowingly converting a quality-of-life operation into a permanent cranial-nerve deficit.

Senior synthesis — ask five questions. INDICATION: is this refractory benign disease, a clearly benign tumor, or possible malignancy, and have gland-preserving options been considered? MAP: where are the marginal mandibular, lingual and hypoglossal nerves relative to the current plane? CONTROL: are the facial vessels and duct being divided under direct identification rather than traction or assumption? BIOLOGY: does tumor behavior require intact oncologic resection and a neck/adjuvant plan rather than a benign shell-out? BAILOUT: if bleeding, scar or uncertainty destroys the safe plane, can you restore exposure and control before continuing? The dangerous errors are removing glands unnecessarily for treatable obstruction, treating an unexplained mass like inflammation, injuring the marginal mandibular nerve in the superior flap, blindly clamping facial-vessel bleeding, dividing the duct before identifying the lingual nerve, traction injury to the hypoglossal nerve, violating a tumor capsule, and persisting through unsafe scar or postoperative airway compromise.

items.prompt: A patient has a firm submandibular-gland mass for which excision is planned after appropriate imaging and tissue evaluation. Which anatomic structures must be deliberately identified/protected during a transcervical excision, and what preoperative or intraoperative finding should change a routine benign-gland plan?
items.answer_text: Plan around the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve, facial vein/artery, lingual nerve, hypoglossal nerve, and Wharton duct while staying in the appropriate gland/fascial plane. Suspicion for malignancy, fixation, perineural symptoms, pathologic nodes, or gross nerve/adjacent-structure invasion should convert the case from simple inflammatory-gland excision to oncologic planning with adequate margins, nodal assessment as indicated, and explicit nerve-management strategy rather than unexpected piecemeal removal.

items.prompt: A 37-year-old with Graves disease has a large hypervascular goiter, compressive symptoms, and active medical treatment with methimazole. She is referred for thyroidectomy because of poor durable control and gland size. What must be optimized before surgery, when is preoperative iodide useful, how do the hypervascular gland and distorted anatomy change operative risk, and what should you do if the patient cannot be rendered conventionally euthyroid or develops concern for thyroid storm?
items.answer_text: Thyroidectomy for Graves disease or toxic goiter begins with control of thyrotoxicosis and a clear reason surgery is favored over continued medical therapy or radioactive iodine. Coordinate with endocrinology to achieve euthyroidism when feasible using a thionamide such as methimazole, add beta blockade for adrenergic symptoms and heart-rate control, and correct major comorbidity or volume/electrolyte problems. Short-course inorganic iodide can be used immediately before Graves thyroidectomy after antithyroid therapy has blocked new hormone synthesis; it decreases hormone release and can reduce gland vascularity. Do not give iodide as unopposed long-term therapy because iodine can provide substrate for new hormone synthesis after escape from the acute inhibitory effect. A large Graves gland is hypervascular and friable, so anticipate greater bleeding and difficult capsular-plane work. Marked enlargement, inflammation, substernal extension, or prior treatment can distort the recurrent laryngeal nerve and parathyroid relationships; meticulous capsular dissection, deliberate RLN identification/monitoring strategy, and preservation of parathyroid blood supply are essential. Obtain preoperative laryngeal examination when voice symptoms, prior neck surgery, invasive disease concern, or other risk makes baseline function important. If urgent surgery is required before conventional euthyroidism can be achieved, use multidisciplinary rapid preparation with beta blockade, thionamide when possible, iodide only after synthesis blockade, glucocorticoid, supportive therapy, and selected adjuncts such as cholestyramine according to severity and endocrine/anesthesia guidance. Thyroid storm is a clinical emergency marked by severe thyrotoxicosis with systemic decompensation such as hyperthermia, marked tachycardia/arrhythmia, CNS dysfunction, heart failure, or GI/hepatic manifestations; treat immediately with supportive resuscitation, beta blockade when hemodynamically appropriate, thionamide, then iodide after thionamide, glucocorticoid, and treatment of the precipitant. The senior principle is that surgical anatomy and endocrine physiology are inseparable: a technically excellent thyroidectomy is unsafe if uncontrolled hormone physiology is ignored, while indefinite delay may also be unsafe in a compressive or otherwise urgent gland.

items.prompt: A 30-year-old with Graves disease is scheduled for total thyroidectomy. Why is potassium iodide (SSKI) given for about 10 days before surgery?
choices: It replaces thyroid hormone after surgery
It reduces gland vascularity and hormone release
It destroys the thyroid like RAI

items.prompt: A 42-year-old has a 2.1-cm thyroid nodule with Bethesda III cytology, no suspicious cervical nodes, and intermediate ultrasound features. She wants to avoid unnecessary surgery but also asks whether a positive molecular panel means she should automatically have a total thyroidectomy. How should you integrate Bethesda category, ultrasound and clinical pretest risk, repeat sampling, molecular test performance, and patient preference into surveillance versus diagnostic lobectomy or a larger initial operation?
items.answer_text: Indeterminate cytology is a risk category, not a cancer diagnosis. Start by confirming the Bethesda category and integrating it with ultrasound pattern, nodule size and growth, cervical-node findings, radiation/family history, compressive symptoms, contralateral disease, and the local malignancy prevalence that determines the patient's pretest probability. For Bethesda III, repeat ultrasound-guided FNA is often reasonable because some nodules are reclassified; molecular testing or diagnostic surgery are alternatives when uncertainty remains. Bethesda IV more often proceeds to molecular risk stratification or diagnostic lobectomy because cytology cannot demonstrate capsular or vascular invasion required to diagnose follicular carcinoma. Molecular testing is useful only when its result is likely to change management. A high-sensitivity/high-negative-predictive-value 'rule-out' result can support surveillance in an appropriately selected low/intermediate-pretest-risk nodule, whereas a 'rule-in' result raises malignancy probability and, depending on the alteration, may provide biologic information. Predictive values are not fixed properties: they change with disease prevalence and pretest risk, so a negative test should not override worrisome nodes or invasive ultrasound findings, and a positive result is not synonymous with a mandate for total thyroidectomy. If surgery is chosen for an isolated indeterminate nodule without independent indication for total thyroidectomy, diagnostic lobectomy frequently provides diagnosis and treatment with less hypoparathyroidism and bilateral recurrent-laryngeal-nerve risk. The extent can increase when established cancer risk, tumor size/extent, suspicious nodes, contralateral disease, high-risk molecular features that truly alter the oncologic plan, or patient preference create an independent reason. Counsel about the possibility of completion thyroidectomy if final pathology reveals features requiring it. The senior question before ordering a molecular panel is: 'What will I do if it is negative, and what will I do if it is positive?' If neither answer changes, the test adds cost and ambiguity rather than decision value.

items.prompt: A 3 cm thyroid nodule has Bethesda IV (follicular neoplasm) cytology. Why can FNA not distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma?

A patient with a pathogenic RET variant is referred for thyroid management and reports episodic headaches and palpitations. What must be addressed before thyroid surgery, and how does the RET diagnosis change counseling and operative timing?
items.answer_text: Evaluate for pheochromocytoma before thyroid surgery and treat a catecholamine-secreting tumor first when present, because unrecognized pheochromocytoma creates major anesthetic risk. RET genotype and age-specific medullary-thyroid-cancer risk guide timing/extent of thyroid surgery, while biochemical evaluation for medullary thyroid carcinoma and hyperparathyroidism informs the operative plan. The diagnosis also requires genetic counseling and cascade testing of at-risk relatives rather than treating the index thyroid lesion as an isolated sporadic cancer.

items.prompt: A 3-year-old carries the familial RET M918T mutation. Why is thyroidectomy recommended within the first year of life?
choices: This codon causes very early aggressive MTC

items.prompt: A 46-year-old patient has calcium 14.6 mg/dL, markedly elevated PTH, nephrolithiasis, bone pain, a 3.5-cm firm inferior parathyroid-region mass and new hoarseness. As the senior resident planning surgery, explain how suspicion for parathyroid carcinoma changes preoperative workup, biopsy decisions, exposure and first-pass resection; how you handle an adherent or invaded recurrent laryngeal nerve, thyroid, trachea or esophagus; what intraoperative findings make you stop a routine parathyroidectomy; and how calcium/PTH kinetics, pathology, CDC73/parafibromin, recurrence and metastatic disease change postoperative management. Include explicit rescue and bailout decisions that prevent capsular rupture, uncontrolled nerve injury or incomplete oncologic surgery?
items.answer_text:
Foundation — parathyroid carcinoma is rare, but missing the diagnosis before or during the first operation can convert a potentially curable operation into a lifelong recurrence problem. Suspect carcinoma when primary hyperparathyroidism is unusually severe: marked hypercalcemia, very high PTH, renal and skeletal complications together, a palpable neck mass, hoarseness or other evidence of local invasion, or a large firm gland on imaging. None of these findings alone proves malignancy. The key resident move is to recognize a high-risk phenotype early enough to plan an oncologic operation rather than treating the lesion as a routine adenoma.

Preoperative localization and staging — confirm PTH-dependent hypercalcemia and stabilize dangerous hypercalcemia before elective surgery. Assess creatinine, phosphate, magnesium, vitamin D, ECG and volume status; severe symptomatic hypercalcemia may require IV isotonic fluid, antiresorptive therapy and calcimimetic treatment in addition to definitive tumor control. Ultrasound can show a large irregular hypoechoic lesion, loss of tissue planes or adjacent thyroid involvement. Multiphase CT or other cross-sectional imaging helps define tracheoesophageal, thyroid, vascular and nodal relationships; imaging is for operative planning and staging, not for histologic proof. Obtain a baseline laryngeal examination when voice is abnormal, prior surgery exists, or invasive disease approaches the recurrent laryngeal nerve. In a patient with suspected carcinoma, avoid percutaneous FNA or core biopsy of the parathyroid mass because cytology is unreliable for distinguishing adenoma from carcinoma and needle disruption risks fibrosis, diagnostic confusion and possible seeding.

Pathology and genetics — the diagnosis cannot be made from cellular atypia alone. Unequivocal invasive behavior such as vascular invasion, lymphatic invasion, perineural invasion, direct invasion into adjacent structures, nodal disease or metastasis establishes malignancy; parafibromin loss and CDC73 abnormalities can support the diagnosis and identify a hereditary cancer-predisposition pathway. Ask about family history of hyperparathyroidism, jaw tumors, renal or uterine tumors and young age. Germline CDC73 evaluation is particularly important when carcinoma is confirmed or strongly suspected. The durable distinction for boards is that a suspicious gland is managed by operative oncologic behavior before final pathology is available; definitive histologic classification follows the intact specimen.

First-operation anatomy — know the tracheoesophageal groove, recurrent laryngeal nerve, inferior thyroid artery, thyroid capsule, strap muscles, esophageal muscular wall, trachea and carotid sheath before committing to tumor mobilization. Carcinoma may feel gray-white, hard, fibrotic and adherent rather than the soft, reddish-brown, easily dissected appearance of a typical adenoma. The operation should proceed from normal tissue toward tumor so that planes are defined before the mass is manipulated. Do not grasp the tumor capsule, shell it out through an adhesive plane or rupture it to gain exposure. Capsular disruption and tumor spillage are major avoidable errors because local recurrence may be difficult to eradicate.

Primary surgery — when carcinoma is suspected and resection is feasible, the objective is an R0 en-bloc resection without capsular rupture. This commonly means removal of the involved parathyroid tumor with the ipsilateral thyroid lobe and any directly invaded soft tissue as one specimen rather than piecemeal parathyroidectomy. Adjacent strap muscle, esophageal muscularis or other structures are resected only when actually required for a clear gross margin; the operation is not a ritualized radical neck dissection. Current AAES guidance specifically discourages prophylactic central or lateral neck dissection in the absence of evidence of nodal disease, while contemporary ESES guidance emphasizes complete initial resection and individualized management of advanced local invasion. Therapeutic nodal dissection is appropriate for clinically or radiographically involved nodes.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve decision — this is a senior judgment point, not a memorized automatic sacrifice. If the nerve is grossly invaded and an R0 resection is otherwise achievable only by nerve sacrifice, oncologic clearance may require resection, with preoperative counseling about voice, aspiration and reconstruction options. If the nerve is merely adherent or entrapped yet functioning, the evidence is weak and expert consensus acknowledges a real tradeoff between R0 clearance and functional preservation. Identify the nerve in normal tissue, use monitoring as an adjunct when appropriate, avoid traction through tumor, and make the decision deliberately rather than tearing tumor off the nerve or sacrificing a functional nerve reflexively.

Rescue and bailout — if the presumed adenoma is unexpectedly rock-hard, densely adherent, invasive or inseparable from thyroid, stop the routine focused-parathyroidectomy script. Do not keep peeling until the capsule tears. Widen exposure, confirm anatomy, assess whether an oncologic en-bloc resection can be completed safely, and call an experienced endocrine/head-and-neck surgeon if needed. If gross invasion of trachea, esophagus, carotid or a functioning recurrent laryngeal nerve creates a morbidity decision that was not consented or cannot be managed safely, it is better to preserve the specimen and defer a planned multidisciplinary operation than to perform uncontrolled piecemeal debulking. Catastrophic bleeding is managed by compression, exposure and vascular control, not blind clamping around the recurrent laryngeal nerve or carotid sheath.

Intraoperative PTH and postoperative calcium — intraoperative PTH can document removal of functioning tissue, but a biochemical fall does not prove oncologic adequacy. Conversely, renal dysfunction can slow PTH clearance and blunt the expected kinetic drop, so failure to achieve a textbook percentage decline should be interpreted with renal function and the operative picture rather than prompting indiscriminate exploration. After removal of a highly functional carcinoma, anticipate profound hypocalcemia and hungry-bone physiology, especially in patients with severe bone disease. Monitor calcium, magnesium and phosphate, replace calcium and active vitamin D as needed, and distinguish expected postoperative hypocalcemia from persistent hypercalcemia suggesting residual functional disease.

Adjuvant therapy boundary — complete surgery is the only established curative modality. Routine adjuvant external-beam radiation after an R0 resection is not supported by strong evidence; older AAES guidance advises against routine use, whereas newer expert discussions allow individualized consideration after unresectable or grossly incomplete local disease because recurrence risk is high and data are sparse. This disagreement should be taught explicitly rather than flattened into a single rule. Cytotoxic chemotherapy has no established standard curative role. In recurrent or metastatic disease, the immediate threat is often uncontrolled PTH-mediated hypercalcemia rather than tumor volume itself.

Recurrent/metastatic disease — confirm biochemical recurrence with calcium and PTH trends and localize disease with neck and systemic imaging. Resectable locoregional or oligometastatic disease can merit repeat surgery when meaningful biochemical or disease control is achievable, but reoperations carry greater recurrent-nerve, hypoparathyroidism, esophageal, tracheal and vascular risk. Control hypercalcemia aggressively with hydration when appropriate, calcimimetics such as cinacalcet, antiresorptive therapy and other endocrine support. For progressive unresectable disease, contemporary ESMO guidance and recent reviews support molecular profiling and individualized systemic therapy in expert centers; antiangiogenic multikinase inhibitors have reported activity, but there is no universal FDA-approved parathyroid-carcinoma drug regimen that should be memorized as standard.

Surveillance — a patient is not “cured” because the calcium normalized at the postoperative visit. Parathyroid carcinoma can recur years later. Follow calcium and PTH long term, reassess the neck and distant sites when biochemistry or symptoms change, and integrate pathology features such as invasion and parafibromin/CDC73 findings. Rising PTH may precede major hypercalcemia and should trigger deliberate evaluation rather than reassurance.

Senior synthesis — before incision, answer four questions: Do the biochemical and imaging features make carcinoma plausible? Can the tumor be removed intact with a meaningful margin? Which adjacent structures, especially the recurrent laryngeal nerve, trachea, esophagus and carotid sheath, could force a morbidity tradeoff? What will make you stop rather than rupture the tumor? During surgery, the most dangerous cognitive error is continuing a routine adenoma operation after the anatomy tells you the diagnosis may be different. The oncologic priority is intact first-pass resection when safely achievable; the safety priority is controlled exposure and a planned bailout when achieving that margin would require an unconsented or technically uncontrolled sacrifice.

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the otolaryngology service. A 55-year-old with calcium 14.8 mg/dL and markedly elevated PTH has a firm 3.5-cm parathyroid-region mass that appears tethered to the ipsilateral thyroid and strap muscle. There is no proven nodal disease. What features should make you suspect parathyroid carcinoma before incision, what should you avoid diagnostically, how should the first operation differ from routine parathyroidectomy, and how do you manage hypercalcemia and recurrent or metastatic disease?
items.answer_text: Suspect parathyroid carcinoma when primary hyperparathyroidism is unusually severe—particularly marked hypercalcemia with very high PTH—when there is a large firm mass, local invasion/adherence, recurrent laryngeal nerve dysfunction, or recurrent disease after a prior suspicious lesion. No single calcium or PTH cutoff is diagnostic, and benign adenomas can be large, so the operative phenotype matters. Avoid percutaneous FNA of a suspected parathyroid carcinoma because cytology cannot reliably distinguish adenoma from carcinoma and needle/capsule violation can complicate the field or seed parathyroid tissue. The first operation offers the best chance for durable control. Resect the suspicious gland en bloc with its capsule intact and remove directly invaded/adherent adjacent tissue as required for a negative oncologic margin; an ipsilateral thyroid lobectomy or involved strap muscle may therefore be part of the specimen, but routine sacrifice of uninvolved structures is not the goal. Do not rupture or shell out the tumor. Assess the recurrent laryngeal nerve carefully and obtain preoperative laryngeal examination when voice symptoms, invasive imaging, prior neck surgery, or other risk makes baseline function important. Therapeutic compartment-oriented nodal dissection is appropriate for clinically involved nodes; routine prophylactic lateral neck dissection without evidence of nodal disease does not improve the operation. Severe hypercalcemia is itself an urgent management problem: restore volume, use calcitonin for rapid temporary effect when needed, antiresorptive therapy as appropriate, and cinacalcet for ongoing PTH-mediated calcium control, while definitive resection is planned. Pathologic diagnosis depends on unequivocal invasive/metastatic features rather than atypia alone. Recurrent or metastatic disease is managed multidisciplinary; reoperation/metastasectomy can be valuable when resectable because controlling functional tumor burden may substantially improve hypercalcemia even when cure is unlikely. Consider CDC73-related disease and genetic counseling/testing when age, family history, jaw/renal/uterine findings, pathology, or clinical context suggests a hereditary syndrome. The senior principle is intact first-pass oncologic resection plus aggressive calcium control: capsule violation converts a potentially local problem into a difficult recurrent one.

items.prompt: A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. Reoperative Hyperparathyroidism is being considered. reoperative primary hyperparathyroidism as a FAILURE/RECURRENCE problem, not simply another presentation of untreated PHPT. Persistent PHPT means failure to achieve normocalcemia within 6 months of parathyroidectomy; recurrent PHPT means hypercalcemia returning after a normocalcemic interval of more than 6 months. When is Reoperative Hyperparathyroidism indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Re-exploration should be TARGET-DIRECTED whenever possible. Enter through the safest anticipated plane, use the prior operative map to predict scar and residual anatomy, and identify/protect the recurrent laryngeal nerve before aggressive dissection around a suspected gland. Intraoperative PTH is especially useful to test whether the localized target explains the biochemistry and whether additional hyperfunctioning tissue remains. Search ectopic or mediastinal sites according to embryology rather than escalating to indiscriminate bilateral scar dissection. If multigland disease is encountered, preserve a viable source of parathyroid function whenever oncologically appropriate; autotransplantation/cryopreservation considerations depend on the amount and quality of remaining tissue and institutional practice. The operative endpoint is durable biochemical cure with acceptable nerve/parathyroid function—not simply removal of something that looks enlarged.

items.prompt: A patient remains hypercalcemic with elevated PTH after prior parathyroid surgery, but the prior operative note is incomplete and current ultrasound is nondiagnostic. What must be established before reoperative exploration, and which steps reduce the risk of an unsuccessful or unnecessarily hazardous scarred-neck operation?
items.answer_text: First reconfirm true biochemical primary hyperparathyroidism and review the prior operative report, pathology, intraoperative PTH data, and any imaging to understand what glands were found or left behind. Obtain preoperative laryngeal examination and pursue high-quality localization with complementary studies such as ultrasound, sestamibi-based imaging, or 4D CT according to the case; selective venous sampling is reserved for difficult nonlocalizing situations. Reoperation should be targeted when benefit justifies the higher recurrent-laryngeal-nerve and hypoparathyroidism risk, with explicit consideration of ectopic or supernumerary glands, mediastinal disease, parathyromatosis, and hereditary/multigland physiology rather than blind bilateral scarred-neck exploration.

items.prompt: A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. Postoperative hypocalcemia after thyroid/parathyroid surgery has several mechanisms and should not be treated as one diagnosis. After thyroidectomy, transient hypoparathyroidism from devascularization/manipulation is common; permanent hypoparathyroidism is less common. After parathyroidectomy for severe hyperparathyroid bone disease, hungry-bone syndrome causes rapid skeletal uptake of calcium, phosphate, and magnesium despite removal of the PTH source. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Mild/asymptomatic postoperative hypocalcemia is managed with oral calcium, often plus calcitriol when PTH is low or risk is high. Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia requires monitored IV calcium with magnesium correction as needed, followed by oral replacement. Hungry-bone syndrome can require large and prolonged calcium/calcitriol replacement because the sink is the skeleton; do not mistake the ongoing requirement for immediate operative failure. After thyroidectomy, taper replacement according to recovering PTH/calcium rather than leaving every transient patient on indefinite therapy.

items.prompt: After removal of a 4 g parathyroid adenoma in a patient with osteitis fibrosa cystica, serum calcium falls to 6.8 mg/dL on day 2 despite a normal PTH. Phosphate and magnesium are also low. What explains this?
choices: Avid mineral uptake by demineralized bone
Inadvertent removal of all four glands
Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve

items.prompt: A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. pleomorphic adenoma (PA) and Warthin tumor as common benign parotid neoplasms, but do not treat 'benign parotid mass' as one disease. PA is classically a slow-growing, painless, firm/mobile mass and often occurs in younger or middle-aged adults; Warthin tumor commonly arises in the parotid tail in older adults, has a strong smoking association, and may be bilateral or multifocal. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Management follows natural history and diagnostic certainty. A resectable PA is generally offered surgery because it tends to grow, can recur after inadequate removal, and carries a small but clinically meaningful long-term risk of carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma. A confidently diagnosed, asymptomatic Warthin tumor may be observed in selected patients, especially when comorbidity or operative morbidity outweighs benefit; growth, symptoms, cosmetic burden, diagnostic uncertainty, or patient preference favor excision. Smoking cessation should be encouraged in Warthin patients because of the strong association and broader health benefit.

items.prompt: A 45-year-old had a pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid tail enucleated 8 years ago. She now has multiple small nodules in the parotid bed. Why did the tumor recur?
choices: Malignant transformation of the original tumor
New tumors arising in intraparotid nodes

items.prompt: A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. sialadenitis as a syndrome of salivary-gland inflammation or impaired drainage, then use the tempo and symptom pattern to decide what is driving it. Acute bacterial disease usually causes a tender, swollen gland with erythema, fever or systemic symptoms and may express purulence from Stensen or Wharton duct. Recurrent swelling and pain that predictably worsen with meals strongly suggest obstruction. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat the cause, not the label. Acute uncomplicated bacterial sialadenitis is managed with hydration, warm compresses, gland massage, sialogogues, meticulous oral hygiene and antibiotics directed at typical oral flora/staphylococcal pathogens and local resistance patterns; drain a true abscess and escalate care for sepsis, airway/deep-neck extension or failure of medical therapy. Obstructive disease requires restoration of drainage—conservative measures for mild episodes, then stone extraction or sialendoscopy when obstruction persists or recurs. Viral disease is generally supportive unless a specific infection changes management. Sjögren care focuses on preserving ocular and oral function: frequent hydration, saliva substitutes/stimulation when appropriate, aggressive dental prevention/fluoride and candidiasis surveillance, ophthalmologic dry-eye therapy, avoidance of unnecessary xerogenic drugs, and rheumatology involvement for systemic disease.

items.prompt: A 78-year-old is dehydrated 3 days after hip surgery and receiving an anticholinergic. She develops a painful, swollen parotid, and massage expresses pus from Stensen duct. What is the main predisposing mechanism?
choices: An allergic reaction to anesthetic agents
Low salivary flow permitting ascending bacteria
A flare of underlying Sjögren syndrome

items.prompt: A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. a this condition as a mucus-extravasation lesion arising overwhelmingly from the sublingual gland rather than as a generic 'floor-of-mouth cyst.' A simple this condition is usually a painless, fluctuant, translucent or blue lateral floor-of-mouth swelling that can elevate the tongue when large. A plunging this condition may present mainly as a soft upper-neck/submandibular swelling with little oral component. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Manage the mucus source rather than treating only the collection. Observation can be reasonable for a small, minimally symptomatic lesion in selected patients, but repeated needle aspiration alone has a high recurrence problem because the leaking sublingual gland remains. For persistent, symptomatic, recurrent, or plunging disease, definitive treatment generally targets the ipsilateral sublingual gland, with decompression/evacuation of the ranula as needed. Marsupialization or micromarsupialization can be considered in selected simple oral lesions, especially when minimizing operative morbidity matters, but recurrence risk and the likelihood of needing subsequent gland-directed treatment should be part of counseling.

items.prompt: A 20-year-old has a soft, painless submandibular neck swelling and a bluish floor-of-mouth cyst that returned after marsupialization. What is the definitive treatment?

A patient is seen in endocrine/head-and-neck surgery clinic. TED severity and inflammatory activity are different axes; proptosis, diplopia/exposure and optic neuropathy do not all require the same treatment. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Coordinate thyroid control, smoking cessation and activity/severity-directed medical/ophthalmic therapy. Urgent vision-threatening disease is different from rehabilitative surgery after inactive disease.

items.prompt: A 45-year-old smoker with Graves disease has new proptosis and intermittent diplopia. Her thyroid function is controlled with methimazole, and RAI is being considered. Why is smoking cessation especially important?
choices: Smoking blocks the action of methimazole

items.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. You are considering AOM / OME / Tympanostomy Decisions. Separate acute otitis media (AOM) from otitis media with effusion (OME). AOM requires acute symptoms plus middle-ear inflammation/effusion, classically a bulging tympanic membrane or new otorrhea not from OE; OME is fluid without the acute inflammatory syndrome. Recurrent AOM and chronic OME are different decision pathways. When is AOM / OME / Tympanostomy Decisions the right test or evaluation, what information does it provide, and what limitation or pitfall should you remember when interpreting it?
items.answer_text: Diagnose AOM by pneumatic otoscopy/otoscopy rather than symptoms alone. For persistent OME, document duration, laterality, hearing status, tympanic-membrane structural change, speech/language/developmental risk and school/listening impact. Audiology is important when OME persists or hearing impact is suspected. Do not obtain routine CT for uncomplicated middle-ear effusion. Recurrent AOM candidacy for tubes depends importantly on whether middle-ear effusion is present at the time of assessment rather than episode count alone.

items.prompt: A 2-year-old in daycare has had four episodes of acute otitis media in 6 months. Why is otitis media so much more common in young children than in adults?

A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. You are considering Pediatric OSA / Adenotonsillar Disease. Pediatric OSA is repetitive upper-airway obstruction during sleep and is not diagnosed simply by tonsil size or snoring. Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is common, but obesity, craniofacial restriction, neuromuscular disease, Down syndrome, mucopolysaccharidosis, nasal obstruction, laryngomalacia and multilevel collapse change severity and treatment response. When is Pediatric OSA / Adenotonsillar Disease the right test or evaluation, what information does it provide, and what limitation or pitfall should you remember when interpreting it?
items.answer_text: Polysomnography is the gold standard when diagnostic/severity uncertainty matters and is particularly important in high-risk children or when symptoms/exam disagree. Interpret AHI with oxygen nadir, CO2/hypoventilation, arousal burden and comorbidity rather than using one number in isolation. Preoperative assessment should identify age, obesity, severe PSG findings, craniofacial/neuromuscular syndromes and cardiopulmonary disease that increase postoperative respiratory risk.

items.prompt: A child has a recurrent lateral neck swelling that becomes tender during upper-respiratory infections. The family reports that it has been present intermittently since infancy. How should location and embryology guide the differential and workup, and when should infection be controlled before definitive surgery?
items.answer_text: Start with age, exact midline-versus-lateral location, relationship to the hyoid and sternocleidomastoid, movement with swallowing or tongue protrusion, skin pits/drainage, compressibility, and history of infection. Ultrasound is often a useful first study for superficial cystic lesions, while CT or MRI is selected when deep extent, airway relationship, vascular anatomy, or a complex malformation must be defined. The differential includes thyroglossal duct cyst, branchial anomalies, dermoid, lymphatic/vascular malformation, thymic lesions, and neoplasm depending on anatomy. Treat acute cellulitis or abscess first when feasible rather than performing elective tract dissection through uncontrolled infection. Definitive surgery should remove the relevant embryologic tract/relationship—not merely the visible cyst—to reduce recurrence; vascular or lymphatic malformations may instead require observation, sclerotherapy, surgery, or combined treatment according to symptoms and anatomy.

items.prompt: A 4-year-old has a painless midline neck mass just below the hyoid that rises when she sticks out her tongue. Which embryologic structure failed to involute?

A patient is evaluated by the otolaryngology service. A previously healthy 2-year-old has a witnessed choking episode while eating peanuts. The severe coughing settles, but unilateral wheeze and decreased breath sounds persist; chest radiography is read as normal. How should a resident decide whether further imaging or bronchoscopy is needed, what features make this an immediate airway-rescue problem, how should rigid bronchoscopy be planned with anesthesia, and what should the team do if ventilation suddenly worsens or the foreign body migrates during extraction?
items.answer_text:
Foundation: treat the aspiration history as major diagnostic evidence. A witnessed choking event followed by persistent unilateral wheeze, asymmetric breath sounds, focal recurrent pneumonia, unexplained cough, or stridor can represent an airway foreign body even when the child later appears comfortable. Many aspirated objects are radiolucent, so a normal chest radiograph does not exclude aspiration. Inspiratory/expiratory films or bilateral decubitus views may show unilateral air trapping, atelectasis, mediastinal shift, or a radiopaque object, but imaging should answer an uncertainty question—not erase a convincing clinical event. CT can be useful in selected stable equivocal cases when it is likely to avoid an unnecessary bronchoscopy, but it should not delay endoscopic evaluation when suspicion remains high.

Application: first separate the stable child from the child with impending or complete obstruction. Severe stridor, rapidly increasing work of breathing, cyanosis, inability to ventilate, altered mental status, or a clearly mobile/proximal object is an airway emergency. In a stable child with a convincing aspiration history, rigid bronchoscopy is both the diagnostic and definitive removal platform in most pediatric cases because the rigid scope provides a ventilating airway and permits secure instrumentation. Flexible bronchoscopy may have a diagnostic or adjunctive role in selected settings, but it should not become a reason to delay definitive rigid removal when clinical suspicion is high.

Before entering the OR, the surgeon and anesthesiologist should agree on the suspected location and object, bronchoscope sizes, optical forceps and backup retrieval instruments, whether spontaneous or controlled ventilation best fits the case and local expertise, how ventilation will be maintained through the bronchoscope, and what the rescue sequence will be if the airway is lost. There is no single ventilation technique that is correct for every foreign body; the senior principle is shared planning that minimizes coughing, air trapping, migration, hypoxemia, and repeated traumatic attempts while preserving the surgeon's ability to see and control the object.

During extraction, expose the object completely enough to understand its axis and surrounding edema before grasping it. Avoid blind instrumentation that can push a partially obstructing object distally or convert it into a complete obstruction. Select a grasp that controls the object rather than merely pinching a fragment; friable organic material may break apart and require multiple pieces to be removed. As the object passes the glottis, keep the bronchoscope, forceps, and object coordinated so the foreign body is not lost at the cords. After removal, re-inspect both bronchial trees for a second object, retained fragments, mucosal injury, bleeding, purulence, or edema before declaring the procedure finished.

Senior decision/rescue: if oxygenation or ventilation deteriorates, stop repetitive extraction attempts and restore a ventilating airway first. Withdraw obstructing instruments, re-establish ventilation through the rigid bronchoscope, suction blood/secretions, and reassess object position. If a proximal object has migrated into a complete tracheal obstruction and cannot be immediately removed, an experienced bronchoscopist may need to displace it into one mainstem bronchus to permit contralateral-lung ventilation as a rescue maneuver while definitive removal is reorganized; this is a bailout, not a routine technique. The team must also be prepared for pneumothorax, airway edema, laryngospasm/bronchospasm, bleeding, or an unexpectedly sharp object. If endoscopic control cannot be maintained, escalate early to the institution's pediatric difficult-airway and surgical rescue plan rather than persisting with repeated blind attempts. The governing principle is oxygenation first, controlled extraction second.

items.prompt: A 2-year-old had a choking episode while eating peanuts 2 days ago and now has a cough and right-sided wheeze. Inspiratory chest X-ray is normal, but the expiratory film shows a hyperinflated right lung. What is the mechanism?

A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Treat this as a candidacy question, not a second AOM/OME lesson. The decision is whether a child with a defined middle-ear disease phenotype is likely to benefit from ventilation tubes now. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Use a guideline-style decision: chronic bilateral OME with hearing difficulty is a strong tube phenotype; chronic OME with meaningful attributable symptoms may also justify tubes; recurrent AOM with effusion supports candidacy, whereas recurrent AOM without effusion generally does not.

items.prompt: A 3-year-old has had bilateral middle-ear effusions for 4 months with a 30 dB conductive hearing loss and speech delay. Why are tubes indicated?
choices: Any effusion lasting more than 2 weeks
To prevent cholesteatoma in all children
To allow topical antibiotics for effusion

items.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Separate conductive, SN and auditory-neural patterns; timing matters because language development is time-sensitive. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Early amplification/CI/communication support and developmental services; treat reversible conductive disease.

items.prompt: An 18-month-old has newly diagnosed bilateral profound sensorineural hearing loss. Family history includes sudden cardiac death. Which test must be included in the workup?

A newborn fails the hearing screen and has a positive saliva CMV PCR at 12 days of life. The infant otherwise appears well. The family asks whether this proves congenital CMV, whether antiviral treatment will preserve hearing, and why repeat hearing tests are needed even if the next audiogram is normal. What should be confirmed now, what findings change antiviral discussions, and how should hearing surveillance and rehabilitation proceed?
items.answer_text: First confirm congenital infection within the diagnostic window. A positive saliva PCR should generally be confirmed with urine PCR because saliva can be contaminated by CMV in breast milk; testing obtained within the first 21 days of life distinguishes congenital from postnatally acquired infection. After that window, retrospective dried-blood-spot testing may sometimes help but a negative result does not reliably exclude congenital CMV because sensitivity is limited. Evaluate the infant for symptomatic disease with the pediatric/infectious-disease team, including neurologic findings, growth, platelet/liver abnormalities, eye disease, and neuroimaging when indicated. Antiviral evidence is strongest for symptomatic congenital CMV, particularly disease with central-nervous-system involvement; valganciclovir-based treatment requires blood-count and hepatic monitoring because neutropenia and other toxicities occur. Treatment of an otherwise asymptomatic infant with isolated sensorineural hearing loss remains an area in which evidence and institutional practice are evolving, so ENT should not promise hearing preservation or start therapy solely from a failed hearing screen without multidisciplinary confirmation of disease category and current protocol. Hearing loss from congenital CMV may be unilateral or bilateral, fluctuate, appear after a normal newborn test, or progress over childhood. Therefore obtain diagnostic ABR/audiology promptly after a failed screen and continue scheduled surveillance even when thresholds normalize. Rehabilitation should follow functional loss without waiting for the disease course to declare itself: optimize hearing aids or bone-conduction options when appropriate, provide early-intervention and speech-language support, and evaluate cochlear-implant candidacy for severe-to-profound loss. The senior pearl is that the 21-day clock is a diagnostic emergency, not necessarily an antiviral-treatment mandate.

items.prompt: A newborn fails the hearing screen. CMV PCR on saliva is positive at 14 days of age. Why is testing within the first 3 weeks essential?
choices: Antivirals are only available in the first week
Hearing loss always appears after 3 weeks
It distinguishes congenital from postnatal infection

items.prompt: A 5-year-old has a midline cystic mass at the hyoid that rises with swallowing and tongue protrusion. What is the initial management, and which findings would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Ultrasound first, to confirm a cyst and a normal orthotopic thyroid, then elective Sistrunk (cyst + central hyoid + tongue-base core) when quiescent. Change course if: there is no orthotopic thyroid or the mass is solid (TSH/free T4, scintigraphy, endocrinology; do not excise); the cyst is infected (antibiotics +/- aspiration, avoid I&D, operate after resolution); there is a solid, calcified, or vascular component (FNA of the solid part, evaluate thyroid and nodes); it recurs after surgery (re-image, then wide central neck dissection).

items.prompt: A 6-year-old has a recurrently infected thyroglossal duct cyst. Why does the Sistrunk procedure remove the central portion of the hyoid bone?
choices: The tract runs through the hyoid

items.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Lateral neck pits/cysts/fistulae follow reproducible embryologic pathways; first/second/third/fourth anomalies have distinct relationships. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat infection first; definitive excision after inflammation settles when indicated.

items.prompt: A 7-year-old has a draining pit along the anterior border of the lower third of the SCM. The tract passes between the internal and external carotid arteries. Where does it end?

A 3-year-old with a known trans-spatial cervicofacial lymphatic malformation presents after a viral illness with rapid enlargement, pain, dysphagia and new noisy breathing. MRI previously showed mixed macro- and microcystic disease extending through the submandibular space and tongue base. As the senior pediatric ENT resident, explain the immediate airway and acute-flare priorities; how current lymphatic-malformation classification, cyst morphology, anatomic extent and symptoms guide observation, sclerotherapy, surgery or systemic therapy; what makes tongue-base/pharyngeal disease and post-sclerotherapy swelling dangerous; and when PIK3CA testing or targeted therapy changes management. Include specific rescue, stop/stage and counseling decisions?
items.answer_text:
Foundation — a lymphatic malformation is a low-flow vascular malformation, not a neoplasm and not simply a 'cystic hygroma.' Head-and-neck lesions can cross fascial spaces, insinuate around nerves and vessels, involve the floor of mouth, tongue, pharynx or larynx, and change dramatically with infection, inflammation or intralesional hemorrhage. Current ISSVA terminology should be used rather than outdated tumor language. Morphology is clinically useful: macrocystic disease contains larger drainable cysts, microcystic disease is infiltrative with many small channels, and mixed lesions contain both. The label predicts treatment behavior but does not replace an anatomic and functional map.

Immediate priority — the child with rapid enlargement, dysphagia and new noisy breathing is first an airway patient. Assess work of breathing, stridor/stertor, voice/cry, secretion handling, oxygenation and progression. Examine the oral cavity and floor of mouth and use flexible nasopharyngolaryngoscopy when it can be performed safely to define tongue-base, pharyngeal and laryngeal narrowing. Do not send a tenuous child away for a perfect MRI before securing a deteriorating airway. Escalate early to pediatric anesthesia/PICU and the vascular-anomalies team. If ventilation or intubation becomes unsafe, use the institution's difficult-airway pathway and prepare a surgical airway rescue appropriate to the child's anatomy rather than repeating traumatic attempts through a progressively narrowed upper airway.

Acute inflammatory or hemorrhagic flare — infection, viral inflammation and bleeding into cysts can abruptly increase lesion volume. Treat a true bacterial infection when supported clinically; provide hydration, analgesia and anti-inflammatory support while monitoring the airway. A hemorrhagic cyst can be painful and rapidly enlarging without bacterial infection. The resident should not reflexively aspirate or incise every enlarging LM: uncontrolled procedures can bleed, infect the lesion, injure traversing structures and offer only transient decompression. Drainage or urgent image-guided intervention is selected when anatomy, airway compromise or a dominant accessible cyst makes decompression beneficial and the procedure can be controlled.
