Imaging and map — ultrasound can characterize superficial cystic spaces and guide procedures, but MRI is the workhorse for defining deep trans-spatial extent, macro/microcystic components and relationships to tongue, pharynx, orbit, parotid, neurovascular structures and mediastinum. CT is useful selectively when speed, airway instability, acute hemorrhage, calcification/bone detail or another diagnosis makes it preferable. Imaging is not an excuse to delay airway rescue. Before any definitive intervention, know whether the lesion is circumscribed enough to treat as a target or infiltrative enough that the treatment goal must be symptom/function control rather than complete eradication.

Observation — an asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic lesion with stable function can be observed, especially when intervention would create more morbidity than the malformation. Observation is active: families need a flare plan and follow-up for growth, pain, recurrent infection/bleeding, dysphagia, speech effects, sleep-disordered breathing, cosmetic burden and psychosocial impact. Growth or a new symptom changes the risk-benefit calculation; 'congenital' does not mean harmless, and 'benign' does not mean intervention-free.

Sclerotherapy — image-guided sclerotherapy is commonly first-line procedural therapy for accessible macrocystic components because they can be aspirated and exposed to a sclerosant. Results are less predictable in diffuse microcystic disease, although specialized techniques and multimodal treatment can still help. Choice of sclerosant belongs to an experienced vascular-anomalies/interventional-radiology team because agents differ in inflammatory swelling, nerve/skin toxicity, pulmonary risk and local practice. The senior ENT role is especially important when the lesion is in the tongue, floor of mouth, pharynx or upper airway: post-sclerotherapy edema can transiently make the airway much worse even when the treatment is ultimately effective. Plan airway protection, observation level and rescue before injecting—not after swelling develops.

Surgery — surgery is appropriate when a discrete or surgically favorable component causes important functional/cosmetic morbidity, when residual disease after other therapy has a correctable anatomic target, when tissue diagnosis is needed because the diagnosis is uncertain, or when urgent decompression/control cannot otherwise be achieved. Complete excision is not always the goal. Diffuse microcystic LM may encase the facial, hypoglossal, lingual or other nerves, salivary structures and major vessels; chasing microscopic disease can create paralysis, dysphagia, hemorrhage or disfigurement. A planned subtotal/debulking operation may be the expert choice when it relieves airway, swallowing or bulk morbidity while preserving critical structures. Stop rather than converting symptom-control surgery into an uncontrolled nerve or vessel sacrifice for the sake of an imaging endpoint.

Macro versus micro versus mixed — macrocystic lesions generally respond better to percutaneous sclerotherapy; microcystic disease is more infiltrative and often needs multimodal therapy; mixed disease should be decomposed into treatable components rather than assigned one modality globally. The 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis reinforces that response differs by morphology and that both sclerotherapy and surgery have roles. It should not be misread as a mandate that every lesion be excised or that one sclerosant is universally superior, because anatomy, functional risk, treatment definitions and study heterogeneity matter.

Systemic therapy — sirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, is used off-label in selected extensive, symptomatic or refractory lymphatic/combined vascular malformations when local therapy is inadequate or excessively morbid. It is not a casual first-line medication for a small asymptomatic macrocyst. Treatment requires a vascular-anomalies team and monitoring for immunosuppression/infection, mucositis, cytopenias, lipid abnormalities and other toxicities. The pediatric head-and-neck systematic review is encouraging but emphasizes limited high-quality evidence, so teach individualized risk-benefit selection rather than a universal regimen.

PIK3CA and alpelisib — somatic PIK3CA pathway mutations explain an important subset of lymphatic malformations and PIK3CA-related overgrowth phenotypes. Consider lesional molecular testing when severe, extensive, atypical or refractory disease may change systemic-therapy options; blood testing can be falsely negative for mosaic disease. Alpelisib is a PI3K-alpha inhibitor with prospective evidence of benefit in children with PIK3CA-associated head-and-neck LM/overgrowth. The FDA regulatory boundary matters: Vijoice is approved for adults and children age 2 years and older with severe manifestations of PIK3CA-Related Overgrowth Spectrum requiring systemic therapy. That is not the same statement as 'alpelisib is FDA-approved for all lymphatic malformations.' A child with isolated LM needs appropriate phenotype/genotype and specialist assessment before extrapolating the PROS indication.

Airway-specific planning — oral tongue, floor-of-mouth, base-of-tongue, pharyngeal and laryngeal involvement can produce chronic sleep obstruction or acute airway compromise during a flare or after treatment. Preoperative endoscopic airway mapping can change where and how treatment is delivered. A lesion that looks modest externally can be dangerous internally. For a procedure expected to swell a narrow tongue base, discuss elective intubation, delayed extubation and PICU observation in advance. If the child cannot safely be extubated because of edema or residual obstruction, maintaining the airway is not a treatment failure; premature extubation can be catastrophic.

Hemorrhage and infection danger zones — rapid expansion after trauma or spontaneously may represent intralesional hemorrhage. Obtain blood counts/coagulation testing when clinically indicated and define whether the child is stable before intervention. Significant systemic infection, cellulitis or abscess-like complication requires antimicrobial/source-control reasoning, but routine antibiotics do not shrink sterile LM inflammation. Avoid blind transoral incision into a vascular-anomaly field. If airway deterioration, uncontrolled bleeding, sepsis or a threatened neurovascular structure emerges, stabilize that threat first and defer elective lesion-reduction goals.

Recurrence and counseling — recurrence or residual disease is common because diffuse LM rarely respects surgical planes. Set goals in terms of breathing, swallowing, speech, pain, infection/bleeding frequency, sleep, function and appearance rather than promising radiographic eradication. Families should understand that several staged sclerotherapy sessions, selective surgery and/or systemic therapy may be needed. Treatment changes as the child grows and as molecular options evolve.

Senior synthesis — make seven decisions: AIRWAY: is this stable, threatened or already failing? FLARE: infection, hemorrhage or sterile inflammation? MAP: which spaces and upper-airway structures are involved? MORPHOLOGY: macro-, micro- or mixed cystic disease? GOAL: observation versus symptom/function control versus a discrete correctable target? MODALITY: sclerotherapy, surgery, systemic therapy or a staged combination? GENETICS: would PIK3CA/other molecular testing change systemic therapy? The expert does not chase every cyst. The expert protects the airway and neurovascular function, targets the component most responsible for morbidity, anticipates treatment-induced swelling and changes course when the intervention becomes more dangerous than the malformation.

items.prompt: An infant has a large, soft, transilluminating left neck mass present since birth. MRI shows several large fluid-filled cysts without solid enhancement. Why is this lesion a good candidate for sclerotherapy?
choices: It is a malignant lesion needing chemotherapy
Microcystic lesions respond better than macrocystic

items.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. this condition is dynamic inspiratory supraglottic collapse, usually presenting in early infancy with inspiratory stridor that worsens with feeding, agitation or supine positioning. Most cases are mild and self-limited, but severity is defined by physiology—not loudness of stridor. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Observe and counsel families for mild disease with adequate growth and no significant hypoxemia/feeding morbidity. Address feeding strategy and comorbid conditions; acid suppression should not be automatic without a clear indication. Supraglottoplasty is indicated for severe laryngomalacia causing clinically important obstruction, cyanotic/apneic events, failure to thrive, significant feeding/aspiration compromise or cardiopulmonary consequence. Persistent OSA after supraglottoplasty requires reassessment for residual/multilevel obstruction rather than assuming the first surgery was technically inadequate.

items.prompt: A 6-week-old has inspiratory stridor that worsens with feeding, crying, and lying supine. She feeds well and is gaining weight along her curve. Laryngoscopy shows an omega-shaped epiglottis and short aryepiglottic folds. What is the best management?

A 3-month-old with inspiratory stridor has flexible laryngoscopy showing shortened aryepiglottic folds and redundant arytenoid mucosa prolapsing into the glottis. The infant now has poor weight gain, feeding-associated desaturations, and increasing work of breathing despite conservative reflux/feeding optimization. Which findings make this laryngomalacia severe enough for supraglottoplasty, what anatomy should be treated or preserved, when should you look for synchronous airway disease, and which postoperative problems require escalation?
items.answer_text: Most laryngomalacia is observed because symptoms peak in infancy and improve with maturation, but supraglottoplasty is considered when dynamic supraglottic collapse produces clinically important obstruction or functional consequences such as failure to thrive, recurrent cyanosis or hypoxemia, significant retractions, severe obstructive sleep apnea, pulmonary hypertension, or feeding/aspiration morbidity attributable to the collapse. Flexible awake laryngoscopy establishes the dynamic diagnosis; direct laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy are appropriate when the presentation is atypical, the severity is disproportionate, intubation history or other findings suggest a second lesion, or the child is proceeding to surgery and the team needs a complete airway assessment. Operatively, tailor treatment to the collapsing structure: divide pathologically shortened aryepiglottic folds and selectively reduce redundant supra-arytenoid/arytenoid mucosa while preserving enough mucosa and supraglottic tissue for sensation, swallowing protection, and scar-free healing. Avoid indiscriminate bilateral deep resection because opposing raw surfaces can produce supraglottic stenosis; also respect the interarytenoid region and neurovascular structures. Postoperatively monitor airway edema/obstruction, oxygen requirement, stridor trajectory, feeding and aspiration, pain/hydration, and need for respiratory support. Children with neurologic disease, significant cardiopulmonary comorbidity, synchronous airway lesions, severe preoperative OSA/hypoxemia, or very young age may need higher-acuity observation and have higher revision or persistent-symptom risk. Failure to improve should trigger reassessment for residual collapse, synchronous lesions, aspiration, neurologic tone abnormalities, or another airway level rather than reflexively repeating the same resection. The senior principle is anatomy-directed reduction of the obstructing tissue while preserving protective supraglottic function; the operation treats severe physiology, not stridor volume alone.

items.prompt: A 3-month-old with severe laryngomalacia has failure to thrive and oxygen desaturations during feeds. Endoscopy shows tight, short aryepiglottic folds pulling the epiglottis into an omega shape. Why does dividing the folds help?

A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Pediatric Subglottic Stenosis is being considered. this condition may be congenital or acquired; acquired disease most commonly follows intubation injury, with risk influenced by tube size, duration, motion/trauma, infection and host factors rather than duration alone. Biphasic stridor, recurrent 'croup,' extubation failure or inability to tolerate an age-appropriate ETT should raise suspicion. Congenital SGS is present without prior airway instrumentation and may reflect abnormal cricoid development;. When is Pediatric Subglottic Stenosis indicated, what key anatomy or decision points determine how you perform it, and what would make you change the operative plan?
items.answer_text: Choose endoscopic treatment for favorable short/soft stenosis where the framework is adequate; choose LTR when expansion can restore lumen while preserving the segment; choose CTR for selected severe mature stenosis where resection offers a better durable airway. Single-stage LTR requires confidence that the reconstructed airway can support extubation without a protective trach; double-stage reconstruction retains/stents the tracheostomy when airway, pulmonary, neurologic or multilevel factors make that unsafe. Preserve recurrent laryngeal nerves and cricoarytenoid function; a technically larger airway with new glottic dysfunction is not a success.

items.prompt: A 2-year-old intubated for 3 weeks as a premature neonate has biphasic stridor. Endoscopy shows 60 percent subglottic narrowing. Why does the subglottis narrow after prolonged intubation?

A tracheostomy-dependent child with subglottic stenosis is being considered for laryngotracheal reconstruction after prior endoscopic treatment. What information must be established before committing to reconstruction, and which findings would make you delay, stage, or choose a different airway strategy?
items.answer_text: Map the entire airway endoscopically, including stenosis grade/length, glottic mobility, posterior glottis, trachea, and any multilevel disease, while assessing pulmonary reserve, aspiration/swallowing, reflux or inflammatory contributors, infection, and the child's ability to tolerate postoperative airway management. Poor pulmonary reserve, uncontrolled aspiration/infection, severe multilevel obstruction, significant glottic dysfunction, or an airway that cannot safely support the planned postoperative course should prompt optimization, staged reconstruction, or an alternative approach rather than forcing a single-stage plan.

items.prompt: A 4-year-old with grade III subglottic stenosis undergoes laryngotracheal reconstruction with anterior and posterior costal cartilage grafts. Why is the airway stented (or kept intubated) afterward?
choices: To deliver steroids into the subglottis
To hold the grafts in place as mucosa heals

items.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Neonatal bilateral obstruction causes cyclical cyanosis/respiratory distress (worse with feeding, relieved by crying); unilateral disease presents later with chronic unilateral symptoms such as persistent unilateral rhinorrhea or congestion, sometimes not recognized until childhood. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Secure neonatal airway first; endoscopic repair timing/technique depends on laterality and stability.

items.prompt: A newborn has episodes of cyanosis that improve when she cries and worsen during feeding. A 6 French catheter cannot be passed through either nostril. Why does crying relieve the cyanosis?
choices: Crying forces the atretic plates open

items.prompt: A 4-year-old has fever, torticollis, drooling, muffled voice, and worsening oral intake. CT shows a 2.8-cm retropharyngeal collection with rim enhancement and mild airway displacement but no mediastinal extension. The child is tachycardic but oxygenating comfortably. How should you decide monitored IV therapy versus drainage, secure the airway if the child deteriorates, and recognize vascular, neurologic, or mediastinal complications that mandate urgent escalation?
items.answer_text: Begin with airway and sepsis assessment rather than the CT size alone. Evaluate work of breathing, stridor, secretion handling, neck position, trismus, hydration, neurologic findings, and the trajectory over hours. Start broad IV antibiotics covering expected aerobic and anaerobic upper-airway flora and provide fluids and analgesia. Selected clinically stable children without airway compromise, septic shock, neurologic or vascular complication, or rapidly progressive disease can undergo a closely monitored trial of medical therapy even when imaging shows a collection, particularly if operative anesthesia itself carries meaningful airway risk. Drainage is favored for airway compromise, large organized or accessible abscess with mass effect, sepsis, progression, complication, or failure to improve after an appropriate medical trial. If respiratory status worsens, coordinate ENT and anesthesia early, preserve spontaneous ventilation when loss of the airway is a concern, and have rigid endoscopy and surgical-airway rescue capability available. Internal-jugular thrombosis, carotid involvement, cranial neuropathy, epidural/intracranial spread, or descending mediastinitis changes the case from routine abscess management to urgent multidisciplinary source control.

items.prompt: A 3-year-old has 3 days of fever, drooling, and refuses to extend her neck after a cold. CT shows a rim-enhancing retropharyngeal collection. Why is this infection most common before age 5?
choices: Retropharyngeal nodes are present and later involute
Young children cannot mount a fever response
The danger space is absent after age 5

items.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Hypernasality, nasal air emission and reduced oral pressure after cleft/palatal or neuromuscular disease suggests velopharyngeal dysfunction; distinguish structural insufficiency from mislearning/articulation errors. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Speech therapy treats articulation/mislearning but not a structural gap. Surgery or prosthetic management is selected for persistent structural dysfunction according to closure pattern and airway risk.

items.prompt: A 6-year-old has new hypernasal speech and nasal air escape after adenoidectomy. Exam shows a bifid uvula and a notch at the posterior edge of the hard palate. What is the underlying problem?
choices: Submucous cleft with a misaligned levator

items.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Confirm that reported 'strep' or sore-throat episodes were true qualifying tonsillitis episodes. Frequency alone is insufficient without severity features and documentation. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Below the usual thresholds, favor watchful waiting: fewer than 7 episodes in 1 year, fewer than 5/year for 2 years, or fewer than 3/year for 3 years. Tonsillectomy may be offered when ≥7 in 1 year, ≥5/year for 2 years, or ≥3/year for 3 years are documented with qualifying features. Consider modifying factors such as PFAPA, multiple antibiotic intolerance/allergy or >1 peritonsillar abscess.

items.prompt: A 9-year-old has had 5 documented streptococcal pharyngitis episodes this year and 6 last year, each with fever over 38.3 C and exudate. Which criterion supports tonsillectomy?
choices: Any child with 3 sore throats per year

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the otolaryngology service. A 4-year-old with a tracheostomy placed for prolonged ventilation is now off the ventilator, tolerates a speaking valve while awake, handles secretions, and has improving swallow function. The family asks whether the next step is simply downsizing and capping until the tube can be removed. What physiologic readiness must be demonstrated, what airway evaluation is required before decannulation, when is polysomnography useful, and what findings should stop or reverse a decannulation pathway?
items.answer_text: Decannulation is the end point of resolution of the original tracheostomy indication plus adequate upper-airway patency, ventilatory reserve, secretion clearance, cough, and swallow/aspiration control; it is not achieved by tube downsizing alone. First confirm that the child no longer needs the tracheostomy for ventilation or airway protection and can manage secretions without frequent suctioning or recurrent aspiration-related pulmonary decompensation. Progression through speaking-valve use, downsizing, and capping can test tolerance, but protocols vary and each step should be interpreted in the context of work of breathing, oxygenation, sleep, and pulmonary reserve. A complete endoscopic airway examination before decannulation is a core safety step: evaluate the supraglottis/glottis, subglottis, trachea, and stoma for granulation, suprastomal collapse, tracheomalacia, stenosis, vocal-fold immobility, or another lesion that could be masked by the tracheostomy. Current pediatric tracheostomy guidance supports bronchoscopy before decannulation and supports polysomnography when objective sleep assessment is needed; PSG is particularly useful when there is significant sleep-disordered breathing risk, marginal capping tolerance, complex airway or neuromuscular disease, or uncertainty that awake performance predicts sleep ventilation. A capped study must be interpreted carefully because a small tracheostomy tube itself can add airway resistance. Stop or reverse the pathway for persistent oxygen desaturation, hypercapnia, increased work of breathing, inability to clear secretions, recurrent aspiration/pneumonia, severe obstructive events, or a fixed/dynamic airway lesion that has not been corrected. After tube removal, observe for early respiratory failure and ensure a rescue plan; persistent tracheocutaneous fistula is addressed later if it fails to close and is clinically important. The senior principle is to prove airway and respiratory independence across wake, secretion burden, and sleep rather than using a successful brief cap trial as a surrogate for the entire physiology.

items.prompt: A 2-year-old with a 3.5 mm tracheostomy tube has sudden respiratory distress at home. The caregiver cannot pass a suction catheter through the tube. What is the most likely cause and response?
choices: Tube cuff overinflation: deflate the cuff
Mucus plug: change the tube immediately

items.prompt: An infant has persistent stridor and feeding difficulty after cardiac surgery; flexible laryngoscopy shows one vocal fold immobile near the paramedian position. How do you distinguish neurogenic paralysis from fixation, evaluate aspiration and recovery potential, and decide observation, injection, reinnervation or airway-widening intervention?
items.answer_text: Confirm laterality, resting position, contralateral motion and the relationship of symptoms to airway and swallowing. The history of cardiothoracic surgery raises recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, but persistent immobility may also reflect cricoarytenoid fixation, posterior glottic scar or central neurologic disease, so direct laryngoscopy with palpation is useful when fixation is plausible or management depends on the distinction. Assess feeding and aspiration clinically and with instrumental swallowing evaluation when symptoms or pulmonary consequence warrant it. Many unilateral injuries may recover, so recovery timing, etiology and symptom severity guide observation versus temporary medialization. Injection can improve glottic closure and swallowing in selected symptomatic unilateral cases while recovery remains possible; reinnervation offers longer-term tone in appropriate persistent paralysis. Bilateral immobility or severe airway compromise requires a separate airway strategy, balancing tracheostomy or airway-widening procedures against voice and aspiration consequences. Progressive respiratory distress, recurrent aspiration pneumonia, failure to thrive or inability to maintain a safe airway should accelerate intervention rather than waiting solely for nerve recovery.

items.prompt: An infant with a lumbar myelomeningocele has new inspiratory stridor with a normal cry. Laryngoscopy shows both vocal folds resting near midline. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Left RLN injury from cardiac surgery

items.prompt: A child with biopsy-proven recurrent respiratory papillomatosis has progressive dysphonia, increasingly frequent procedures, papilloma approaching the anterior commissure, and intermittent inspiratory symptoms. How should an otolaryngology resident balance airway safety, voice-preserving surgery, procedure timing, systemic bevacizumab, pulmonary surveillance, and malignant-transformation risk in juvenile RRP, and what must be understood about PAPZIMEOS when counseling families about future adult care or comparing pediatric management with the new adult treatment landscape?
items.answer_text:
Foundation: recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP) is a chronic HPV-driven disease, classically associated with HPV 6 and 11, in which benign squamous papillomas recur throughout the respiratory mucosa, most often the larynx. Juvenile-onset disease may be particularly aggressive and can require repeated procedures during years of laryngeal growth. The resident's goal is not to 'eradicate every visible papilloma' at any cost. The durable surgical objective is a safe airway and useful voice with the least iatrogenic injury necessary to control clinically important disease. Recurrence reflects persistent viral biology; it is not proof that the preceding surgeon failed to remove enough tissue. Document disease distribution, airway symptoms, voice impact, procedure frequency, prior scarring/web formation, HPV type when available, and whether disease extends below the glottis.

Application — surgery: operate for clinically important airway compromise, voice/function burden, diagnostic uncertainty, or disease that requires debulking while medical therapy is being considered or has failed. Use precise endoscopic removal with microdebrider and/or appropriate laser/energy technique according to location and surgeon expertise, but preserve normal epithelium and avoid deep indiscriminate injury. At the anterior commissure, bilateral opposing raw surfaces can create a web that permanently worsens voice and can complicate the airway; staged or deliberately conservative treatment may be safer than chasing microscopic disease. Obtain tissue when the diagnosis is first established and re-biopsy when phenotype changes—rapid growth, ulceration, fixation, unexpected pain, progressive pulmonary lesions, or other features concerning for dysplasia or squamous malignancy.

Airway boundary: tracheostomy is not routine RRP therapy and should be avoided when a safe alternative exists because severe RRP requiring tracheostomy is associated with distal tracheobronchial spread and instrumentation can contribute to mechanical dissemination. But this is an association and a management caution, not permission to tolerate impending obstruction. If oxygenation/ventilation is failing, stridor is progressing with poor air movement, or a secure endoscopic airway cannot be maintained, perform the safest lifesaving airway available. The senior error is either automatic tracheostomy for recurrent disease or delaying a necessary airway because of fear of distal seeding.

Pediatric systemic-therapy layer: systemic bevacizumab has become an important disease-modifying option for selected severe juvenile-onset, highly recurrent, refractory, or pulmonary RRP. Current pediatric evidence, including a 2026 systematic review, supports meaningful reductions in disease burden and procedure frequency, but the evidence base remains dominated by nonrandomized reports and does not create one universal pediatric protocol. Use multidisciplinary selection and monitoring, especially for pulmonary disease or children whose cumulative operative burden threatens airway, voice, development, or quality of life. The 2024 systemic-bevacizumab consensus provides practical candidate-selection and monitoring principles even though individual pediatric dosing and duration require specialty judgment.

Adult regulatory pivot — know it without misapplying it to the child: on August 14, 2025, the FDA approved PAPZIMEOS (zopapogene imadenovec-drba), an HPV 6/11-directed immunotherapy, for adults with RRP. The pivotal study enrolled adults requiring at least three surgeries per year and 18 of 35 achieved the FDA-defined complete response of no surgical intervention for 12 months after treatment, but do not convert that study entry threshold into a false label restriction: the trial population, not the wording of the adult indication, carried the >=3-procedure requirement; the FDA indication is adults with RRP. PAPZIMEOS currently has an adult FDA indication, so do not silently extrapolate adult regulatory status to a child. This matters both when families hear about the new therapy and when adolescents transition to adult care.

The 2026 RRP Foundation adult position statement recommends that HPV-specific immunotherapy be discussed early rather than withheld until an arbitrary procedural threshold is reached and positions systemic bevacizumab as second-line medical therapy for adults after HPV-specific immunotherapy. This position statement is influential contemporary guidance, not a substitute for individualized shared decision-making, access considerations, contraindication review, and the FDA label. It updates the older mental model of serial debulking until disease becomes 'severe enough' for an adjuvant, but it should not be back-projected as a pediatric approval.

Pulmonary/malignancy layer: distal disease changes the stakes in both children and adults. Current pulmonary-RRP consensus recommends HPV typing at diagnosis, chest CT to monitor pulmonary disease, biopsy of suspicious pulmonary lesions when feasible, multidisciplinary management, and consideration of systemic therapy. In a child, tailor radiation exposure and surveillance intervals to actual disease risk rather than ordering indiscriminate repeated CTs, but do not ignore distal disease in an aggressive phenotype. The 2026 adult RRPF position statement additionally recommends that adults consider low-dose noncontrast chest CT screening and longitudinal surveillance. Pulmonary RRP is uncommon but carries a markedly higher malignant-transformation risk than larynx-limited disease. A changing lesion should trigger diagnostic reassessment rather than automatic assumption that it is simply more papilloma.

Senior decision: run four parallel goals—maintain the airway, preserve laryngeal function, reduce cumulative procedure injury, and identify biology that changes treatment. For juvenile RRP, track trajectory rather than one procedure in isolation: shortening interoperative interval, lower-airway extension, worsening scarring, or increasing airway/voice burden should trigger deliberate systemic-therapy discussion rather than endless identical debulkings. Involve pediatric laryngology, oncology or other systemic-therapy expertise when appropriate, and pulmonology/thoracic teams when distal disease is present. Continue endoscopic surveillance even when medical therapy produces a major response. Medical therapy may reduce repeated procedures, but medical therapy never substitutes for immediate airway rescue, nor does apparent response remove the need to investigate suspicious transformation.

OR rescue rule: when using laser or other ignition-capable energy in the shared airway, use a deliberate fire-prevention plan with anesthesia—minimize oxidizer concentration when clinically feasible, avoid nitrous oxide, protect the tube/cuff as appropriate, keep wet materials and saline immediately available, and stop energy delivery if airway control becomes uncertain. If an airway fire occurs, stop ventilation and oxidizer flow, remove the burning airway device/material, extinguish with saline, re-establish ventilation, and evaluate the airway for thermal injury. RRP is recurrent; an avoidable scar, web, distal injury, or airway fire can create morbidity that persists long after today's papilloma is gone.

items.prompt: A 4-year-old with hoarseness needs debridement of laryngeal papillomas every 6-8 weeks despite complete removal each time. Why do they keep recurring?
choices: Surgery seeds papillomas into the trachea

items.prompt: An infant has recurrent 'croup' with progressively persistent biphasic stridor and increased work of breathing between viral illnesses. How do you confirm a subglottic hemangioma, stabilize the airway, use beta-blocker therapy safely, and decide when endoscopic or open airway intervention is required?
items.answer_text: The changing pattern—progressive or persistent biphasic stridor rather than episodic uncomplicated croup—should trigger airway evaluation. Flexible laryngoscopy can assess the supraglottis and vocal folds, but direct laryngoscopy/bronchoscopy may be needed to define subglottic location, degree of obstruction and alternative lesions; imaging is selective when extent or diagnosis remains uncertain. In a stable infant with a typical infantile hemangioma, systemic propranolol is foundational therapy after appropriate cardiovascular/feeding safety assessment and with dosing/monitoring coordinated to age and comorbidity. The airway plan comes first in a child with significant distress: minimize agitation, maintain oxygenation and involve pediatric anesthesia/airway expertise early rather than forcing an examination that precipitates obstruction. Failure to improve on appropriate medical therapy, severe fixed obstruction, recurrent life-threatening events or inability to maintain a safe airway can require endoscopic debulking or other airway intervention, with tracheostomy/open reconstruction reserved for selected refractory situations. Feeding intolerance, hypoglycemia risk during illness and associated cutaneous/distribution clues should also inform management.

items.prompt: A 3-month-old has progressive biphasic stridor that worsens with crying and a hemangioma covering the chin and jaw. Endoscopy shows a smooth, compressible posterolateral subglottic mass. What is first-line treatment?

An infant with prior esophageal-atresia/tracheoesophageal-fistula repair has recurrent barking cough, cyanotic spells with agitation, repeated pneumonias, and difficulty weaning from positive-pressure ventilation. CT suggests anterior vascular contact, but the child also appears to have posterior membranous intrusion. How should you prove whether clinically important tracheomalacia, bronchomalacia, or both are present; avoid an anesthetic/endoscopic examination that masks the disease; decide when supportive treatment is enough; and choose an anatomy-directed operation or bailout when symptoms are severe?
items.answer_text:
Foundation — tracheomalacia and bronchomalacia are dynamic large-airway disorders, not simply a small static lumen. Tracheomalacia involves excessive expiratory collapse of the trachea; bronchomalacia involves one or both main bronchi, and tracheobronchomalacia involves both. Disease may be primary/intrinsic because the cartilaginous framework and posterior membrane do not maintain caliber, or secondary/extrinsic because the airway is compressed or distorted by adjacent cardiovascular, esophageal, skeletal, postoperative, or inflammatory anatomy. Important pediatric associations include prematurity and prolonged airway instrumentation, esophageal atresia/tracheoesophageal fistula, vascular rings or slings, aberrant innominate-artery compression, and other congenital airway abnormalities. The symptom pattern should fit dynamic physiology: barky or brassy cough, expiratory noise or fixed wheeze, recurrent lower-respiratory infections, secretion-retention problems, exercise/feeding intolerance, cyanotic or near-death spells, and inability to wean respiratory support can all occur. A percentage of collapse alone does not define the clinical severity; physiology and consequences matter.

Dynamic diagnosis — the key test is an airway examination that actually allows the airway to demonstrate its native behavior. Current ERS teaching favors flexible bronchoscopy in a free-breathing child for diagnosis, while dynamic CT or MRI can complement endoscopy when distal airway anatomy, vascular compression, or operative planning needs clarification. During bronchoscopy, describe the location and length of collapse, anterior versus posterior versus circumferential geometry, relationship to the carina, and whether the right or left mainstem bronchi are also involved. Inspect the entire tracheobronchial tree rather than stopping after seeing one dramatic tracheal segment. A major OR trap is evaluating the child only under substantial positive-pressure ventilation: positive pressure pneumatically stents a malacic airway and can make the collapse appear much less severe. Coordinate anesthesia so the dynamic portion is assessed under physiologic spontaneous/free breathing when safe, then change ventilation strategy as needed for airway control. Do not create danger merely to preserve spontaneous breathing; if oxygenation or ventilation is failing, stabilize the child first and interpret the study in light of the support being applied.

Separate intrinsic from extrinsic anatomy — bronchoscopy shows what collapses, while cross-sectional dynamic imaging and vascular imaging help explain why. Anterior pulsatile compression should trigger deliberate evaluation for innominate-artery compression, vascular ring/sling, enlarged cardiovascular structures, or postoperative mediastinal relationships. Posterior membranous intrusion points toward a different mechanical problem and may coexist with anterior compression. Left-mainstem or diffuse bronchial disease matters because a trachea-only operation may leave the clinically important obstruction untreated. Before choosing surgery, define the airway geometry rather than equating every severe tracheomalacia case with an automatic aortopexy.

Supportive management — mild disease without dangerous events, major infection burden, failure to thrive, or respiratory-support dependence can often be observed while the airway grows and associated disorders are addressed. Airway-clearance strategies, hydration/secretion management, prompt treatment of bacterial lower-respiratory infection when present, and multidisciplinary pulmonary/ENT care are often more useful than empiric medication lists. If respiratory support is needed, CPAP is the most commonly used noninvasive pneumatic-stenting strategy. The contemporary evidence distinction is important: bronchodilators, antimuscarinic agents, mucolytics, reflux treatment, and other medications may be appropriate for a separate demonstrated indication, but the ERS statement notes limited evidence that medication itself fixes pediatric airway malacia. Do not prescribe chronic acid suppression or systemic steroids merely because malacia exists.

When severity changes the plan — escalation is driven by consequential physiology: recurrent cyanotic/brief-resolved-unexplained-event or near-death spells, recurrent pneumonias with secretion trapping, inability to extubate, persistent need for positive-pressure ventilation, progressive respiratory failure, or major feeding/growth consequences despite appropriate support. These are senior-decision findings because repeated conservative care may simply reproduce the same emergency. The operative goal is not to reach an arbitrary collapse number; it is to relieve the mechanism responsible for clinically important obstruction while preserving adjacent structures.

Choose the operation by geometry. Anterior aortopexy is most logical when the anterior trachea is being compressed by the aorta/innominate relationship and anterior suspension will reliably open the airway. Posterior tracheopexy directly addresses excessive posterior membranous intrusion by fixing the posterior airway to a stable posterior structure; combined anterior and posterior procedures may be required when collapse is multidirectional. Distal or left-mainstem disease may require a descending-aortopexy or bronchus-directed strategy at experienced centers. Contemporary systematic reviews support substantial symptom improvement after both aortopexy and posterior tracheopexy in selected severe pediatric patients, but the evidence is predominantly observational; these procedures should therefore be anatomy- and symptom-directed rather than taught as interchangeable universal cures.

Bailout and special situations — tracheostomy with positive pressure can provide a route for prolonged pneumatic stenting when disease is severe or reconstruction is not immediately feasible, but tracheostomy is not the automatic endpoint for every child with malacia and may not bypass long distal disease. Internal airway stents and external splints/stents can be useful in highly selected complex or rescue situations, but migration, granulation, erosion, infection, growth, and adjacent-structure concerns prevent routine use as a simple first-line solution. Newer external-stent/tracheopexy approaches are promising but should be described as evolving evidence rather than a settled standard.

Failure analysis — persistent symptoms after an operation demand a new dynamic airway map, not reflex repetition of the same procedure. Ask whether the original mechanism was wrong, whether bronchomalacia was missed, whether posterior intrusion remains after anterior aortopexy, whether vascular or esophageal anatomy still compresses the airway, whether fixation failed, and whether infection/aspiration or another airway lesion is driving the current physiology. Acute desaturation or cyanotic spells require immediate airway/oxygenation rescue first; diagnostic purity comes second.

Senior synthesis — use four questions. PHYSIOLOGY: are the spells, infections, secretion problems, or ventilator dependence severe enough to justify intervention? DYNAMICS: was the airway actually observed during free/spontaneous breathing rather than only while positive pressure held it open? GEOMETRY: is the dominant problem anterior vascular compression, posterior membranous intrusion, circumferential collapse, bronchomalacia, or a combination? MATCH: does the proposed treatment actually correct that geometry — CPAP for pneumatic support, aortopexy for appropriate anterior compression, posterior/combined tracheopexy for posterior or multidirectional collapse, and selected rescue strategies for complex refractory disease? The dangerous alternatives are diagnosing from a static airway, letting positive pressure hide the lesion, grading severity by collapse percentage alone, missing vascular compression or bronchomalacia, treating reflux or steroids as a malacia cure, assuming every severe child will simply outgrow the disease, and choosing aortopexy before defining the direction and extent of collapse.

items.prompt: An infant who had repair of esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula has a barking cough and expiratory wheeze that worsen with crying. Why does the trachea collapse mainly during expiration?
choices: Inspiration pulls the intrathoracic trachea closed
Mucus plugs form only on expiration
The vocal folds adduct during expiration
Rising pleural pressure compresses a weak trachea

items.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. External-ear deformity may coexist with canal/middle-ear anomalies and conductive hearing loss; bilateral loss threatens language access. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Provide hearing access early; coordinate auricular reconstruction/prosthesis and atresiaplasty or bone-conduction options.

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the otolaryngology service. A 14-month-old with recurrent pneumonias coughs with thin liquids and has poor weight gain. Flexible laryngoscopy shows mobile vocal folds without an obvious mass. How should you localize aspiration physiology, choose FEES versus modified barium swallow, decide when direct laryngoscopy/bronchoscopy is needed for a laryngeal cleft or other structural lesion, and determine whether feeding modification, injection, cleft repair, or enteral support is appropriate?
items.answer_text: First separate oropharyngeal discoordination from a structural airway-protection problem. History should address consistency-specific coughing, wet voice or breathing, recurrent pneumonia, neurologic disease, prior cardiothoracic surgery, prematurity, and growth. An instrumental swallow study is usually required when pulmonary or nutritional consequences are meaningful. Modified barium swallow is useful for oral and pharyngeal timing, bolus flow, aspiration timing, and testing compensatory strategies; FEES is valuable for secretion burden, laryngeal sensation, residue, and repeated bedside assessment, although the actual moment of the swallow is obscured by white-out. Persistent aspiration despite appropriate therapy, unexplained aspiration with suggestive symptoms, or concern for laryngeal cleft, tracheoesophageal fistula, subglottic disease, or occult airway lesion warrants direct airway evaluation, often including palpation of the interarytenoid region because a subtle cleft can be missed on office examination. Management should match mechanism: thicken or alter flow/position when strategies demonstrably improve safety, treat neurologic or inflammatory contributors, consider temporary injection for selected glottic or interarytenoid insufficiency, repair a clinically important structural cleft when conservative therapy fails, and use enteral support when nutrition cannot be maintained safely. A feeding tube supports nutrition but does not eliminate secretion or reflux-related aspiration.

items.prompt: A 1-year-old with developmental delay has had three pneumonias. She coughs rarely during feeds and a bedside feeding assessment was normal. Why is an instrumental swallow study needed?
choices: To treat aspiration during the study

items.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Permanent congenital/early-onset SNHL should trigger etiologic thinking early because genetic diagnosis can predict progression, syndromic risks and cochlear-implant considerations. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Ensure early language access through amplification, CI evaluation and educational support while the etiologic workup proceeds. A genetic result can guide surveillance of vision, thyroid, renal, cardiac or neurologic disease in syndromic conditions.

items.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Children with cleft palate/craniofacial syndromes commonly have chronic OME/hearing loss, velopharyngeal dysfunction, nasal obstruction and sleep-disordered breathing that evolve with growth and reconstruction. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat hearing loss proactively, use tubes when indicated, and coordinate VPI/airway treatment with speech outcomes. Avoid fixing one problem in a way that predictably worsens another.

items.prompt: An infant with an unrepaired complete cleft palate has bilateral middle-ear effusions at 4 months of age. Why do nearly all infants with cleft palate develop effusions?
choices: The tensor veli palatini cannot open the tube
Milk reflux alone fills the middle ear
Hearing loss leads to fluid formation

items.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Recurrent painful unilateral or bilateral parotid swelling in a child, often beginning in early childhood and resolving by adolescence, suggests this condition after excluding suppurative infection, stones and autoimmune disease. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Acute episodes are treated with hydration, massage, analgesia and antibiotics only when bacterial infection is suspected. Recurrent severe disease may benefit from sialendoscopy with irrigation/dilation.

items.prompt: A 6-year-old has had five episodes of painful unilateral parotid swelling with fever over 2 years. Ultrasound between episodes shows multiple small hypoechoic areas; HIV testing and Sjögren antibodies are negative. What is the typical natural history?
choices: Progression to Sjögren syndrome in adulthood

items.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. A persistent pediatric neck mass is more often inflammatory/congenital than malignant, but hard/fixed nodes, supraclavicular location, B symptoms, cranial neuropathy or progressive growth require oncologic evaluation. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treatment is histology-specific and often multidisciplinary. Preserve long-term growth, cranial nerve, swallowing, hearing and endocrine function whenever oncologically safe.

items.prompt: A 12-year-old has a firm, painless 3 cm left supraclavicular node that has persisted for 6 weeks despite antibiotics. She reports night sweats. Why is excisional biopsy recommended?
choices: All enlarged pediatric nodes need biopsy
FNA is never performed in children
Supraclavicular nodes carry high malignancy risk

items.prompt: A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Differentiate articulation/phonologic disorder, motor speech disorder, resonance/VPI, hearing-related language effects and voice disorder before assigning an ENT cause. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Treat the mechanism with speech therapy, hearing access, structural surgery or neurologic/developmental support as appropriate.

items.prompt: A 4-year-old has persistent mouth breathing, snoring, and speech that sounds as if he has a cold, with nasal consonants (m, n) sounding like b and d. What is the most likely cause?

A child is evaluated in pediatric otolaryngology. Not every sleepy, restless or poorly sleeping child has obstructive sleep apnea; insomnia, parasomnias, circadian disorders, restless sleep and central disorders enter the differential. What is the initial management strategy, and what finding, response, or failure would change the next step?
items.answer_text: Use behavioral/sleep-medicine pathways for nonobstructive disorders and avoid adenotonsillectomy when the physiology is not obstructive.

items.prompt: A 7-year-old has episodes 1-2 hours after falling asleep in which she sits up screaming, appears terrified, and cannot be consoled. She has no memory of them in the morning. What is the diagnosis?

items.topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
items.canonical_topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
items.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the otolaryngology service. A 9-month-old with an unrepaired cleft palate has nasal regurgitation, chronic middle-ear effusions, and emerging speech-sound delay but is growing appropriately without obstructive breathing. The family asks what palatoplasty is trying to restore beyond simply closing the visible gap, when ear tubes are considered, and what later findings would suggest velopharyngeal dysfunction or a complication requiring additional treatment. How should you frame the operative anatomy, timing, surveillance, and escalation plan?
items.answer_text: The functional target of palatoplasty is a mobile, length-appropriate palate with restoration of the levator veli palatini sling, not merely mucosal closure. The abnormal palatal muscles insert along the posterior hard palate rather than forming a transverse sling, contributing to poor velopharyngeal closure and Eustachian-tube dysfunction. Primary repair is commonly performed in late infancy, often around 9–12 months depending on the cleft team, growth, airway, and technique, to support speech development while balancing maxillary-growth considerations. The operation closes nasal and oral layers and reorients the levator mechanism while avoiding excessive tension and neurovascular injury. Persistent bilateral effusion or hearing loss is assessed audiologically; tympanostomy tubes are commonly considered at the time of palate repair or earlier when hearing or infection indications warrant, but the child still needs longitudinal surveillance because otitis media with effusion can persist for years. After repair, monitor feeding, fistula, obstructive symptoms, hearing, resonance, articulation, and speech development. Hypernasality, audible nasal emission, weak pressure consonants, or compensatory articulation after adequate speech development should prompt cleft-speech assessment and instrumental evaluation of velopharyngeal function before secondary surgery. A palatal fistula is repaired when symptoms such as nasal regurgitation, hygiene problems, or speech effects justify the morbidity. The senior principle is to distinguish structural velopharyngeal insufficiency from learned articulation errors: speech therapy treats compensatory mislearning, whereas a true anatomic closure gap may require secondary palatal or pharyngeal surgery after the closure pattern and airway risk are defined.

items.topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
items.canonical_topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
items.prompt: An infant with an isolated cleft palate is scheduled for palatoplasty at 10 months. Why is repair timed before about 12-18 months of age?
choices: To allow the lip to fuse
Because palatal growth stops at 1 year

items.prompt: A patient is evaluated by the otolaryngology service. A 7-year-old with unilateral grade III microtia and congenital aural atresia has normal hearing in the opposite ear and wants auricular reconstruction. The family asks whether the ear canal should be opened first, whether autologous rib or porous-polyethylene reconstruction is better, and how hearing rehabilitation fits into the plan. How should you sequence hearing assessment, temporal-bone imaging, atresia candidacy, auricular reconstruction, and long-term complication counseling?
items.answer_text: Start by separating two parallel goals: hearing rehabilitation and creation of an external ear. Obtain age-appropriate audiology early because bilateral conductive loss requires prompt amplification, while a child with normal contralateral hearing may choose among observation, non-surgical bone-conduction options, implantable hearing devices, or selected atresiaplasty based on functional needs and anatomy. High-resolution temporal-bone CT is generally deferred until the child is old enough that operative candidacy is being considered; it defines the ossicular chain, facial-nerve course, middle-ear space, cochlear/vestibular anatomy, and other features used in atresia-candidacy frameworks such as the Jahrsdoerfer score. Auricular options include observation or prosthesis, osseointegrated prosthesis, autologous costal-cartilage reconstruction once sufficient rib cartilage is available, and porous-polyethylene reconstruction at a younger age in selected centers. The choice depends on age, anatomy, skin/soft-tissue envelope, prior scars, surgeon expertise, tolerance for staged surgery, donor-site morbidity, implant exposure risk, and patient preference; there is no universally superior technique. Sequencing with canal surgery must be planned jointly. Uncoordinated atresiaplasty can scar or consume tissue needed for auricular reconstruction, and temporoparietal fascia is particularly important for alloplastic framework coverage. Many autologous-rib pathways place atresia repair after the framework stages, whereas alloplastic pathways require individualized sequencing so vascularized coverage is not jeopardized. Counsel that atresiaplasty can restenose or develop chronic drainage/cholesteatoma and may not provide stable normal hearing; bone-conduction devices often give more predictable hearing. Autologous frameworks can distort or calcify and have chest donor-site morbidity; alloplastic frameworks avoid rib harvest but carry exposure/infection risk. The senior decision is multidisciplinary sequencing: never choose canal or framework surgery in isolation from the hearing plan and the tissue requirements of the eventual reconstruction.

items.prompt: A 7-year-old with grade III unilateral microtia and congenital aural atresia has normal hearing in the opposite ear. The family asks whether the child should first undergo canal surgery, rib-cartilage auricular reconstruction, porous-polyethylene reconstruction, or simply wait. How do you build a coordinated microtia plan that addresses hearing first, chooses the reconstructive pathway and timing appropriately, and avoids sequencing one operation in a way that compromises the next?
items.answer_text:
Foundation — microtia is not only a cosmetic pinna problem. Begin with a complete craniofacial and otologic assessment: characterize the microtia grade and lobule/skin remnant, examine facial symmetry and syndromic features, document the contralateral ear, and establish hearing status early. Microtia and congenital aural atresia frequently coexist, so every child needs age-appropriate audiologic evaluation rather than assuming unilateral disease is functionally irrelevant. Bilateral conductive loss requires prompt hearing rehabilitation; unilateral atresia still deserves counseling about localization, hearing in noise, classroom function, and options for bone-conduction support.

Hearing comes before the decorative framework — reconstruction of the auricle does not restore hearing. Infants and young children with bilateral atresia generally need early bone-conduction hearing access, initially with a non-surgical band/adhesive system when appropriate. Surgically implanted bone-conduction systems, active transcutaneous systems, or atresiaplasty are later options chosen according to age, anatomy, hearing goals, skin/soft tissue, and the planned auricular reconstruction. In unilateral cases, the urgency is different, but hearing surveillance and functional counseling still belong in the plan.

Define anatomy before promising canal surgery — high-resolution temporal-bone CT is not a newborn screening test for every microtia patient. It is obtained when the child is old enough and when the result will change candidacy/planning for atresia repair or another intervention. Atresiaplasty candidacy depends on favorable middle-ear anatomy, including ossicular and facial-nerve relationships, aeration and overall Jahrsdoerfer-type anatomy; a poor candidate should not be sent for canal surgery simply because an external canal is absent.

Choose the auricular pathway deliberately. Autologous costal-cartilage reconstruction uses the child's own rib to carve a three-dimensional framework. Its advantages are durable living autologous tissue and long-term integration; disadvantages include donor-site morbidity, the need for adequate rib cartilage, technically demanding framework carving, and usually staged surgery. Timing is therefore tied to chest/cartilage development and technique: classic autologous reconstruction is commonly performed in school-age children, often roughly 6-10 years depending on the chosen Brent/Nagata-type technique and surgeon preference rather than a single mandatory birthday.

Porous-polyethylene reconstruction can often be performed younger and avoids rib harvest. It provides a prefabricated framework with strong definition, but it is an alloplastic implant that depends on durable vascularized soft-tissue coverage and carries different failure modes — exposure, infection, trauma vulnerability and possible implant loss. The family should hear those tradeoffs explicitly instead of being told that one material is universally superior. Canal surgery changes postauricular skin and vascularity and can alter the tissue needed for auricular reconstruction. With autologous costal-cartilage reconstruction, atresiaplasty is generally coordinated after the auricular framework stages so the microtia surgeon can preserve the skin envelope and place the ear correctly. With porous-polyethylene reconstruction, the sequence may differ: experienced integrated teams may perform atresia repair before or concurrently with alloplastic auricular reconstruction because the vascularized fascial coverage and incision planning are different. Plan the ear in three dimensions. Use the normal contralateral auricle when available to guide height, projection, axis and landmark relationships, while accounting for craniofacial asymmetry. Assess whether the vestigial lobule and local skin can be incorporated, whether the hairline is low, and whether scars or prior surgery threaten the skin pocket or temporoparietal fascial blood supply. Autologous reconstruction requires enough healthy skin for a tension-free pocket and enough donor cartilage for framework definition; alloplastic reconstruction requires reliable vascularized coverage. A beautiful framework under ischemic or scarred soft tissue is a setup for exposure.

ANATOMY: is atresiaplasty anatomically reasonable, and when should CT be obtained? AURICLE: autologous cartilage, porous polyethylene, prosthesis, or no reconstruction based on age, tissues, donor site, risk tolerance and goals? SEQUENCE: which operation must occur first so canal work does not compromise the auricular skin/vascular plan? Failure/rescue — early swelling, skin compromise, framework exposure, infection, hematoma or loss of projection requires prompt reconstructive assessment because delayed management can convert a salvageable soft-tissue problem into framework loss. After autologous harvest, monitor donor-site pain, pneumothorax risk and chest-wall contour; contemporary systematic review data reinforce that donor-site deformity is real and technique-dependent, so rib harvest should be meticulous and perichondrial preservation matters.
